sections.heading: Papers, weightings and command terms: what a grade is actually made of
paragraphs: Parents are told a grade is the sum of the papers. It is closer to the truth to say a grade is the sum of what the mark scheme can pay for. In a Diploma subject, internally assessed work typically carries around a fifth of the grade, and the written papers carry the rest, split between a shorter paper testing recall and precision and a longer one testing structured explanation. Higher Level mathematics adds a third paper, worth a fifth on its own, built on unfamiliar extended problems. In Cambridge IGCSE the written papers usually carry the whole grade, with practical skills assessed separately in the sciences.

Inside every one of those papers, the command term governs the answer. 'State' wants one line with no reasoning. 'Describe' wants what happens, in order. 'Explain' wants a mechanism with a causal link in it. 'Compare' wants both sides addressed in the same sentences rather than in two separate paragraphs. 'Evaluate' and 'discuss' want two sides and a judgement, and they are not interchangeable. 'To what extent' wants a position stated and then defended against its strongest objection. A student who answers all of these with an essay will be marked down on four of them.

This is the most transferable thing a tutor can teach, and it is the reason a student can gain a grade without learning any new content. Mark schemes are public. Reading one next to a student's own answer, line by line, and showing them which of their sentences earned nothing is a session that changes how they write for the rest of the course. Most students have never done it, and in a small school with a young programme, many have never seen a graded exemplar either.
The table lists the command terms that cost AlUla students the most marks in our experience of this cohort, with what each one wants and the specific mistake that loses the mark.

table.caption: COMMAND TERMS AND WHAT THEY PAY FOR
rows: One line, no reasoning, no hedging
A paragraph that buries the answer
A mechanism with a causal link
A description with the word 'because' added
Both sides handled together, point by point
Two separate paragraphs with no link
Both sides plus a supported judgement
A list of advantages and disadvantages
A stated position defended against the strongest objection
Fence-sitting with no position at all

sections.heading: Grade boundaries, predicted grades, and why neither is a promise
paragraphs: Grade boundaries are set after papers have been marked, not before they are sat. The awarding body reviews how candidates actually performed and sets the mark required for each grade so that the standard is comparable with previous series, which is why boundaries move between series and between subjects. A paper that felt hard usually has lower boundaries; a paper that felt easy has higher ones. The practical consequence for a student is that chasing last series' boundary number is pointless, and the only sensible target is the mark scheme itself.

Predicted grades are a different object entirely. They are the school's professional judgement of what a student is likely to achieve, submitted for university applications, and they are based on the evidence the teacher has: classwork, mock papers, internally assessed drafts. They are not a forecast anybody is bound by, they are not negotiable as a favour, and they are not a promise. A tutor cannot change a predicted grade and should never suggest they can. What a tutor can do is help generate better evidence, which is a different and legitimate thing.

In a school with a young Diploma programme the evidence base is thinner, and predictions tend to be cautious. If a prediction looks low, the productive route is to ask the school what evidence it rests on and what further evidence would be considered, then produce that evidence: a timed paper sat under conditions and marked against the published scheme, a coursework draft that meets the top criterion descriptors. Arguing about the number without new evidence rarely moves anything and damages a relationship the student needs.

One honest note on what support can do. We do not guarantee a grade, a point total or an improvement, and no tutor can. What a well-matched specialist changes is the proportion of what a student knows that the mark scheme is able to pay for, which is usually larger than families expect and is still not a certainty.
bullets: Boundaries are set after marking, so they move between series and between subjects
A predicted grade is the school's judgement on the evidence it holds, not a forecast or a promise
A tutor cannot change a prediction; a tutor can help produce better evidence
Ask the school what evidence it would consider before disputing a number

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, the seasonal rhythm, and keeping a slot alive
paragraphs: The school week here runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. Sunday evening is a school night. Thursday evening is not. Any tutor working from a Monday-to-Friday assumption will keep proposing slots that make no sense, and copy written for a British or Indian audience does exactly that. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving, so a slot agreed with a tutor in Europe or the Americas will drift by an hour twice a year unless it is written down in Saudi local time. We write it down in Saudi local time.

AlUla adds a seasonal layer that most of the Kingdom does not have. The county's visitor season concentrates in the cooler months, and a significant part of the parent community works in hospitality, events and site operations during exactly those weeks. That means the term when examination pressure rises is also the term when parental working hours are least predictable. Families who survive this plan around it: a slot that does not depend on a parent being home, a second fallback time agreed in advance, and a written note after each session so a parent who missed it is not relying on a teenager's summary.

Ramadan shifts earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, so it moves through the academic year rather than sitting in a fixed place. School days shorten during it and study patterns move later into the evening. Lessons usually continue, moved later and often shortened; some families pause entirely and resume afterwards. Either is fine, but decide which, in advance, rather than cancelling week by week. The same applies to the autumn and midyear breaks and to the long summer, when a slot can be held rather than released.

Schools here set their own calendars. Ministry of Education schools run a two-semester year that opens in late August and closes in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break; international and British-curriculum schools mostly run three terms and publish their own dates, which differ school by school within the same city. Work from your own school's published calendar, not from ours or anyone else's.

sections.heading: What happens when it is not working, and how we end it
paragraphs: Most of what is written about tutoring describes the good case. The useful part is what happens in the bad one, because that is where a family's money and a student's term actually go. There are three bad cases and they need different answers. The match is wrong; the plan is wrong; or the student does not want this at all. Diagnosing which one you are in takes one honest conversation and is usually obvious from the marked work.

A wrong match looks like sessions that go pleasantly and marked work that does not move, or a student who cannot say what they worked on last week. We change tutor rather than asking a family to persist, and we do it on request without an argument about whether the fit was really that bad. A wrong plan looks like genuine progress on something that was not the problem: technique sharpening while a content gap widens, or vice versa. That is our error and it is fixed by redoing the diagnostic, not by adding hours.

A student who does not want support is the hardest case and the one where more lessons are least likely to help. Sometimes the answer is to reduce frequency and raise the stakes of each session. Sometimes it is to stop, and let a school report arrive without a tutor standing between the student and it. We would rather tell a parent that than bill a slot the student has mentally cancelled. Nobody is well served by a lesson a teenager attends in protest.

Ending is deliberately easy. Lessons are per session or per agreed block rather than an open subscription, so stopping does not require escaping anything, and a slot can be paused and held if the family expects to return. We ask for one piece of feedback on the way out — what the tutor should have done differently — because in a market this small the same family often needs a different subject eighteen months later, and we would rather know.
bullets: Three bad cases: wrong match, wrong plan, or a student who does not want it
Marked work tells you which one, faster than a conversation about effort will
Tutor changes happen on request, without a debate about whether the fit was bad enough
Per-session or per-block payment, so stopping needs no negotiation

process.title: Say which of the four options you are actually choosing between
process.description: Start with the structural question rather than the tutoring one. Is this one Higher Level subject with no specialist, or three compromised subjects and a vanished peer group? The answer decides whether weekly video tuition is proportionate or whether you should be looking at a school in Riyadh or Jeddah. We will say which we think it is.

process.title: Name the subject, the level and the component
process.description: 'Economics HL, the portfolio commentaries and Paper 3' is a brief. 'Help with economics' is not. Tell us the school and the year group too, and whether the student arrived from another board, because exam conventions travel badly and that is often the real problem rather than the content.

process.title: We match on the syllabus, then on the clock
process.description: A specialist in that exact subject and level first; only then do we check that their own working week can hold a stable AlUla evening slot on Arabia Standard Time. You get their subject background and examining experience before the trial lesson, so you can question it rather than take it on trust.

process.title: A free trial used as a diagnostic
process.description: The first session works on real material — a past paper, a returned assessment, a live coursework draft — and ends with a written component-level read: what is secure, what is weak, the order to fix it in. That document is yours whether or not you continue, and it is useful even if you choose a different provider.

process.title: Four weeks, then a decision on evidence
process.description: Weeks two and three teach the first items on the list; week four sits a timed piece marked against the published scheme. At that point you hold marked work rather than impressions, and we recommend continuing, changing tutor, changing the target component, or stopping. We make the recommendation explicitly, including when it is to stop.

process.title: Term reviews on marked work only
process.description: Each term we compare marked work against the component list we started with. Movement, no movement, or movement in the wrong place — and the plan changes accordingly. Slots are held through breaks if you tell us the dates early, which matters here because a scarce Higher Level specialist may not be free again in the autumn.

whyPoints.title: The comparison comes first
whyPoints.description: This page puts boarding, relocation, waiting and online tuition on one table before recommending anything, because in a county with a small resident cohort the structural decision matters more than the choice of tutor. Families who choose a school in Riyadh after reading it have still made a good decision.

whyPoints.title: Specialists for the subjects nobody here can staff
whyPoints.description: The gaps in a small school are predictable: Higher Level physics, Mathematics AA at Higher Level, Higher Level computer science, a science supervised by a teacher from an adjacent discipline. Those are exactly the cases where matching by syllabus rather than by distance changes what the student can attempt.

whyPoints.title: Decisions made on marked work
whyPoints.description: A four-week cycle that ends in a timed piece marked against the published scheme, then an explicit recommendation to continue, change or stop. Tutoring fails most often by drifting pleasantly for three terms, and a scheduled decision point is the cheapest protection against that.

whyPoints.title: Built for the Sunday-to-Thursday week
whyPoints.description: Sunday is a school night here and Thursday evening is the weekend. Slots are written down in Arabia Standard Time so a tutor abroad changing their clocks does not move your evening, and the seasonal working pattern in this county is planned around rather than discovered in week three.

whyPoints.title: Clear about predictions and boundaries
whyPoints.description: We explain how grade boundaries are set and what a predicted grade actually is, and we make no claim to influence either. What a specialist changes is how much of what a student knows the mark scheme can pay for. That is a real effect and it is not a guarantee of anything.

whyPoints.title: A stated line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Feedback on the student's own drafts against the published criteria, with a record of what was discussed. No drafting, no rewriting, no model answer on the student's own title. Several providers in this market blur that line and a parent is entitled to ask the question directly.

faqs.question: How is a starting point diagnosed for a student in AlUla whose previous school used a different board?
faqs.answer: On real work rather than on a questionnaire. The first session uses a past paper from the board the student is now entered for, plus any returned school assessment, and the tutor watches where the approach breaks down. With a board change, the break is usually convention rather than content: the student knows the material and answers in the house style of their old examination. That shows up within twenty minutes. The session ends with a written list separating genuine content gaps from convention problems, because the two take very different amounts of time to fix.

faqs.question: What does the first month of online tuition for an AlUla family actually produce on paper?
faqs.answer: Four documents. A written component-level read from the diagnostic session, naming what is secure and what is weak with a priority order. Two sets of marked homework from the middle weeks, each with a short note on whether the targeted weakness held. And a timed piece sat under conditions in week four, marked against the published scheme. Together those let you judge the month on evidence instead of atmosphere, and they support an explicit recommendation from us to continue, change tutor, change the target, or stop.

faqs.question: Our school in AlUla cannot offer the subject at Higher Level — how is a plan agreed and who owns it?
faqs.answer: The plan is written after the diagnostic and it belongs to you. It names the subject, the level, the components in the order they will be addressed, and what evidence will show each one has moved. Where the school teaches the subject with a non-specialist, the plan concentrates on what a non-specialist cannot cover: the Higher Level extension topics, examiner expectations on extended responses, and coursework supervision. Share it with the school if you want to. Teachers generally welcome it, and it prevents the tutor and the school teaching across each other.

faqs.question: When should an AlUla family expect to see movement in marked work rather than in confidence?
faqs.answer: Confidence moves in two or three sessions and tells you almost nothing. Technique shows in marked work inside four weeks, because command-term discipline, structure and showing working are mechanical changes an examiner can see immediately. A genuine content gap takes a term, sometimes two, and the honest early signal is that the gap list is shrinking rather than that a grade has jumped. If nothing has moved in marked work after six weeks, that is a change-the-plan conversation, not a reason to add hours.

faqs.question: What happens if the first tutor turns out not to suit a student in AlUla?
faqs.answer: We match again, on request, without asking the family to justify it. A mismatch is usually visible by the third session: pleasant lessons and static marked work, or a student who cannot say what was covered last week. Because the local pool of alternatives here is effectively empty, we would rather change tutor quickly than have a family conclude that tutoring in general does not work for their child. Tell us what did not fit — pace, manner, level of challenge — and the next match is better informed for it.

faqs.question: How do lessons fit around a Sunday-to-Thursday school week when the family works through the visitor season?
faqs.answer: Two adjustments do most of the work. First, the slot is set so it does not depend on a parent being home, and a short written note after each session replaces the conversation a working parent would otherwise miss. Second, a fallback time is agreed in advance for weeks when a roster collides, rather than improvising a cancellation. Sunday evening is a school night here and Thursday evening is the weekend, so the stable slots tend to sit Sunday to Wednesday, with Friday or Saturday morning as the fallback.

faqs.question: Does the Kingdom change its clocks, and what does that mean when our tutor is based in Europe?
faqs.answer: No. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 all year and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving. Europe does, so an unpinned slot drifts by an hour twice a year and families discover it when a tutor appears an hour early in the autumn. We write the slot down in Saudi local time, which means the tutor's own clock moves and yours does not. In practice a European tutor finds your early evening easiest in their summer and slightly harder in their winter, when the same slot falls in their mid-afternoon teaching day.

faqs.question: How do shorter school days during Ramadan change a weekly lesson slot in AlUla?
faqs.answer: School days shorten, the household rhythm moves later, and study tends to happen in the evening rather than straight after school. Most families keep their lessons and move them later, often shortening a 90-minute session to 60 minutes. Some pause for the month and resume afterwards. Both work; what does not work is deciding week by week, because a held slot can be protected and an abandoned one may be taken by another family. Agree the arrangement in advance, and remember Ramadan moves earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year.

faqs.question: What happens to our AlUla slot during the autumn break and the midyear break?
faqs.answer: It is held rather than released, provided you tell us the dates reasonably early. Ministry of Education schools run a two-semester year with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break, while international and British-curriculum schools mostly run three terms on calendars they publish themselves, so breaks do not line up even within one city. Lessons are charged per session or per agreed block, so a pause costs nothing. Some families use the midyear break for a short catch-up block instead, which suits a student with a content gap.

faqs.question: Can an AlUla student keep the same tutor if the family relocates to Madinah or Tabuk mid-term?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is the main practical advantage of video lessons for families on contracts that move. The tutor, the plan and the component list travel unchanged; only the slot may need adjusting around a new school day and commute. If the move also changes school, tell us early, because a new school may run a different board, a different term structure and a different option block, and the plan should be rewritten against the receiving school's scheme of work rather than carried over unexamined.

faqs.question: How do grade boundaries work, and why do they move between one series and the next?
faqs.answer: Boundaries are set after papers are marked, not before they are sat. The awarding body looks at how candidates actually performed and fixes the mark needed for each grade so the standard stays comparable with earlier series. A paper that candidates found hard generally ends with lower boundaries, and an easier paper with higher ones. For a student this means last series' numbers are not a target worth chasing; the mark scheme is. For a parent it means a raw mark on a past paper is only meaningful alongside the boundaries published for that paper.

faqs.question: What is a predicted grade, who decides it, and what can we do if it looks too low?
faqs.answer: It is the school's professional judgement of the grade a student is likely to achieve, submitted for university applications and based on the evidence the teachers hold: classwork, mocks, coursework drafts. Nobody is bound by it and it is not a negotiation. If it looks low, ask the school what evidence it rests on and what further evidence would be considered, then produce that evidence — a timed paper sat under conditions and marked against the published scheme, or a coursework draft meeting the top descriptors. A tutor cannot change a prediction and should never claim to.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 'evaluate' and 'discuss' in a mark scheme, and why does it change the mark?
faqs.answer: Both require two sides, and that is where the similarity ends. 'Evaluate' asks for a judgement supported by the stronger evidence, so an answer that balances perfectly and concludes nothing loses the top marks. 'Discuss' asks for the considerations to be set out and related to each other, where a premature verdict can cost you the breadth marks. The practical test is to look at what the scheme awards marks for: if there is a mark for a reasoned conclusion, you must reach one. Most students write the same answer for both terms.

faqs.question: How much of a Diploma subject grade is marked by the school rather than by an external examiner?
faqs.answer: In most subjects the internally assessed component carries around a fifth of the subject grade. The school marks it against the published criteria and the IB moderates a sample, which can move the whole cohort's marks up or down if the school's standard differs from the IB's. That matters in a school with a young programme, where the internal standard is still settling. It also means a fifth of the grade is decided by work done under supervision over months rather than in an examination hall, which is the part a family has the most influence over.

alula.closingHeading: Start with the structural question, not the tutoring one
alula.closingBody: Tell us how many subjects are actually a problem and which components inside them, and we will tell you whether a weekly specialist over video is the proportionate answer or whether you should be weighing a school in Riyadh or Jeddah instead. If it is the former, we match on the syllabus first and the clock second, run a free trial as a diagnostic, and give you a written component-level read whether you continue or not. Four weeks later you hold marked work and an explicit recommendation. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, Sunday to Thursday, pinned to Arabia Standard Time.

arabic-speaking-ib-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Arabic inside the IB framework and support English-medium subjects for Arabic-speaking students. Each profile names the pathway, the level and the components the tutor has taught, so a family can match a child's actual paper rather than a job title.

intro.heading: Two different tutors hide behind one search phrase
paragraphs: The phrase "Arabic speaking IB tutor" is doing two jobs at once, and the gap between them explains why so many families hire the wrong person. One family means a specialist in IB Arabic: a teacher who knows that Arabic A: Language and Literature is examined on unseen text analysis and comparative essay writing, and that Arabic B lives or dies on the receptive paper. Another family means a maths or chemistry teacher who happens to speak Arabic, because their child moved into an English-medium Diploma from a national-curriculum school and is losing marks to the language of the question rather than to the content.

Those are not the same hire. An eloquent native speaker with a literature degree can be close to useless for a Year 12 student who cannot read a Physics Paper 2 data question in English, and a bilingual physics teacher cannot mark an Arabic HL essay against its criteria. The honest first question is therefore not "are you Arabic speaking?" but "which of these two problems is my child actually having?" A single diagnostic session answers it, usually inside forty minutes, by putting a past paper in front of the student and watching where the hesitation sits.

This page is built around the evidence rather than the pitch. It starts with what measurable movement in Arabic looks like over a term, works back through the four Diploma pathways and their components, sets out where marks are genuinely lost, reports what providers in the Kingdom advertise for this work, and finishes with the questions that separate a tutor who has taught the syllabus from one who has only spoken the language. Every figure quoted is attributed to the kind of source that published it.

It helps to know why the local pool is thin. Arabic is taught in almost every school in the Kingdom, so fluent teachers are everywhere; teachers who have taught Group 1 Arabic to an external mark scheme, or marked a component for a board, are not. A school running one Diploma cohort may have a single Arabic A teacher and no second opinion in the building. That is the gap an outside specialist fills, and it is a staffing gap rather than a reflection on the school.

One thing is fixed. Lessons for Saudi families are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an address in Riyadh, Jeddah or anywhere else in the Kingdom; home visits are a service offered only in India. For this subject that constraint is close to an advantage: the pool of teachers who have examined IB Arabic is small and thinly spread, and no family should be choosing from only the ones who live within a half-hour drive of their compound.

sections.heading: What measurable progress in Arabic looks like over one term
paragraphs: Start with evidence rather than a promise. Most families arrive holding one of two documents: a report card carrying a middling grade in Arabic A, or a predicted grade that has slipped a band since the first Diploma term. Neither document says what to fix. The first useful move is to turn the complaint into something countable, which Arabic makes easy. Reading speed on an unseen passage, how long an individual oral runs before the student stalls, whether an analysis paragraph names a technique or only retells the plot.

A first session should produce four or five numbers like those, written down. They are not for the parent's reassurance; they are the baseline the next eight weeks are measured against. A student who reads an unseen passage at a crawl and needs three attempts to find the thesis of it is not short of vocabulary. The problem is decoding speed, and the fix is daily short reading under a clock rather than longer lessons.

By the end of a term, honest progress shows in those same numbers rather than in a grade. Grades move late, because boundaries shift and a single internal test samples a narrow part of the course. What moves early is the structure of an answer: a comparative essay that states its line of argument in the first sentence, an oral that fills its time without rescue, a reading paper finished with minutes to spare. No tutor can promise a specific grade, and anyone who does should be treated with real scepticism.

sections.heading: One search phrase, two different tutors
paragraphs: The table below is the fastest way for a family to work out which hire they are making. Read down the first column until a row describes your child, then read across. The distinction matters because the two tutors are drawn from different pools, cost different amounts, and are verified in completely different ways. Hiring across the line is the single most common waste of money in this corner of the market.

The hardest case to diagnose is the third row. A student who speaks Arabic at home, studies in English, and is sliding in one science subject will often be described by the school as having a language problem, which sends the family looking for an Arabic teacher. Frequently the real issue is that nobody has taught the command terms: the student knows the content but reads "outline" and writes an essay, or reads "explain" and writes a list. That is a subject-teaching fix delivered bilingually, not an Arabic lesson.

The fourth row is the one families underestimate. A child who is going to sit Arabic A: Literature needs somebody who has taught literary analysis in Arabic to an external mark scheme, which is a narrower skill than fluency and a much narrower one than conversation. Ask directly which works the tutor has taught and which components they have marked. A tutor who answers with a book list and a component name is in the right pool; one who answers with their nationality is not.

sections.heading: The four Arabic pathways, component by component
paragraphs: Arabic A: Language and Literature studies literary and non-literary texts together. At both levels there is a guided analysis of an unseen text and a comparative essay on studied works, plus an individual oral built around a global issue and two extracts. Higher Level adds a written essay on one studied work. The analysis paper carries the largest single share at both levels, so unseen-text technique is the highest-return thing to teach first.

Arabic A: Literature narrows the field to literary works only, with the same assessment logic and a heavier reading load. Arabic B is a language acquisition course: productive writing on one paper, listening and reading on the other, and an individual oral based on a visual stimulus at Higher Level or a text at Standard Level. The receptive paper is the biggest component of the Arabic B grade by a wide margin, and listening is the part families never practise because it is tedious to practise alone.

Arabic ab initio exists at Standard Level only and assumes no prior knowledge. The trap is obvious once stated: a student who speaks Arabic at home and is entered for ab initio has an easy year and a capped outcome, because the course does not ask hard enough questions to show what they can do. Pathway and level are school decisions, changeable only before the entry deadline. Ask your coordinator to confirm the component list and weightings in writing, because the published scheme is what the examiner marks against.

sections.heading: Where Arabic marks actually go missing
paragraphs: On the Group 1 analysis paper, the commonest failure is retelling. A student writes four accurate paragraphs about what happens in the passage and scores poorly, because the paper rewards an argument about how meaning is constructed: structure, register, imagery, the effect of a choice the writer made. The second commonest is a thesis that appears in the last line instead of the first. Both are fixable in a handful of sessions, because both are structural habits rather than gaps in knowledge.

On the comparative essay, students lose marks by writing two separate essays stapled together. The mark scheme wants the works held against each other continuously, which means a paragraph plan built on points of comparison rather than on works. In the individual oral, the usual collapse is the global issue: a student picks something too broad to evidence in the time, then spends the oral describing extracts instead of using them. Choosing a narrow, arguable issue is most of the work.

For Arabic B candidates the losses cluster on the receptive paper. Listening sections punish students who have only ever heard their teacher's accent, and reading sections punish students who translate word by word instead of skimming for structure. The productive paper loses marks on text type: a candidate asked for a blog writes a formal letter and forfeits the register marks regardless of how good the Arabic is. Each of these is diagnosable from one past paper, which is why the first session is a diagnosis rather than a lesson.

sections.heading: What providers in the Kingdom advertise for this work
paragraphs: Rates in this market are published by tutoring companies and marketplaces, not by any regulator, so every figure below is an advertised rate from that kind of source rather than a market average and not a quote from IB Gram. Tutoring-platform listings for general, non-specialist online tutoring in the Kingdom start around SAR 55 an hour. Budget platforms advertise IGCSE one-to-one online from roughly SAR 35. A tutor-marketplace guide puts general private tuition in Riyadh at about SAR 50 an hour for primary and over SAR 200 for senior-school examination subjects.

For IB work specifically, tutoring-company listings in Riyadh advertise subject tutoring from about SAR 180 an hour, with Higher Level and premium tracks quoted around SAR 200 to 220. International providers that quote in dollars sit near sixty dollars an hour, which a Saudi family should convert before comparing. In-home tuition carries a travel loading on top of all of these, which is a cost with no academic return attached to it.

What moves the number, in order of weight: scarcity of the exact pathway, examiner or marking experience, level, whether the tutor travels, and package length. Arabic A: Literature at Higher Level is scarcer than Arabic B, and a teacher who has marked for a board is scarcer again. A bilingual Physics Higher Level specialist is scarcer than either. Ask any provider what fees cover beyond the hour itself, because reports, past-paper packs and written feedback on drafts are sometimes inside the rate and sometimes not.

sections.heading: Checking the claim: fluency and syllabus competence are different evidence
paragraphs: Nothing in this market is harder to verify than "I am an Arabic speaking IB tutor", because both halves of the claim sound self-evidently true when spoken by a fluent graduate. Fluency is audible in thirty seconds; syllabus competence is not audible at all. So the verification has to be done with specifics, and the trial lesson is the place to do it. A family should come to that session with one past paper and three questions, not with a general conversation.

Ask which pathway and level the tutor has taught, by name, and for how many cohorts. Ask which components they have marked and whether that marking was for a school or a board, because only one gives a view across many candidates. Ask them to talk through a mark scheme on one question from your child's paper, explaining where an answer sits and why. A teacher who has done this work does it comfortably; a fluent speaker who has not will drift into discussing the content of the passage instead.

Ask what they would and would not do with assessed work. The correct answer is narrow and should come without hesitation: they will teach the criteria, question a line of argument and model technique on a different text, and they will not draft any part of the submission. A tutor who is vague here is a risk to the candidate, because malpractice findings fall on the student. Then ask how progress will be reported against the first session's numbers.

sections.heading: Arabic, the bilingual Diploma, and the Qiyas tests
paragraphs: Arabic is not only a subject on the timetable in the Kingdom; it sits on two routes that matter after school. The first is the bilingual Diploma. A candidate who completes two Language A subjects, or who studies an individuals-and-societies or sciences subject in a language other than their Language A, can be awarded the Diploma with a bilingual designation. The exact conditions are published by the IB, and a Diploma Programme coordinator will confirm whether a combination qualifies.

The second route is the Saudi university pathway, where Arabic resurfaces in a way most international-school families do not expect. An international certificate needs an equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate; that applies to the IB Diploma as much as to A Levels. Alongside it sit the Qiyas tests run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission: Qudurat, which tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and Tahsili, which covers science-stream subjects and English.

Tahsili is the one that catches international-curriculum students, and the reason is structural rather than linguistic. Its content follows the Saudi national curriculum, so an IB student meets familiar material in unfamiliar framing and ordering. Qudurat can be sat in Arabic or in English, a real choice for a student schooled in English with Arabic as a first language. No thresholds or weighting formulas appear here because they differ by university and programme; check the university's own published admission criteria.

whyPoints.title: Honest limits on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach criteria and give feedback on the student's own drafts. Nothing in a submission is produced for the candidate, and that boundary is stated to the student directly.

whyPoints.title: Measured, not promised
whyPoints.description: Progress is tracked against numbers taken in the first session. No grade, score or admission outcome is guaranteed, and any provider offering one is making a claim nobody can keep.

faqs.question: How does an online tutor share Arabic script and vowel markings clearly on screen?
faqs.answer: Through a shared whiteboard with Arabic typing and handwriting input, so text is built right to left in front of the student rather than pasted in. Diacritics are added live, which matters when a reading error comes from a missing short vowel rather than from vocabulary. Past papers are opened as the student will see them, annotated on screen, and the annotated copy saved for revision.

faqs.question: Can a parent who does not read Arabic follow what happens in these lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes, because the report after each session is written in English and is about technique rather than content. It names the component worked on, what the mark scheme wanted, where the answer fell short and what the next task is. A parent who cannot judge the Arabic can still judge whether the thesis now appears in the first sentence, and whether reading speed on an unseen passage is improving.

faqs.question: What happens if the connection drops in the middle of an individual oral rehearsal?
faqs.answer: The rehearsal restarts from the beginning of the extract rather than being stitched together, because the component is timed and continuity is part of what is being practised. Tutors keep the extract set and the global issue notes in the shared workspace, so nothing is lost on reconnecting. If a drop costs more than a few minutes the time is made up by extending the next session.

faqs.question: Are oral rehearsal recordings kept, and who is allowed to see them?
faqs.answer: Recordings are made only when the family asks, because hearing the first attempt next to the fourth is the fastest way to show progress on an oral. Where one exists it is shared with the family and the tutor and nobody else, and it is deleted on request. Nothing is published, used as a sample or shown to another student. School-submitted recordings are a separate matter and are made and held by the school under its own rules.

faqs.question: Why is an Arabic A: Literature tutor quoted higher than an ab initio one?
faqs.answer: Scarcity, and the kind of marking involved. Teaching literary analysis in Arabic against an external mark scheme is a narrower skill than teaching a beginner course, and the pool who have done it is small. Higher Level adds an essay component needing criterion-level feedback on a student's own draft, which is slow, skilled work. Tutoring-company listings in the Kingdom advertise premium Higher Level tracks well above their general rate.

faqs.question: What does the free trial lesson for Arabic actually cover?
faqs.answer: A diagnosis, not a sample lesson. The student works one past paper question from their own pathway while the tutor watches where the time goes, then reads a short unseen passage aloud so decoding speed can be judged. The session ends with four or five written observations and a recommendation about which component to attack first. It also answers this page's opening question: Arabic itself, or reading English papers under time pressure.

faqs.question: Is a small group ever better value than one-to-one for Arabic B listening?
faqs.answer: For listening specifically, a pair can work well, because hearing a second learner's answer exposes the mishearing rather than just the mistake, and the audio is the same for both. For the productive paper and the individual oral, grouping wastes most of the hour: text type, register and oral fluency need individual airtime. Most families run one-to-one weekly and add paired listening before a series.

faqs.question: Do fees change if we want one tutor for Arabic and for maths taught in Arabic?
faqs.answer: Usually this is two tutors rather than one rate, because the pool of people who can teach Arabic A to an external mark scheme and also teach Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches properly is very thin. Where one person genuinely covers both, the higher of the two rates applies for all sessions, since the scarcer qualification sets the price. Splitting the work across two specialists is usually better taught.

faqs.question: What should a family expect to pay in SAR for feedback on an Arabic HL essay?
faqs.answer: Providers in the Kingdom do not usually price written feedback separately; it is billed as session time at the tutor's hourly rate, and advertised Higher Level IB rates from tutoring-company listings in Riyadh sit around SAR 200 to 220 an hour. A realistic piece of work is one session on the research question, one on a draft against the criteria, and one after redrafting. Ask whether reading time outside the session is charged.

faqs.question: How do we check a tutor knows the current IB Arabic syllabus, not just Arabic?
faqs.answer: Ask for the component list of your child's pathway from memory, with the shares each component carries, and compare it with what your coordinator gave you in writing. Then ask which studied works they have taught and whether they have marked that component for a school or for a board. A teacher inside the syllabus answers in component names and criteria; a fluent speaker outside it talks generally about the language.

faqs.question: Does being a native Arabic speaker make someone a good Arabic A teacher?
faqs.answer: No. Fluency is a prerequisite and nothing more. Arabic A is examined on unseen textual analysis, comparative argument and an oral on a global issue, none of which a fluent adult does naturally without training. The useful question is what the tutor has taught and marked, not how they speak. A non-native teacher with years of Group 1 marking is frequently the better hire.

faqs.question: Can we ask for a tutor of a particular gender for Arabic oral practice?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a straightforward request to meet. One-to-one online lessons let a family choose the tutor directly, which is why the choice is wider online than it would be from whoever is available locally. State the preference when you describe the pathway and it is applied to the shortlist before any trial is arranged. The same applies to a preference for a tutor who has taught in the Kingdom.

faqs.question: What if the Arabic tutor is good but our child's maths is the real problem?
faqs.answer: Then the plan changes rather than the tutor being defended. The trial lesson is designed to catch exactly this, which is why it uses a paper rather than a conversation, but it sometimes surfaces a term in. Bilingual subject support is a separate service: a maths or sciences specialist who teaches content and command terms together and then moves the student to answering wholly in English, often as a short block alongside weekly Arabic.

faqs.question: What does examiner experience mean for an Arabic B tutor, and how is it verified?
faqs.answer: It means the tutor has marked that component for a board across many candidates, which gives a view of where the marks sit that no single classroom provides. Verify it by asking which component, for which board, and what it taught them about the receptive paper. A convincing answer is concrete and unglamorous, usually about how narrowly the listening section is marked. A vague answer about years of experience is not the same claim.

One past paper worked live online will tell you which of the two tutors on this page you need, and you will have the numbers in writing before anyone asks you for money. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time.

intro.heading: Nobody can tell you who the best tutor is, so here is what you can check
paragraphs: Search for the best IB home tutor in Saudi Arabia and the results will be confident. Sites will claim to be the top choice, quote a satisfaction percentage with no sample behind it, show a star rating from an unnamed source, and promise a grade improvement. None of that is verifiable, and the reason is structural rather than cynical: there is no register of tutors in the Kingdom, no licensing body for private tuition, and no authority that could rank one tutor above another even if it wanted to. Any page that says otherwise is describing a system that does not exist.

What does exist is regulation of schools, and understanding it is genuinely useful. Private and international schools are licensed by the Ministry of Education. School evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which also operates services for national school accreditation and for approving international accreditation bodies. The IB authorises schools to offer its programmes. Cambridge and Pearson approve examination centres. Every one of those processes stops at the school gate. Not one of them says anything about a private tutor.

So the search for a good tutor is a search a parent has to run themselves, and the good news is that it is runnable. The evidence is concrete: which subject guide the tutor has taught, at which level, with which options and extensions; whether they have marked that component for a live series, and across how many; what they will and will not do with assessed work; and what they propose for the first month in terms a parent can check without knowing the subject. Those four things are checkable in a single trial lesson by somebody who has never read a Diploma syllabus.

The second half of this page is about something families underestimate: the difference between the right tutor and the available one. A home tutor is selected from the people who can physically reach your address at the hour your child is free. In a city that takes an hour to cross, that is a sector rather than a city; in Jubail, Abha or the inland Eastern Province it can be a handful of people, or nobody at all with a Higher Level specialism. The online pool is the same search without the travel constraint, which is why it contains more specialists in every subject and every level.

Timing matters too, and it is why this page runs forward through the school year rather than through a feature list. The right tutor for a student at the start of a course is not the right tutor for one in the final term, and several of the decisions that actually determine an outcome — subject levels, examination entries, equivalency paperwork, when a curriculum switch is realistic — have deadlines a family will miss if nobody tells them the order. Those are set out in a table further down, with no calendar year named, because your school and the regulator hold the real dates.

One plain statement before any of it. Lessons for Saudi families are delivered online, one to one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an address in the Kingdom, and home visits in Saudi Arabia are not a service we sell; in-home teaching is something we run only in India. The phrase at the top of this page is the phrase parents search, and we would rather use it and then tell you exactly what we do than let anybody book expecting a knock at the door.

best-ib-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The IB runs four programmes and a Saudi family will usually meet one or two of them. What matters for this page is recognition: what each one leads to, and which of them a Saudi university or an overseas one will expect to see.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led with no external examinations, reported against learning outcomes rather than marks. There is nothing here for a university to recognise, which is the point: the programme is building habits rather than producing a certificate. The useful hire at this stage is a primary specialist who can name a gap a report card has not named, not a Diploma subject expert working downwards.
programmes.countryNote: In the Kingdom the practical question at primary level is which route the child will take afterwards, because a PYP primary can feed into an MYP stream, a Cambridge Lower Secondary stream or an MoE school, and each of those marks work differently. Families relocating mid-primary should ask the receiving school how it assesses, not only what it teaches, since that is where a settled child suddenly looks behind.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, with the Personal Project in the final year. The MYP certificate is not what universities look at, but the programme decides whether a student arrives in the Diploma able to write at length and research independently. Criterion coverage, rather than content, is what caps marks here, and it is the thing an examination-trained tutor most often misreads.
programmes.countryNote: MYP provision in the Kingdom is thinner than Diploma provision, so plenty of students reach DP1 from Cambridge IGCSE or an MoE route instead. That is not a disadvantage, but it changes what has to be built before the Diploma: an IGCSE student usually has the content and less experience of independent written research, which is exactly the gap the MYP exists to close.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at two levels, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. This is the qualification that has to be recognised, both by overseas universities, which publish points and Higher Level subject requirements, and by Saudi universities, which require a Ministry of Education equivalency decision before treating a foreign certificate as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students here face one extra administrative step that British or American students at home never think about. The certificate itself is not enough for a Saudi university application; equivalency is a separate decision made by the Ministry, and it applies to an IB Diploma, A Levels and an American high school diploma alike. Families who learn this after results are published have lost time they did not need to lose.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The IB's fourth programme combines Diploma courses with a career-related study and a core of its own. It is offered by relatively few schools worldwide and recognition varies much more than it does for the Diploma, so a family considering it should ask the receiving universities directly rather than assuming parity. Where it is offered, the subject courses are taught against the same guides as the Diploma.
programmes.countryNote: Availability in the Kingdom is limited enough that most families will not meet this programme at all, and a school offering it should be asked specifically which universities have accepted its leavers. Where a student is taking Diploma courses inside a Career-related Programme, subject tutoring works exactly as it does for a Diploma student, because the subject guide is the same document.

best-ib-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Subject choice is where the regulatory and university endgame becomes concrete, because prerequisites are stated in subjects and levels. This grid reads each subject twice: what it is needed for afterwards, and what the local staffing reality usually is.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The level and the course both appear in university prerequisites, and engineering, physics, economics and computing programmes frequently name Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level specifically. It is also among the hardest subjects for a school with one mathematics department to staff properly at Higher Level alongside the other mathematics course.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: A full Diploma mathematics course, but not interchangeable with Analysis and Approaches for prerequisite purposes, and that catches families late. Check the stated requirement of the courses your child is likely to apply to before the level is locked, because a change afterwards is a timetable problem rather than a preference.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Named at Higher Level by many engineering and physical-science programmes. The Higher Level extension has no Standard Level equivalent, and it is the part of the course most often compressed at the end of the year by a department with a single specialist, which is why outside requests cluster there.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: A standard prerequisite for medicine, pharmacy, dentistry and chemical engineering, usually at Higher Level. Its content also overlaps with the chemistry section of the national Achievement Test, though the framing differs, which matters for students applying inside the Kingdom as well as outside it.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Required or strongly preferred at Higher Level for medicine and the life sciences in most systems. The content volume is the teaching challenge and the data treatment in the internal investigation is the marking one; neither is helped by a tutor who knows biology but has not marked the component.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Rarely a hard prerequisite, frequently an advantage, and a common Higher Level choice for business and finance applicants. Diagrams and quantitative method carry marks that students assume are presentational, and Higher Level Paper 3 is the component most often under-taught locally.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Serves both as a Diploma group 1 subject and, in many cases, as evidence of English proficiency for university entry, though each university states its own position. For students taught in English who speak another language at home, the gap is precise critical vocabulary rather than fluency.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Relevant both to the Diploma's language requirements and to a family thinking about study inside the Kingdom, where Arabic-medium provision and the national tests are a live consideration. Availability of Arabic A as a group 1 subject varies by school and should be confirmed before enrolment rather than assumed.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Increasingly named by computing and data programmes, and one of the thinnest subjects to staff anywhere. A school running it with one teacher often cannot also run the Higher Level case study properly, which is a recurring and very specific outside-teaching request.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Together these contribute points through the Diploma matrix, so they can decide whether a student meets a points-based offer. Both are marked against published criteria and both are supervised at school, which makes them the part of the Diploma where the line between legitimate tutoring and misconduct matters most.

best-ib-home-tutor.regionsTitle: What a drivable radius actually looks like, city by city
best-ib-home-tutor.regionsIntro: The phrase home tutor implies a geography, so it is worth being concrete about what that geography contains. In each of these places, the in-home pool is the set of tutors who can reach an address and get home again on a weekday evening — and in most of the Kingdom that is a much smaller set than families assume.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: Roughly an hour across in traffic, which means an in-home tutor serves a sector rather than the city. A family in the north and a family in the south are choosing from different lists, even though both are in Riyadh, and the specialist they want may be on the other list.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur. Travelling the length of it in the late afternoon is not a realistic weekday commitment for a tutor, so the practical in-home pool is a stretch of the spine rather than the whole of it.

regions.name: Dhahran, Al Khobar and Dammam
regions.note: One conurbation and one labour market, with the King Fahd Causeway putting Bahrain inside a day trip. The in-home pool here is better than most of the Kingdom and is still narrow by subject, because the number of Higher Level specialists in any one subject is small everywhere.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: An industrial city with international schooling and a transient professional population. The local pool is small enough that the question is rarely which tutor is better; it is whether anybody within reach has taught the subject at the level the student is sitting.

regions.name: Al Ahsa and the inland Eastern Province
regions.note: An hour and a half inland from the coastal cluster, far enough that the coastal tutor pool is not reachable on a weekday evening at all. Families here are choosing between the few local options and the national online pool, and often there is no local option in the subject.

regions.name: Makkah and Madinah
regions.note: Makkah sits roughly 80km east of Jeddah, so a Jeddah-based tutor is not a weekday option. Pilgrimage seasons also shape the local calendar and the practical availability of evenings, which makes a fixed, agreed slot more valuable here than a flexible arrangement.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Twin cities about 25km apart in 'Asir at high altitude, sharing one catchment. Distance from any large international cluster means a Higher Level specialist in a given subject may simply not live within driving distance, whatever a family is willing to pay.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: A fast-changing north-west with newly arriving families and a young school market. Students here are often the only ones in their year sitting a particular subject combination, and an in-home search frequently returns nothing at the right level.

regions.name: Thuwal, Yanbu and Ha'il
regions.note: Smaller markets with narrow senior provision, including a campus community north of Jeddah on the coast. In each, the realistic choice is between relocating, boarding a child, or keeping schooling local and buying the subject teaching from the national pool.

schoolClusters.note: The city's licensed international schools between them cover the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma Programmes, which makes a continuous IB route realistic here. Whether an individual Higher Level subject runs in a given year still depends on how many students pick it, which is a question to ask before enrolling rather than after.

A mix of IB and Cambridge provision along the coast plus the campus school at Thuwal. Families in Makkah's catchment commonly school their children in this cluster, which is a daily commitment rather than a short journey and shapes what time a weekday lesson can start.

The International Schools Group runs several campuses here and the Diploma is offered at some and not others, which surprises families who assume one curriculum across a group. British-curriculum schools in the same conurbation run to A Level, so moving between them changes the qualification rather than only the address.

It is the cheapest useful version of tutoring and the one families buy least, because nothing is on fire yet. It is also the only version that can change a habit rather than patch a gap.

sections.heading: Why there is no official answer to this search
paragraphs: A parent typing this query is asking for a ranking, and the honest response is that no ranking exists and none could be produced legitimately. There is no register of private tutors in the Kingdom, no licensing requirement to teach privately, and no public body that inspects or grades tuition. A tutoring company can call itself the top choice on Tuesday and nothing happens, because there is nothing to contradict it.

That matters because of what the vacuum fills with. Across this market you will find satisfaction percentages with no sample size and no date, star ratings from unnamed sources, student counts nobody audits, and promises of a specific grade improvement. Every one of those is unverifiable, which makes it worthless as evidence even when it happens to be true. A claim a parent cannot test does not help a parent decide, and a market full of such claims is one where the loudest page wins rather than the best teacher.

The second thing the vacuum fills with is proximity. If quality cannot be judged, families fall back on what can be observed: who is nearby, who is available this week, who came recommended by a neighbour whose child takes a different subject at a different level. Those are not bad instincts, they are simply weak evidence. A neighbour's excellent Mathematics Standard Level tutor tells you very little about Physics at Higher Level, which is a different subject taught by a different and much smaller group of people.

What is left is a short list of things that genuinely can be checked, and the rest of this page is built on them. Which subject guide and level the tutor has taught, with which options. Whether they have marked that component for a live series, and across how many. What they will not do with assessed work. And what they propose for the first month, stated so that a parent who does not know the subject can verify it at the end of the month. None of that requires trust. All of it can be tested in one free hour.

sections.heading: What the Ministry and ETEC actually regulate, and where it stops
paragraphs: Families are often reassured by the word accredited without knowing what is accredited, so it is worth separating the layers. Private and international schools operate under licences from the Ministry of Education. School evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which operates e-services for national school accreditation and for approving the international accreditation bodies that schools also use. Those processes are about institutions: premises, governance, staffing, curriculum provision.

On top of that sit the curriculum bodies, which authorise schools rather than people. The IB authorises a school to offer the Primary Years, Middle Years, Diploma or Career-related Programme, and that authorisation is the school's. Cambridge and Pearson approve examination centres, which is why a private candidate has to find a centre that holds that approval rather than simply turning up. Again, these are institutional arrangements and they say nothing about an individual tutor.

Then there is the Ministry's other role, which Saudi families meet at the end of school rather than the beginning: equivalency, or mu'adalah. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision from the Ministry before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate, and that applies to an IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. It is an administrative step with its own requirements, and it is the single thing most international-school families in the Kingdom learn about too late.

Where all of this stops is the tutor. No licence is required to teach privately, no body inspects private tuition, and no authority certifies a tutor's competence in a subject or a syllabus. IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership from the Ministry, from ETEC, from Qiyas, from the IB, from Cambridge or from Pearson, and neither does anyone else in this market who claims one. Anybody implying otherwise is describing something that is not available to be held.

sections.heading: The available tutor and the right tutor
paragraphs: In most families' experience these two are the same person, because availability is what the search actually returned. A home tutor is selected from the people who can reach an address and get home again on a weekday evening, filtered further by who happens to have a free slot at the hour the student is free. Subject specialism enters that process last, if at all. The result is a competent person teaching slightly outside their specialism, which works until the Higher Level extension topics arrive.

The difference shows up in specific, diagnosable ways. A tutor working inside their specialism anticipates where a question is going and can say, before the student has finished writing, which of three standard errors is about to happen. A tutor working a chapter ahead responds to the error after it appears. Both are helpful; only one of them changes how the student approaches the next question. At Standard Level that gap is tolerable. At Higher Level, in a subject with an extension that has no Standard Level equivalent, it is the whole thing.

There is a second difference, in what gets taught. A specialist teaches to the mark scheme because they know what it rewards: which command terms change the required answer, what a six-mark response must contain, where candidates give away marks they had already earned. A generalist teaches the content correctly and leaves the student to work out how to be paid for it. This is why marking experience is worth a premium, and why it should be stated as board, subject, component and number of series rather than as a general claim.

None of this is an argument that every family needs the scarcest tutor available. For a Standard Level subject where the student simply needs structure and accountability, a good generalist is the right purchase and a specialist is an expensive one. The argument is only that the family should know which they are buying, and should not discover that they bought availability when a Higher Level paper arrives. Ask what the tutor's own subject and level are, then ask what they have taught at the level your child is sitting.

sections.heading: Why a national pool holds more specialists than a drivable one
paragraphs: This is arithmetic rather than advocacy. Senior subject specialists are a thin slice of any teaching workforce, everywhere, because a school needs one or two of each and the market trains accordingly. Restrict that slice to the people who can drive to a particular address on a weekday evening and the number falls sharply — not because Saudi teachers are scarce, but because any geographic filter on a small population leaves a very small population.

Put numbers to the shape of it without inventing any. Riyadh takes about an hour to cross in traffic, so an in-home tutor realistically serves a sector of the city, which means a family is choosing from a fraction of even the local pool. Jeddah runs as a long spine and the same applies along it. The Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran conurbation behaves as one market and is therefore the best case in the Kingdom. Al Ahsa is an hour and a half inland from that conurbation, which removes it from that pool entirely. Abha and Khamis Mushait share a catchment at altitude far from any large cluster. In the last two cases the honest answer is that a Higher Level specialist in a given subject may not live within reach at any price.

Removing travel changes two things at once. The pool becomes everyone who teaches that subject guide and can hold an evening slot on Arabia Standard Time, which is a far larger group, and the journey disappears from the price — travel is either billed or absorbed, and senior in-home subject tuition in the Kingdom is advertised at the top of the local range partly for that reason. Published rates in this market run from roughly SAR 35 an hour on budget platforms to about SAR 200 to 220 for Higher Level tracks; those are advertised figures from platforms and tutoring companies, not a market average and not our price.

What online teaching does not do is replace the things an in-home tutor is genuinely better at. Somebody in the room is harder for a teenager to ignore, reads body language more easily, and can take a book out of a student's hands. Those are real advantages, and a family whose problem is motivation rather than specialism should weigh them seriously. The case for the online pool is specific: it is strongest at Higher Level, in scarce subjects, and anywhere outside the three largest urban markets.

sections.heading: The decision calendar, and what it costs to leave each item late
paragraphs: Several of the things that determine an international-school outcome in the Kingdom are administrative, dated and easy to miss, and a family that meets them in the wrong order pays for it in options rather than in money. The order below runs forward through a student's school career rather than through an academic year, and it names no year because every school sets its own dates and the authorities publish their own.

Three of the items catch families repeatedly. Subject levels get locked earlier than parents expect, and because university prerequisites are stated in subjects and levels, a Higher Level decision made casually in the spring can close a course two years later. Examination entries close months ahead of a series, and a private candidate must arrange an approved centre themselves rather than assume their school will do it. And equivalency is applied for after results, which sounds obvious until a family realises the application is a separate process with its own requirements and timelines, sitting between a certificate and a Saudi university offer.

The fourth is the quietest. Predicted grades are produced by the school from evidence it already holds, during the application cycle, which means the moment to improve the evidence is the year before the prediction and not the week after it. A family that reads a disappointing prediction and hires help that month is asking for something no tutor can deliver, because the judgement was formed from work that has already been marked.

Two calendar facts to hold alongside all of this. The school week runs Sunday to Thursday, and MoE public schools run a two-semester year starting in late August and ending in late June with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break, while international and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms. Two schools in the same city can therefore be on different years, which matters enormously when a family is moving a child between them. Always work from your own school's published calendar rather than a general one.
