Treat a one-teacher Higher Level option as a risk to plan around

sections.heading: The six checks, in the order they are worth running
paragraphs: First, the component test. Ask what the tutor would look at first, given your child's most recent marked work. A specialist names a component and a reason inside one sentence. A generalist names the subject, or talks about building confidence, which is a statement about manner rather than about teaching. This single question filters more effectively than any credential, because it cannot be prepared for without the underlying knowledge.

Second, the course test: have they taught this course, at this level, to a mark scheme, and which version of the subject guide. Third, the marked-work test: send one piece of your child's marked work in advance and ask what they see in it. Fourth, the trial test: the trial lesson must be taught rather than pitched, and you watch what happens when the student gets something wrong, because the response to a wrong answer is the whole craft. Fifth, the honesty test: ask what they will do if a coursework draft arrives in poor shape two days before a school deadline. The only acceptable answer involves the student doing the work and, where appropriate, the school being told.

Sixth, the exit test. Ask what happens if this is not working after a term, and listen for whether stopping is on the list. A provider who cannot describe the circumstances in which they would tell you to stop paying them has an incentive problem they have not thought about. None of these six requires expertise on your part, none takes more than a few minutes, and together they separate a subject specialist from a confident generalist more reliably than anything published about either.

sections.heading: Examiner experience: what it is worth, and what it is not
paragraphs: Marking or moderating for a board is the one credential in this market that genuinely changes what a tutor can teach, and it is also the one most loosely claimed. Someone who has marked a component has read several hundred scripts against a mark scheme and knows two things a non-marker usually does not: precisely what the scheme credits, and precisely what it refuses to credit despite the answer being correct in substance. That second category is where competent students lose grades, and it is nearly impossible to learn from a textbook.

The claim is checkable in the way that matters, which is by asking which component. A real marker says the component, the paper and roughly how long ago, and will talk about the experience concretely: the standardisation process, the kinds of answer that caused trouble, what the scheme would not accept. A loose claim stays general, attaches to a company rather than to a person, or slides between examiner, marker and moderator as though those were the same job.

What examiner experience is not is a teaching qualification, and families sometimes over-pay for it. A marker who cannot explain a topic to a struggling fifteen-year-old is less useful than a patient specialist who has never marked. The two profiles suit different jobs: for exam technique and mark-scheme work in a final year, marking experience is worth paying for; for rebuilding a weak foundation in the middle of a course, teaching skill matters more. A current classroom teacher also brings scheme-of-work awareness that a full-time tutor may lack, while a full-time tutor sees more schools and more boards. All three are legitimate, and none of them is best in the abstract.
bullets: Ask which component, which paper, and how recently

sections.heading: Why the right tutor for Higher Level is often the wrong one for Standard Level
paragraphs: Families buy a subject when they should be buying a level. In several Diploma subjects the Higher Level course rests on a component that Standard Level candidates never sit, and it is usually the hardest one in the course. History Higher Level carries a regional-option third paper worth more than a third of the grade. Economics Higher Level carries a quantitative paper with no Standard Level counterpart. Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches Higher Level carries a third paper of extended problems. A tutor who has taught the Standard Level course has not, by that fact, taught any of these.

The reverse mistake costs money rather than marks. A Higher Level specialist teaching a Standard Level student may teach beyond the syllabus, which feels impressive and wastes paid hours on content that will never be examined. Scarce specialists also cost more everywhere, for ordinary supply reasons, so a family paying a premium rate for a Standard Level subject is frequently buying nothing extra. This is the single most common way tuition budgets are misallocated across a Diploma.

The useful allocation follows the consequence. Put the money where the grade decides something: the Higher Level subject that a university offer depends on, or the subject where a predicted grade is at risk. Accept a cheaper and perfectly competent generalist for a Standard Level subject that only needs homework discipline and structure. Saying that out loud costs us revenue on some matches, which is rather the point of a page about how to check a provider.
bullets: Buy a level and a component, not a subject name
Ask explicitly whether they have taught the Higher Level third paper
Do not pay a specialist premium for a Standard Level subject

sections.heading: Equivalency: the step that makes an international certificate usable here
paragraphs: This is the biggest gap in the Saudi tutoring market and the part where bad information is most expensive. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, the mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. It applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. It is a documentary process with its own requirements, and some universities also state a maximum age for the certificate they will accept, which matters for a student taking a gap year.

Timing is what families get wrong. Equivalency is treated as an administrative task for the end of the final year, and by then the decisions it interacts with have already been taken. Subject choices made two years earlier may or may not satisfy a programme's prerequisites. A course-results route rather than a full Diploma may read differently. The right moment to read the requirements is the first Diploma year, because that is when the choices that matter are still open and a change is still possible without disruption.

What nobody can offer is an outcome. No provider can promise a university place or a particular equivalency decision; those sit with institutions that do not take instructions from tutoring companies. What a tutor can do is make sure the subjects your child is sitting match what the target programmes expect, that the Higher Level combination is right rather than merely comfortable, and that the family is reading the university's own published criteria rather than a third-party summary of it. We will point you at the document holder and decline to guess.

sections.heading: Qudurat, Tahsili, and why international-curriculum students struggle with one of them
paragraphs: The two Qiyas tests do different jobs and are prepared for differently. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, assesses verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and is sat in Arabic or in English. Because it tests reasoning, familiarity with the question formats and timing is most of the preparation, and a strong IB student usually adapts to it without great difficulty once they have seen enough of it.

Tahsili, the Achievement Test, is the one that catches international-curriculum students out, and the reason is worth stating plainly because almost nobody does. Tahsili covers the science-stream subjects, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum. An IB or Cambridge student has studied the same material and has studied it well, but through different framing, different terminology, different emphasis and a different style of question. The overlap is real and the fit is not, which is why strong students sometimes under-perform on a test of material they genuinely know.

The preparation that works accepts that framing problem instead of treating it as a revision problem. Working through national-curriculum style questions, learning the terminology as it is used in that syllabus and practising the question formats under time is a different activity from revising for a Diploma paper. We publish no thresholds here and you should distrust any page that does: universities set their own admission formulas combining school results with the Qiyas tests, those weightings differ by university and by programme, and the competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili. Read the university's own criteria.

sections.heading: What a good provider says instead of a promise
paragraphs: There is a short list of things no tutoring provider in this market can honestly offer, and a family that knows the list can sort providers quickly. No grade or score can be guaranteed, because the papers are marked by a board and boundaries are set after the event. No improvement figure can be guaranteed, because it depends on work the student does when nobody is watching. No university outcome can be promised. No statistic about results should be published without a sample size, a date and a method attached, and almost none in this market has any of the three.

What can be offered instead is specific and testable. A named tutor with a stated subject background rather than a network. A trial lesson that is taught. A written diagnosis naming the component after the first working session. Work set and marked every week, because that is where progress actually happens. A written note after each session and an honest review at the end of term, including whether to stop. The commitment to change the tutor rather than argue when a match is wrong. Each of those is a thing you can observe happening or not happening within a month.

And one refusal, which is worth more than any of it. Assessed work, internal assessments, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the reflective project, must be the student's own. A tutor reads, questions and maps the draft against the published criteria, then the student redrafts. Nothing is written for them, ever, including when a deadline is two days away and everybody is anxious. A provider willing to cross that line is offering to put an entire Diploma at risk of a malpractice finding in exchange for a few marks, which tells you precisely how much they are weighing your child's interests.

faqs.question: Is there an official register of IB tutors in Saudi Arabia I can check a name against?
faqs.answer: No. Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, but there is no public register of individual private tutors, no licence number to request and no body that adjudicates on private teaching quality. That absence is why the verification has to be yours, and why a short list of specific questions is worth more than any amount of browsing. Ask what they have taught, at what level, and what they see in your child's marked work.

faqs.question: Does the Ministry of Education license private tutors the way it licenses schools?
faqs.answer: It does not. The licensing regime applies to schools as institutions: permission to operate, to deliver a curriculum, to admit students. An individual teaching privately over video for an hour a week sits outside it. The practical consequence is that no tutoring provider can point to a licence as a credential, and any that implies regulatory standing is telling you something about its honesty. Judge a tutor on subject background, on what they have taught to a mark scheme, and on how they handle a wrong answer in a trial lesson.

faqs.question: What does ETEC do, and what does it not do for a family hiring a tutor?
faqs.answer: The Education and Training Evaluation Commission runs school evaluation and accreditation, and operates e-services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. It describes schools as organisations. It does not assess individual tutors or tutoring companies, so an evaluation outcome tells you about your child's school and nothing at all about the person you are about to employ. Read it for what it is: context on provision, leadership and curriculum delivery, which is useful when choosing a school and irrelevant when choosing a tutor.

faqs.question: How do I check a claim about results when no statistic in this market can be verified?
faqs.answer: You stop trying to check it and check something else instead. A success percentage without a sample size, a date and a method is not evidence, and almost none published in this market has any of the three. What is checkable is specificity: which component would they look at first in your child's marked work, which subject guide version have they taught, what did they do when the student got something wrong in the trial lesson. Those answers are produced live, in front of you, and cannot be manufactured in advance.

faqs.question: Should the tutor who suits Standard Level teach the Higher Level option as well?
faqs.answer: Not automatically, and in some subjects definitely not. History, Economics, Business Management and the analysis-and-approaches mathematics course all carry a Higher Level third paper that Standard Level candidates never sit, and in History it is worth more than a third of the grade. A tutor who has taught only the Standard Level course has not taught that paper. Ask the question directly. Conversely, do not pay a Higher Level specialist's rate for a Standard Level subject that needs structure and homework discipline rather than depth.

faqs.question: What does a tutor need to know about my child's school scheme of work?
faqs.answer: Enough not to teach against it. Schools order the syllabus differently, choose different options within a subject, and set internal deadlines that are theirs rather than the board's. A tutor who teaches topics in a different order from the school produces a confused student, and one who does not know which option the school chose may teach content that will never be examined. Send the scheme of work or the term plan if the school publishes one, and expect the tutor to ask for it rather than having to be prompted.

faqs.question: How many students should one IB tutor be carrying at once?
faqs.answer: There is no correct number, but there is a diagnostic in the answer. A tutor who marks written work between sessions, writes a short note after each one and remembers what happened three weeks ago has a workable load. A tutor who cannot produce last week's marked work, or whose notes arrive days late, is carrying too many whatever the figure. Ask how work gets marked and when, rather than asking for a headcount, because the marking is the first thing to be dropped when a tutor is over-committed.

faqs.question: What single question in a trial lesson separates a specialist from a generalist?
faqs.answer: Hand them your child's most recent marked work and ask which component they would look at first and why that one. A specialist answers in a sentence, names a component and gives a reason tied to the mark scheme. A generalist names the subject, talks about confidence or asks what you would like to focus on. The question works because it cannot be prepared for: answering it requires knowing both the assessment structure and what the script in front of them actually shows.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether an IB tutor has taught inside the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: Less than families assume, with two real exceptions. The assessment is international, so a tutor who has taught the subject guide anywhere has taught the same course. The exceptions are scheduling and the university endgame. A tutor who has worked with Saudi families already understands the Sunday-to-Thursday week and will not propose a Friday slot thinking it is a weekday. And a tutor who has walked a family through equivalency and the Qiyas tests before is more useful in the final year than one meeting them for the first time.

faqs.question: What is Ministry of Education equivalency, and when should a Diploma family start looking at it?
faqs.answer: Equivalency, the mu'adalah, is the Ministry of Education decision that makes a foreign or international school certificate equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate for university purposes. It applies to the IB Diploma, A Levels and an American high school diploma alike, and some universities also state a maximum age for the certificate they will accept. Read the requirements in the first Diploma year rather than the last, because they interact with subject choices that are still open then and effectively closed later. The decision itself is documentary and sits with the Ministry.

faqs.question: Why do international-curriculum students find Tahsili harder than their own examinations?
faqs.answer: Because Tahsili content follows the Saudi national curriculum. The subjects it covers, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, are subjects an IB or Cambridge student has studied properly, but the framing, terminology, emphasis and question style belong to a different syllabus. The overlap is genuine and the fit is not, so a strong student can under-perform on material they know. The preparation that works is practice in that syllabus style and terminology rather than more revision of their own course.

faqs.question: Is Qudurat sat in Arabic or in English, and does the choice matter?
faqs.answer: Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is available in Arabic and in English. It assesses verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, so the verbal section is the part where language choice has real consequences: reasoning about text is harder in a language a student reads more slowly. The sensible approach is to try sample material in both and choose on performance rather than on principle, early enough that the decision is not made under pressure. Check the current arrangements with the National Center for Assessment directly.

faqs.question: Where should a family check a Saudi university's actual admission criteria?
faqs.answer: On the university's own admission pages, for the specific programme, and nowhere else. Universities publish their own formulas combining school results with the Qiyas tests, the weightings differ by institution and by programme, and competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili. Third-party summaries disagree with one another and go stale. Read the primary source in the first Diploma year, then read it again before applying, because a change to prerequisites is far easier to accommodate two years out than two months out.

faqs.question: Can a student apply to Saudi and overseas universities in the same cycle?
faqs.answer: Families do it regularly, and the two routes ask for different things on different timetables, which is the part to plan for. Overseas applications lean on predicted grades, subject prerequisites at Higher Level and references, and predicted grades are issued by the school long before the papers are sat. A Saudi route leans on the equivalency decision and the Qiyas results. Running both means satisfying both sets of prerequisites with one set of six subjects, which is a decision taken before the Diploma starts rather than during it.

faqs.question: What should happen in the first fortnight if the tutor turns out to be wrong for my child?
faqs.answer: You say so and the tutor changes, without a negotiation. A match can fail for reasons unrelated to competence: pace, manner, whether a particular student will admit confusion to a particular adult. Two sessions is usually enough to tell, and persevering out of politeness costs a term. Describe what specifically did not work, because that is what makes the second match better rather than merely different, and expect the new tutor to be briefed on the written diagnosis the first one produced.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a school's accreditation and a tutor's qualification?
faqs.answer: They answer different questions and families routinely treat them as one. Accreditation and evaluation describe an institution: its governance, processes and provision, assessed against a published framework. A tutor's qualification describes a person: their subject background, the courses they have taught and whether they have marked for a board. A school's accreditation says nothing about the individual teaching your child privately, and a tutor's credentials say nothing about the school. Ask for both separately and do not accept one as evidence of the other.

intro.heading: Judge a home tutor on the hour you actually have, then on the teaching
paragraphs: The in-home tutoring market in the Kingdom works on a simple constraint that nobody advertises: a visiting tutor can serve two, perhaps three households on a weekday evening, and they are all competing for the same ninety minutes. School finishes, the run home takes what traffic decides it takes, and the usable study window in most families opens somewhere between five and six and closes when a teenager stops being able to think. A tutor who has to arrive, set up, teach and leave has to be slotted into that window with travel attached at both ends.

That arithmetic determines who is available, and it has nothing to do with who is good. The tutor who has marked Cambridge 0620 Chemistry scripts for a board may live on the wrong side of Riyadh, which is roughly an hour across in traffic, or in a different city, or in a different country. The tutor who can reach your district by 5.30 is whoever happens to live nearby and wants the work. Families searching for the best IGCSE home tutor are usually shown the second list and told it is the first.

So this page runs in that order: the window first, the calendar second, the teaching third. It sets out what a Sunday-to-Thursday week genuinely leaves, what Arabia Standard Time does to a tutor working from India, the United Kingdom or further afield, and what happens to a fixed slot through a Ramadan timetable, an autumn break and a long summer. Only then does it get to what separates a good IGCSE tutor from an adequate one, because a brilliant tutor who cannot meet your hour is of no use to your child.

The whole middle of the page is the academic year read backwards from the examination series. Saudi IGCSE candidates sit the June series as the main sitting, with November available for resits and November-entry candidates. The February and March series that appears in so much online guidance is an India-only arrangement and is not open to a candidate here. Counting backwards from the papers rather than forwards from today is what turns vague intentions into dated decisions, and most of those decisions belong to the school rather than to the tutor.

One thing stated plainly, early. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Teaching for families in the Kingdom is delivered one-to-one over live video on Saudi local time. The reason that is worth considering is in the paragraphs above rather than in any claim about online learning being superior: it removes travel from the hour, removes geography from the shortlist, and makes a fixed weekly slot something that can survive a whole academic year.

best-igcse-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Four stages, each with a different relationship to the clock. What a tutor can usefully do in a week depends heavily on which of these a student is in, because the amount of school work already filling the evening changes completely between them.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessment runs against criteria across a long project cycle rather than against timed papers, so the weekly homework load is uneven: quiet for a fortnight, then heavy as a deadline approaches. Tuition in this programme is best placed on a fortnightly rhythm that can absorb those peaks, with the work aimed at timed closed-book writing, which the programme itself does not demand.
programmes.countryNote: Middle Years Programme schools in Riyadh and Jeddah feed into either Cambridge IGCSE or straight into the Diploma Programme, and the first timed paper a student meets is often an IGCSE mock. Families here have the most scheduling freedom of any group on this page, and the least urgency, which is exactly why support at this stage is both cheap and under-used.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year course built from components specified by syllabus code, with many subjects tiered between Core and Extended. Year 10 evenings still have room in them; Year 11 evenings do not, because mock seasons, internal examinations and coursework deadlines arrive together. A slot agreed in Year 10 and kept is worth far more than a slot negotiated under pressure in the spring term of Year 11.
programmes.countryNote: Saudi Cambridge candidates sit June as the main series and November for resits. Entries close several months ahead of the papers and the school's examinations officer holds the exact date, which is the single most important thing to ask for in writing. Schools in the Kingdom set their own term dates, so two candidates in the same city can be at different points in the syllabus in the same week.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Graded on the 9 to 1 scale, with its own specification codes — 4MA1 for Mathematics A, 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1 for the sciences. Paper structures, formula provision and the balance of short-answer to extended-response items differ from the Cambridge equivalents. A tutor moving between the two boards needs preparation time, and a good one will tell you that rather than claim the subject is the subject.
programmes.countryNote: Schools in the Kingdom choose boards subject by subject, so a single Saudi candidate can sit Cambridge sciences and Edexcel Mathematics in the same June series. That matters for scheduling as well as teaching: two boards means two sets of past papers, two mark-scheme styles and two revision rhythms inside the same already-narrow weekly window.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two years after IGCSE, where the evening load roughly doubles. Internal assessments, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge all generate deadlines that do not align with the examination timetable, and a student who never learned to protect a weekly study slot at IGCSE level struggles to build one here. The habit is more transferable than the content.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma Programme schools in the Kingdom sit the May session, and the subject-selection deadline falls well before a student's first Diploma lesson. For Saudi families the useful sequence is that IGCSE results arrive, Higher Level choices are confirmed with the school's Diploma Programme coordinator, and any prerequisite gap is closed in the break rather than carried into the first term.

best-igcse-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: The subjects Saudi families most often book a weekly IGCSE slot for, with the component that usually justifies the slot. Where a subject needs marking between sessions rather than teaching inside them, that is said, because it changes how long a plan actually takes.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 · Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The most common weekly booking in this market, and the one most dependent on marking between sessions. Written working has to be read line by line to see where credit was available and not taken, which cannot be done inside a live hour. Expect a plan where the tutor's preparation time is as long as the lesson.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Sat alongside 0580 by students heading towards Higher Level Mathematics. It introduces calculus, vectors and heavier trigonometry, and it exposes anybody who learned Extended-tier algebra as a set of remembered procedures. A weekly slot here is content-shaped and benefits from being booked from the start of Year 11 rather than the middle.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 · Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.description: Two separate demands on an hour: multi-step numerical work where units and rearrangement decide the mark, and the experimental component, which is screen work and teaches efficiently online. A sensible plan separates them rather than alternating, because they reward different kinds of practice between sessions.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 · Edexcel 4CH1)
subjects.description: Definitions are marked strictly here, and writing them out is homework rather than lesson time. The hour is better spent on moles, electrolysis, the qualitative analysis tables and the extended-response questions. A tutor who spends a live session reading definitions aloud is spending your money on something a student can do alone.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 · Edexcel 4BI1)
subjects.description: Recall is the easy half and students over-invest in it. The weekly hour earns its place on data questions, experimental design, control variables and the gap between describing a trend and explaining it. Progress here is measurable session to session, which makes it a good subject to test a new tutor on.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0653 · 0654)
subjects.description: One or two grades awarded across all three disciplines, which makes the first job triage: establishing which strand is dragging the award down. That diagnosis takes a session and saves a term, because spreading a single weekly hour evenly across physics, chemistry and biology is the least efficient plan available.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500)
subjects.description: Reading and writing are credited separately, so a confident writer who does not evidence close reading of the passage hits a ceiling quickly. Almost all the value sits in marked drafts returned between sessions, with the live hour used to rebuild the approach rather than to read the text together.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 · 0511)
subjects.description: An entirely different examination from 0500, with its own mark scheme: precise information transfer, summary to a word limit, register. Students placed here when they could manage First Language English often find out too late to change the entry, so the tier conversation matters more in this subject than in most.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies (Cambridge 0455 · 0450)
subjects.description: Both are decided on data-response and case-study questions where command terms carry the marks. These subjects suit a shorter, more frequent rhythm — two half-hour blocks of structured writing beat one long session — which is worth asking about when a provider only sells sixty-minute slots.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478 · 0984)
subjects.description: The written papers examine pseudocode, trace tables, logic and data representation. Most candidates write working code more easily than they read somebody else's and predict its output, and trace-table practice is the highest-yield use of a weekly hour in this subject by a wide margin.

best-igcse-home-tutor.regionsTitle: What the evening window looks like, city by city
best-igcse-home-tutor.regionsIntro: The usable study hour is set locally: by how far the school run is, whether the family lives on a compound, and how the city moves at five in the afternoon. These are the patterns that actually decide what time a weekly IGCSE slot can start.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: An hour across in traffic north to south, so two families at the same school have different realistic start times. A household in Al Olaya and one in Al Narjis negotiate completely different evenings, and a visiting tutor can serve one of them on a given night, not both.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur. A tutor living at one end of it loses most of an evening reaching the other, which is why in-home availability in Jeddah is effectively a map problem rather than a staffing one.

regions.name: Dhahran, Al Khobar and Dammam
regions.note: One school and labour market across three cities, with families routinely living in one and schooling in another. Compound timetables add their own fixed points, and the binding constraint here is almost always the calendar rather than the supply of teachers.

regions.name: Jubail and Ras Tanura
regions.note: Industrial communities with a narrow set of schools and long internal distances. A weekday evening slot after an industrial shift pattern and a school bus route is genuinely hard to place, which makes a fixed online slot unusually valuable here.

regions.name: Al Ahsa and Qatif
regions.note: Al Ahsa sits about an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster — far enough that a visiting tutor from Al Khobar is not a weekday proposition at all. Families here are usually choosing between an online specialist and nobody.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Roughly 25km apart at altitude in 'Asir, sharing one catchment and a small pool of IGCSE teachers. The realistic evening window is wide here compared with Riyadh; what is narrow is the list of people who have taught the specification.

regions.name: Tabuk, AlUla and NEOM
regions.note: Mid-term arrivals dominate. A family relocating into the north-west part-way through Year 10 needs a slot that starts immediately rather than one negotiated over a month, and the catching-up work does not wait for a tutor to become locally available.

regions.name: Madinah, Makkah, Taif and Yanbu
regions.note: Makkah is roughly 80km east of Jeddah and some families commute into the Jeddah school market, which lengthens the day at both ends. Where the school run is long, the only workable study hour is often after the evening meal.

schoolClusters.note: British, American and IB provision across the city, with several schools running Cambridge IGCSE into A Levels or the Diploma Programme. Term dates and mock timetables differ between campuses, so two students in the same district can be in different parts of the syllabus in the same week.

Long-established British, German, American and Indian international schools, with Cambridge provision common. Thuwal serves the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology campus community, which brings a steady stream of mid-year arrivals into the western school market.

The International Schools Group runs several campuses across the Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran area and in Jubail, and provision differs between them. British and Cambridge curricula are well represented, and compound life shapes the study week for a large share of these households.

best-igcse-home-tutor.modesIntro: Three shapes a weekly arrangement takes, distinguished by what they do to the calendar rather than by price. Families usually pick the first by default when the second or third fits the household better.

modes.title: One fixed slot, held for the year
modes.description: The same evening, the same time, booked against Arabia Standard Time so it does not drift when the tutor's own country changes its clocks. This is the right shape when a subject needs sustained content work, and its real value is cumulative: a slot that survives a mock season and a long holiday is worth more than one renegotiated every few weeks.

modes.title: Two short sessions instead of one long one
modes.description: Forty minutes twice a week rather than ninety once. This suits households where the window is genuinely narrow and students who stop absorbing after half an hour, and it suits subjects built on structured writing — Economics, Business Studies, English — where frequency beats duration. Rarely offered by in-home providers, because travel makes it uneconomic for them.

modes.description: Two or three sessions a week across the weeks before the June or November papers, aimed at timing, question selection and the technique marks that are available without new content. Deliberately finite: it is booked against a date the school has confirmed, and it ends when the papers do rather than rolling on.

sections.heading: Start with the window: what a Sunday-to-Thursday week actually leaves
paragraphs: The Saudi school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. That single fact reorganises everything, and most tutoring copy aimed at this market has been written for a Monday-to-Friday week and never adjusted. It means Sunday carries the weight that Monday carries elsewhere, that Thursday evening behaves like a Friday evening, and that a tutor whose own working week runs Monday to Friday is offering their Thursday to a family for whom it is the last school night.

Inside that week the usable hour is narrower than parents expect once it is counted honestly. School ends, the run home takes what traffic allows, and there is a gap for food and decompression that a teenager will take whether or not it is scheduled. In a dense Riyadh district the study window realistically opens around six and closes when concentration does, which is earlier than willpower suggests. Pushing a session to eight because that is when the tutor is free produces an hour that is paid for and not used.

A visiting tutor has to fit inside that window with travel at both ends, which is why in-home availability clusters so tightly. The tutor who can be in your district by half past five is the one who lives near it. Everybody else is offering you a time that does not exist in your household. Removing the journey does not create extra hours, but it does mean the hour you have can be matched to a person rather than the person to a journey.

The table below audits a weekday evening across four household patterns common in the Kingdom. It is worth doing this exercise honestly before shortlisting anybody, because the answer tends to eliminate most of a local shortlist and all of the scheduling arguments that follow.

sections.heading: Arabia Standard Time against a tutor's own working week
paragraphs: The Kingdom sits on Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, and does not change its clocks. That is an advantage families rarely use deliberately. A slot agreed with a tutor in a country that does observe daylight saving will drift twice a year unless it is pinned to Saudi local time rather than theirs, and the drift is the most common reason a working arrangement quietly falls apart after a few months. Fix the slot in Saudi terms once and the problem never arises.

The offsets matter for a second reason: they decide whether a 6pm Riyadh session falls in a tutor's working day or their night. A tutor in India sits two and a half hours ahead, so your early evening is their late evening, which is workable but caps how many Saudi families they can reasonably take. A tutor in the United Kingdom is two or three hours behind depending on the time of year, so your 6pm is their mid-afternoon, which is the easiest fit of all. A tutor in eastern Australia is seven or eight hours ahead, which makes the same slot the middle of their night, and no amount of goodwill makes that sustainable across a school year.

This is why asking where a tutor is based is a scheduling question rather than a credentials question. Nothing about location predicts teaching quality. What it predicts is whether the hour your household can actually use is an hour that person can teach well in, week after week, through a mock season and a run of marking. A tutor teaching at the wrong end of their own day will be reliable for a month and then start rescheduling.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the autumn break and the long summer: what happens to the slot
paragraphs: Three predictable disruptions hit a weekly arrangement each year, and a good tutor has a policy for each one before you ask. Ramadan shortens the school day and moves the household's whole rhythm: study happens later, concentration arrives at a different hour, and a 6pm slot that worked all autumn becomes the worst possible time. Ramadan also drifts roughly eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, so it lands in a different part of the academic year each time and never has a fixed relationship to a mock season.

The sensible response is to move the slot rather than suspend it, usually later in the evening, and to shorten sessions while keeping their frequency. Continuity matters more than duration at this stage of a plan. Where Ramadan falls close to the June series, the honest conversation is about what can be achieved in a compressed window and what has to be front-loaded into the weeks before, which is a reason to agree the plan early rather than improvise it.

The other two are simpler. Ministry of Education public schools run a two-semester year with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break, while international and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, so term dates differ school by school within the same city. A short break is best handled by keeping the slot and reducing intensity; a long summer break is best handled by pausing the slot explicitly, with the time held, and agreeing what the student will do with the gap. The dead-stop summer is where a year's momentum is most often lost.

None of this needs a date on a web page, and deliberately has none. Confirm your own school's published calendar, ask the examinations officer for the entry deadline in writing, and build the plan against those two documents rather than against a generic assumption about when terms run in the Kingdom.

sections.heading: The year counted backwards from the series
paragraphs: Planning forwards from today produces intentions. Planning backwards from the papers produces deadlines, and almost all the important ones belong to the school rather than to the tutor. Saudi candidates sit the June series as their main sitting, with November available for resits and November-entry candidates, so there are two fixed points in the year and everything else is negotiable around them.

The first deadline is the furthest out and the most consequential: the tier entry in subjects that are tiered. Core is graded C to G in Cambridge IGCSE, Extended A* to E, and the entry is a school decision usually taken on Year 10 evidence. It is reversible only before entries close. A family that asks about it in the autumn term of Year 11 still has room to argue the case with new evidence; a family that asks after entries close has none for that series.

The second is the entry deadline itself, which falls several months ahead of the papers. Your school's examinations officer has the exact date and will give it to you if asked. After it passes, the component list, the tier and the board are fixed for that sitting. The third and fourth are softer but no less real: the point at which content teaching has to be essentially complete, and the point at which the work becomes timing and technique rather than syllabus.

Counted this way, the plan writes itself. The table below is the sequence, with who holds each deadline, and it is worth taking to the school rather than to a tutor, because the tutor cannot move any of the dates and the school can confirm all of them.

sections.heading: What "best" can honestly mean once the logistics are settled
paragraphs: No register ranks IGCSE tutors in the Kingdom. The Ministry of Education licenses schools and the Education and Training Evaluation Commission handles school evaluation and the approval process for international accreditation bodies, but neither body rates private tutors, and any provider implying otherwise is describing something that does not exist. So the word in this search has to be converted into something checkable, or it means nothing at all.

Four things are checkable, and they are all specific. Has this person taught the exact components your child is entered for, by code, to examination? Have they applied the mark scheme to somebody else's scripts, which is a different skill from teaching the content? Can they tell you, from a marked paper, what is being lost and why, before they have taught a single lesson? And will they commit in writing to what the plan is aiming at and how many sessions it should take? A tutor who answers all four is not necessarily the finest teacher available, but the claim is at least falsifiable.

What is not checkable, and should be discounted accordingly, is a list of satisfied families with no sample or method, a star rating out of five with no source, a stated success percentage, or any statement about a grade a student will reach. Nobody can promise a grade, and the providers in this market who do are the ones to leave off the list. Ask instead what happens if the plan is not working after a month, and listen for a specific answer rather than a reassuring one.

The practical test is the free trial lesson. A specialist spends it reading evidence and forming a hypothesis; a generalist spends it establishing rapport and describing their experience. Both are pleasant hours. Only one of them tells you anything.

sections.heading: The first month: the diagnostic, the plan and the first report
paragraphs: A first session that teaches a topic has skipped a step. The useful first hour is diagnostic: the tutor reads a marked mock or a recent script before the lesson, forms a view about which component is leaking and why, then tests that view against the student with real questions from the specification. By the end they should be able to say something narrower than "the student needs to work on algebra" — something closer to "credit is being lost because the working is not written down on the non-calculator paper, and here are three questions that demonstrate it".

From that comes a plan with a shape and an end. It should name the components it is aiming at, say how many sessions it expects to need, and state what will be different and observable if it works. A plan that is simply "weekly sessions until the examination" cannot be judged, which is convenient for the provider and useless for the family. The reason to insist on this in the first month is that it is the only point at which changing direction is cheap.

The first written report should arrive inside the first few weeks and should contain four things: what the diagnostic found, what has been taught since, what the student did between sessions and how it was marked, and what the next step is. It should not contain a grade prediction, because no tutor has the evidence base for one after three hours. It should be short enough to read in two minutes and specific enough to disagree with.

Then there is the review. After roughly a month, the same paper or an equivalent one, sat under timed conditions and marked against the published scheme. Either the targeted component has moved or it has not. Both results are informative, and the second is the one that justifies changing tutor or changing approach rather than waiting another term in the hope that effort converts into marks.

sections.heading: Why the same raw mark gives different grades in different series
paragraphs: Families treat a mock percentage as a grade and are then baffled when the real result differs. The two are separated by several mechanisms, and understanding them removes most of the anxiety around mock season. A candidate's raw marks on each component are first combined according to the weightings published in the syllabus, which are not always equal; in many Cambridge IGCSE subjects the two written papers carry comparable weight, but the specification for your child's subject is the only authority on that and it is published openly.

The weighted total is then compared against grade boundaries set for that series. Boundaries move, and they move for a defensible reason: a paper that turned out harder than intended would otherwise punish a cohort for the question-setting rather than for their performance, so the boundary is adjusted to keep a grade meaning roughly the same thing across sittings. This is why a mock marked against last series' boundaries can mislead in either direction, and why a teacher saying "that is a strong six, but the boundary could move" is being accurate rather than evasive.

On top of that sits the tier. In a tiered Cambridge subject, Core is graded C to G and Extended A* to E, so two candidates with identical weighted totals on different entries receive different grades, and one of them cannot receive a top grade at all. Edexcel's 9 to 1 scale has its own structure. None of this is hidden; it is simply never explained to families, who reasonably assume a percentage converts.

The predicted grade is a fourth thing again, and the one most often misunderstood. The table separates them, because confusing any two of these four is the root of most disputes between parents, schools and tutors in the final year.

sections.heading: Coursework, practical components and the line a tutor does not cross
paragraphs: Some IGCSE subjects carry coursework or a school-assessed component, and Middle Years Programme students have a Personal Project, which places a boundary around what outside help may legitimately do. The rule is simple and absolute: a tutor teaches the skill, explains the criteria, discusses the student's own plan and gives feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor does not write, draft, redraft or complete any part of an assessed submission, and no honest provider will offer to.

This matters commercially as well as ethically, because several providers competing for this search do exactly that. A school that detects it treats it as malpractice, and the consequences land on the student rather than on the person who was paid. If a tutor's pitch includes producing coursework, that is a reason to end the conversation rather than negotiate the scope.

Inside the line there is a great deal a tutor can usefully do. They can explain what a criterion is asking for in plain language, which schools often assume students already understand. They can look at a draft the student wrote and point to where the evidence is thin without supplying the evidence. They can teach the experimental reasoning that practical components assess, using described methods and other people's data, which is screen work and loses nothing in an online lesson. They can set up a record of what was discussed, so there is a trail showing the work is the student's.

The practical component deserves one more note, because families assume it cannot be supported remotely. The assessment does not ask a candidate to handle apparatus in the examination; it asks them to interpret a described set-up, read a scale from a diagram, process results, plot and criticise. Working through twenty flawed described methods with somebody who has marked those papers is among the most efficient things a tutor can do, and it happens as well over video as in a room.

sections.heading: When it is not working: how to tell, and what to change
paragraphs: Tuition that is not working rarely announces itself. The sessions happen, the student is polite, the tutor is pleasant, and nothing moves. Because the cost is spread weekly, families carry an arrangement for two terms that a month would have condemned. The defence against this is set up at the start: a plan that named a component, a session count and an observable change, plus a review booked against it.

There are three distinct failure modes and they need different responses. The first is a wrong match — the tutor is competent but does not have the specification, or the personalities do not work. Change the tutor; this is a routine request rather than a complaint, and asking for it early is cheaper than enduring it. The second is a wrong diagnosis: the plan is being executed well against the wrong problem. Re-diagnose from a fresh marked paper rather than persisting. The third is a wrong instrument — weekly teaching bought when the problem was one component, or a short block bought when a term of content was missing.

The fourth possibility is that nothing is wrong except the timetable. A student with four evenings of homework and a fifth taken by a session is not failing to learn; they are out of hours. The right answer there is sometimes to drop the subject back to one session a fortnight, or to stop until a holiday, which is a conversation a good tutor will raise before a parent does. A provider that only ever recommends more hours is telling you something about its business model.

Whatever the cause, the decision should be made against written evidence rather than impressions. That is the whole reason to insist on a diagnostic note, a plan with a session count, and a short report after each session: three documents that together make it possible to say, after a month, that this is working, or that it is not.

process.title: Audit the window before shortlisting anybody
process.description: Write down when the school run actually ends, when the household eats, and when your child stops being able to concentrate. That gives you a real window rather than an aspirational one, and it eliminates most scheduling arguments before they start. Tell us the window first; it narrows the tutor list more usefully than the subject does.

process.title: Get the entry facts from the school in writing
process.description: Which board, which tier, which component codes, and the entry deadline for the series. The examinations officer holds all four and will confirm them on request. These decide what a tutor can and cannot change, and they are the facts most families discover too late to act on.

process.title: Use the free trial lesson as a diagnostic
process.description: Send a marked mock or a recent script beforehand. The tutor reads it, forms a view about which component is losing marks and why, tests that view with real questions, and tells you the plan they would propose. You are assessing their reasoning, not their manner.

process.title: Fix the slot in Saudi local time
process.description: The session is booked against Arabia Standard Time, inside the Sunday-to-Thursday week, so it holds when the tutor's own country changes its clocks. Agree the Ramadan arrangement and the long-holiday arrangement at the same time, rather than when they arrive.

process.title: Review against the diagnostic after a month
process.description: The same paper, or an equivalent, sat to time and marked against the published scheme. Either the component has moved or it has not. A plan that is not working gets changed or stopped, and changing tutor at this point is an ordinary request rather than a complaint.

whyPoints.title: The slot is pinned to your clock, not the tutor's
whyPoints.description: Sessions are booked in Arabia Standard Time, which does not change all year, so the arrangement survives a tutor's own daylight-saving shift twice over. A fixed slot inside the Sunday-to-Thursday week is the single strongest predictor of whether a weekly plan is still running in the spring term.

whyPoints.title: Travel is not inside the hour you pay for
whyPoints.description: An in-home arrangement prices a journey into the evening at both ends, which is why visiting availability clusters around whoever lives nearby. Live video removes the journey, so the hour is teaching and the shortlist is drawn from people who have taught your child's components rather than from people who can reach your district.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before a plan, and a plan you can judge
whyPoints.description: The first session is diagnostic and produces a written note. The plan that follows names the components it targets, the number of sessions it expects to need, and what will be observably different if it works. A plan with no end point cannot be assessed, which suits a provider and not a family.

whyPoints.title: Nothing assessed is ever produced for a student
whyPoints.description: A tutor explains criteria, discusses the student's own plan and gives feedback on work the student has written. No tutor will draft, redraft or complete coursework, a Personal Project or any school-assessed component. A school that detects that treats it as malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student.

whyPoints.title: Claims that can be checked, and none that cannot
whyPoints.description: No success percentages, no ratings out of five, no tutor headcounts, no statements about the grade a student will achieve. What you are told is which components a tutor has taught or marked, what the trial lesson found, and what the review after a month showed.

faqs.question: How late can an IGCSE session start if the school run in a dense Riyadh district finishes after five?
faqs.answer: Later than most providers offer, and that is usually the deciding factor. Where the run home ends after five, the realistic window opens around seven once the household has eaten, and a session starting then needs to finish before concentration goes rather than before the tutor's day does. Online slots can run into the late evening because nobody has to drive home afterwards, and a tutor several hours behind Saudi time is in the middle of their working afternoon at that point. What does not work is pushing a session later than the student can genuinely use, which is an hour paid for and wasted.

faqs.question: What happens to a weekly IGCSE slot when the tutor's own country puts its clocks forward?
faqs.answer: Nothing, if the slot was booked against Arabia Standard Time in the first place. The Kingdom does not change its clocks, so a session fixed at 6pm Saudi time stays at 6pm Saudi time all year; what moves is the tutor's local time, which becomes their problem to absorb rather than yours. Arrangements that quietly collapse after a few months are usually ones agreed in the tutor's time zone, where the hour drifts twice a year and each drift triggers a renegotiation. Ask explicitly which clock the booking is held in before the first session, because changing it later means renegotiating the whole week.

faqs.question: Do IGCSE lessons run on a Friday or a Saturday in the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: They can, and for some households the weekend is the only place a long session fits. Friday and Saturday are the Saudi weekend, so a two-hour block on a Saturday morning is often easier than two weekday evenings, particularly for a student in Year 11 carrying several subjects. The trade-off is retention: one long weekend session spaced seven days from the next is less effective for technique work than two shorter ones in the week, because the gap between practice and feedback is longer. Where the weekday window genuinely does not exist, a weekend slot is better than no slot, and worth structuring differently.

faqs.question: How do shortened school days during Ramadan change an IGCSE lesson plan?
faqs.answer: The school day shortens, the household rhythm moves later, and the hour that worked all autumn becomes the wrong hour. The sensible adjustment is to keep the frequency and move the time, usually to later in the evening, while shortening each session. Continuity matters more than duration at this point in a plan. Because Ramadan drifts roughly eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, it lands in a different part of the academic year each time and has no fixed relationship to mock season, so the arrangement is worth agreeing in advance rather than improvising. Where it falls near a series, front-load the content work into the weeks before.

faqs.question: What happens to the regular slot during the long summer break between Year 10 and Year 11?
faqs.answer: The honest options are to pause the slot with the time held, or to use the break deliberately for one narrow thing. A dead stop is where a year's momentum is most often lost, particularly in Mathematics, where algebraic fluency decays quickly without use. A short block of six to eight sessions on a single named weakness is usually better value than light revision across four subjects, and it is the cheapest point in the year to buy teaching because nothing is urgent. Agree before the break which of the two you are doing, because an unspecified pause tends to become a quiet end.

faqs.question: Can a Year 11 student take two IGCSE subjects in one evening without losing the second hour?
faqs.answer: Rarely well. Two consecutive hours of one-to-one teaching asks for sustained output, not passive attention, and most students are noticeably weaker in the second. Where both subjects genuinely need weekly support, splitting them across two evenings works better even if each session is shorter. If one evening is the only option, the better structure is a full session on the harder subject followed by a short, tightly defined block on the other — marking review, a timed question, feedback — rather than two full sessions. Two siblings sharing an evening is a different matter and is usually straightforward.

faqs.question: How much notice is needed to move a fixed IGCSE slot to a different evening?
faqs.answer: A single session can usually be rescheduled at short notice for a school trip, an internal examination or an illness, and that should be treated as routine rather than exceptional. Moving the regular slot permanently is harder, because the tutor has built their week around it and the new time may already be held by another family. A week or two of notice is a reasonable expectation. Ask about this before booking rather than after: a provider with no stated policy will improvise one in the moment, and the improvisation generally favours the provider.

faqs.question: What does the diagnostic in the first IGCSE session actually test?
faqs.answer: Not knowledge in general. A good diagnostic starts from evidence the tutor has already read — a marked mock, a recent script, a report — and tests a specific hypothesis about where credit is being lost. That means a handful of questions from the actual specification, chosen because they discriminate: one that separates recall from application, one that exposes whether working is written down, one that checks whether a command term is being read. The output is a narrow statement about a component rather than a general assessment of ability, and it should be written down so it can be tested again a month later.

faqs.question: What should the first written report from an IGCSE tutor contain?
faqs.answer: Four things, and ideally nothing else. What the diagnostic found, stated specifically enough to be wrong. What has been taught since. What the student produced between sessions and how it was marked. What the next step is and why. It should be readable in two minutes and specific enough that a parent could disagree with it. What it should not contain is a predicted grade, because no tutor has the evidence base for one after a few hours, and a confident forecast early on is a sales document rather than an assessment.

faqs.question: How soon after starting should a parent expect to see movement in an IGCSE subject?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on whether the problem is technique or content, which is why the diagnostic matters so much. Technique problems — command terms misread, working not written down, time mismanaged in a paper — can move measurably within four to six sessions, because the student already knows the material. Content gaps move on the timescale of consolidation, which is a term rather than a month, and no amount of teaching quality compresses that much. A tutor who promises visible movement in a fortnight on a content problem is describing a sales timeline rather than a learning one.

faqs.question: What happens if the first IGCSE tutor is the wrong match after two sessions?
faqs.answer: You ask for a different one, and it should be an ordinary request rather than a complaint. Mismatches happen for reasons that have nothing to do with competence: the tutor knows the subject but not the board, the explanation style does not land, the student will not speak. All three are visible within two or three sessions and none improves with patience. The useful thing to do alongside changing tutor is to say what specifically did not work, because that sharpens the next match. Enduring a poor fit for a term is the single most expensive mistake available in this market.

faqs.question: How do we decide whether to continue IGCSE tuition after one term?
faqs.answer: Against the plan agreed at the start, not against a feeling. If the plan named a component, a session count and an observable change, a term is more than enough evidence either way. Re-sit the same paper or an equivalent under timed conditions and have it marked against the published scheme. If the targeted component has moved, continue with the next target. If it has not and the diagnosis still looks right, change the approach. If it has not and the diagnosis looks wrong, re-diagnose. Continuing by inertia, with no measurement, is how families pay for a year of nothing.

faqs.question: What should a parent be doing between IGCSE sessions, if anything?
faqs.answer: Protecting the time and nothing else, in most cases. The highest-value parental contribution is making sure the set work happens before the next session, because a plan built on marked written work collapses when there is nothing to mark. Beyond that, resist the urge to teach: a parent re-explaining a method differently from the tutor is a common source of confusion, particularly in Mathematics, where notation and method marks matter. If you want a role, ask your child to explain one thing they learned each week. Being unable to explain it is useful information for the tutor.

faqs.question: Why does the same raw mark give different IGCSE grades in different series?
faqs.answer: Because the mark is converted twice before it becomes a grade. First, component marks are combined using the weightings published in the syllabus, which are not always equal between papers. Then the weighted total is compared against grade boundaries set for that specific series. Boundaries move so that a grade means roughly the same thing across sittings: if a paper turned out more demanding than intended, the boundary falls rather than the cohort being penalised for the question-setting. This is why a mock marked against an older boundary can mislead in either direction, and why a teacher who hedges about a borderline grade is being accurate.

faqs.question: Who decides an IGCSE predicted grade, and what is it based on?
faqs.answer: The school does, usually the subject teacher, drawing on classwork, mock performance and professional judgement about trajectory. It is not a board product and it is not a forecast a tutor can issue. Its purpose is to support an application to the next stage — a sixth form, a Diploma Programme place, a university — and it is explicitly not a promise about the result. Where a family disagrees with a prediction, the productive route is evidence: a timed paper marked against the published scheme, shared with the school, rather than an argument about effort. A tutor's job there is to produce the evidence, not to issue a competing number.

faqs.question: How much of an IGCSE grade can be decided by components other than the written papers?
faqs.answer: It varies by subject and by board, and the syllabus for your child's subject is the only authority on it. Some subjects are entirely examined by written papers; others carry coursework or a school-assessed component that is internally marked and then moderated by the board, which means the school's marking is checked against the board's standard rather than taken at face value. The practical question for a family is which components make up the specific entry the school has made, and that is a one-line answer from the examinations officer. Plan around the actual component list rather than a general assumption about the subject.

best-igcse-home-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for the best IGCSE home tutor in Saudi Arabia, do two things before you shortlist anyone. Write down the hour your household genuinely has free on a school night, and ask the school in writing for the board, the tier, the component codes and the entry deadline. Those five facts eliminate most of the decisions people agonise over. Then send them to us with a marked paper if you have one, and the free trial lesson will test a specific idea about what is going wrong. intro.heading: There is no best IGCSE tutor, only the right one for this term
paragraphs: No register ranks IGCSE tutors, in the Kingdom or anywhere else. There is no league table, no scoring body and nothing a provider can point at to justify the word, which is why every page that claims the title is marking its own work. The search still means something concrete, though. A parent typing it is saying: I do not want to make this decision twice, and I would like the person who is right for this child, this subject and this term, at the first attempt.

The practical substitute for a ranking is a fit test, and fit turns out to be mostly a question of timing. A Year 9 student who has not yet chosen subjects needs something different from a Year 11 Extended candidate reading a disappointing mock paper. The same tutor can be the obvious choice for one and the wrong purchase for the other, and no amount of experience changes that. So this page is laid out as a calendar rather than a list of virtues: the honest answer to best depends on where in the two-year course you are standing when you ask.

The other half of the answer is money, because value and price are different questions. Advertised rates in this market run from around SAR 35 an hour on budget platforms to SAR 200 and above for senior examination subjects, and the distance between those figures is not teaching ability alone. Subject scarcity, marking experience, the level being taught and whether anybody has to drive across a city all move it. A page that names the best without explaining what moves the price has answered the easy half of the question.

Lessons at IB Gram are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. We do not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. The gain is not only the travel that comes out of the fee. It is that a family in Madinah or Khamis Mushait can reach an Additional Mathematics specialist at all, instead of choosing between the two people in the city who teach any mathematics at senior level. The rest of this page works forward through the course and puts numbers against each stage.

One caveat before the detail. Everything below assumes the school's own teaching is sound and the gap is in practice, feedback and technique, which is the usual case. Where a subject is being taught by a non-specialist, or a school cannot staff a set at Extended level at all, outside teaching is doing a different job and needs more hours than this page implies. Ask the school directly who teaches the senior set and how long they have taught that specification. The answer changes what you should be buying, and schools answer it readily when asked plainly.

sections.heading: What a search for the best IGCSE online tutor is trying to buy
paragraphs: Nothing ranks IGCSE tutors. No register exists, no body scores them against each other, and no provider can point to an external measure that would justify the word, so a claim to be best is self-issued by definition. That does not make the search irrational. It makes it a request for a shortcut past a decision the parent has no way to audit from the outside.

The substitute worth having is a test you can run yourself, in one hour, before money changes hands. Ask for the syllabus code and the tier. Ask which paper the student is weakest on and how the tutor knows. Ask what the first hour would contain. A tutor who answers those three with specifics has demonstrated more than any badge, and a tutor who answers them with reassurance has also told you something.

The second thing the search is buying is protection against buying twice. Families who change tutor in the spring term of Year 11 have usually lost a term, not an hour, and that is the real cost of a poor first choice. Getting it right early is worth paying a little more for, which is a different claim from paying more being better. One more thing is worth saying about the word itself: the tutor who suits an organised student stuck on one topic is rarely the person who suits a capable student who has stopped working, and a provider that treats those two as one problem will solve neither of them.

sections.heading: Where your child is in the IGCSE year, and what that does to the value of an hour
paragraphs: Work forward rather than backwards. An IGCSE course runs two years, and the same hour of teaching does a different amount of work depending on which term it lands in. In the autumn of Year 10, an hour spent on algebraic fluency changes every mark the student will later earn in Mathematics and in the sciences. In the final weeks of Year 11 the same hour can only redistribute marks that are already nearly within reach.

This is not an argument for starting early whatever the cost. It is an argument for buying the right thing at each stage. Early hours should track the school's teaching and close gaps in the week they appear, because a topic half-understood in Year 10 is the one that collapses under timed conditions a year later. Later hours belong almost entirely to technique: command terms, timed questions, mark schemes, and the two or three topics a mock has exposed as weak.

The table sets the stages out in order. Read the right-hand column as the thing to raise with a prospective tutor, because anyone who proposes the same programme to a Year 9 student and to a Year 11 candidate eight weeks from the papers has not looked at the calendar. Where a school runs three terms rather than two semesters, the stages shift by a few weeks and the order stays the same. Take the stage from the student's position in the course rather than from the month.
