buraidah.programmesIntro: Four programmes cover the Al-Qassim enquiries. They are described here by what each one actually assesses, because that is the detail a family needs when the school down the road runs something else and nobody in the building can explain how the grade is produced.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: There is no external assessment in the Primary Years Programme, so nothing is reported as a grade and nothing is moderated. What exists instead is a set of learning expectations and a portfolio of the child's own work. The output that matters is written fluency in English, number sense and the willingness to explain reasoning rather than produce an answer, because every later qualification pays for the explanation.
programmes.countryNote: Primary enquiries from Al-Qassim are usually from families planning several years ahead, often because an older sibling is already on an international route or a relocation is expected. The sensible early work is English reading volume and written explanation, both of which transfer into any later curriculum and neither of which requires choosing one yet.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessment runs on four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight against published descriptors, converted at the end into a subject grade. Some schools add external eAssessment in the final year. The Personal Project is a long independent piece with its own criteria. Because marking is descriptor-based rather than mark-per-question, a student can hold the content and still sit in a middle band for two years.
programmes.countryNote: An MYP tutor in Al-Qassim is most often engaged by a family whose child is enrolled with a school elsewhere or online, and who therefore has criteria to satisfy but no classroom to calibrate against. Reading two or three of the student's own marked tasks against the descriptors shows within an hour whether the gap is knowledge or presentation.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: A papers-based qualification, one grade per subject, taken a subject at a time. Cambridge runs Core and Extended tiers on many syllabuses, with different grade ceilings and overlapping content. The sciences carry either a practical test or an alternative-to-practical written paper, and which one a candidate sits is set by the entry rather than by the student. Some Edexcel syllabuses offer a coursework route and a papers-only route.
programmes.countryNote: This is the bulk of the work in Al-Qassim. A Cambridge IGCSE tutor in Buraidah is frequently teaching the entire syllabus, setting the mock papers and tracking the entry window, because the student is attached to a centre rather than to a department. Candidates here enter the June series or the November series, which gives a Year 11 student two realistic windows.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, each graded one to seven, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. The Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay grades combine in a published matrix worth up to three further points, so the ceiling is forty-five. Every subject has an internally assessed component, and the Diploma is awarded against a published pass requirement rather than a simple total.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma enquiries from this province are either from families whose child boards or commutes to a school in Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province, or from families who have relocated inward mid-course. An IB Diploma tutor in Buraidah is usually asked for one or two Higher Level subjects plus Extended Essay guidance, with the school holding the core process.

buraidah.subjectsIntro: These Diploma subjects are described by what a university does with them, because that is the lens Al-Qassim families use. A subject choice made in the first year of the Diploma decides which degree applications are open two years later, and in a province with no local Diploma cohort there is nobody in the corridor to point that out.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The course engineering, physics, computer science and most economics degrees expect, with several departments naming the Higher Level version outright. It is algebra-led, with proof and calculus extensions at Higher Level that have no Standard Level equivalent. It also carries the heaviest overlap with the mathematics section of Tahsili, which makes it the most efficient subject to be strong in for a student applying inside the Kingdom.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology-led problem solving, accepted widely for business, social science, design and health-related degrees, and declined by some quantitative engineering departments at Standard Level. It is not an easier course, only a differently weighted one. Students pick it to avoid pure algebra and then find the marks sit in written interpretation of a result rather than in the calculation itself.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: A named prerequisite for most engineering and physical-science degrees, frequently at Higher Level. Its content overlaps substantially with the physics section of Tahsili, though the question style does not. The internally assessed investigation needs equipment or a defensible data source, which is a real planning problem for a student not attached to a school laboratory and is best solved in the first weeks rather than the last.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Required for medicine, pharmacy, chemical engineering and most life-science degrees, usually at Higher Level. Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms account for most of the lost marks; the data booklet is permitted and routinely underused. Like Physics, it overlaps with a Tahsili section, so a student preparing for both can plan one body of content rather than two.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Expected for medicine, dentistry, biomedical science and agricultural science, which matters in a province built on agriculture. Definitions are examined strictly, and the command terms distinguish, outline, explain and discuss each demand a different structure that the mark scheme pays for. The statistical content surprises students who chose the subject to avoid mathematics.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: A language-acquisition course, not a literature one, assessed on reading, listening, writing and a spoken component. For students in Al-Qassim schooled partly in Arabic it is often the correct choice over English A, and the decision is worth getting right in the first term because the two courses are examined quite differently and a late move costs ground.

subjects.name: Arabic A
subjects.description: A literature or language-and-literature course for fluent speakers, examined on a literary register that conversational fluency does not supply. It is frequently the strongest subject on a Diploma transcript for a student from this province, and it is also the one where families most often underestimate the written analysis demand until the first marked essay comes back.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study driven, with a prescribed stimulus for one paper and an internally assessed project. Accepted for business and management degrees everywhere and treated as a social science rather than a quantitative subject by most admissions offices. Marks are lost by answering with general theory where the question named a specific firm in the material.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Assessed on written papers plus fieldwork, with the Higher Level extension adding global interactions. The fieldwork requirement needs a site and a method, which is manageable in Al-Qassim with planning and awkward without it. Useful for environmental science, planning and development degrees, and a strong complement to Economics.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams carry marks for axes, labels and the shift itself, and incomplete diagrams are the commonest loss on the paper. The Higher Level extension questions add quantitative work that Standard Level candidates never see. Several economics degrees ask for Higher Level mathematics alongside it, so the two choices should be made together rather than separately.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Research methods, studies and evaluation, with an internally assessed experimental study. It is a popular choice and a frequently misjudged one: the marks come from critical evaluation of evidence, not from recalling studies. Admissions treatment varies widely, so check whether a target degree counts it as a science before it occupies a Higher Level slot.

buraidah.igcseSubjectsIntro: IGCSE is where most Al-Qassim work sits, and the syllabus code decides the paper structure, so it is given here alongside each subject. A tutor who does not know the code does not know how many papers the candidate sits or whether a practical test is involved, and that is not a detail a family can afford to discover late.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (0580)
igcseSubjects.description: The tier decision caps the grade before any revision starts, and for a candidate attached to a centre rather than a school it is a decision the family effectively makes. Extended is the route into Diploma mathematics and into A Level, and a student who can cope with it should be entered for it even if the first mock is uncomfortable.

igcseSubjects.name: Additional Mathematics (0606)
igcseSubjects.description: Taken alongside Extended mathematics by students heading for a mathematics-heavy sixth form. It introduces calculus and formal algebra a year early and is the single best bridge into Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, which makes it unusually valuable for a student with no Diploma class to ease them in.

igcseSubjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (0654)
igcseSubjects.description: Biology, chemistry and physics in a double award rather than three separate qualifications, with fewer papers and less total content. For a candidate teaching themselves the sciences with one tutor it is often the realistic entry, and it is accepted for most sixth-form science routes, though a few expect the separate sciences instead.

igcseSubjects.name: First Language English (0500)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and directed writing at native-speaker level, with a composition component. Students who read widely in English still lose marks here by analysing content and ignoring the writer's method. It is the stronger qualification to hold for later study, and the wrong one to be entered for if the reading demand is genuinely out of reach.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language (0510 and 0511)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading, writing and listening, with the summary question functioning as a technique rather than a comprehension exercise. Many Al-Qassim candidates sit this rather than First Language English, and the two are worth comparing honestly with a diagnostic reading task before the entry is made rather than after a disappointing result.

igcseSubjects.name: Information and Communication Technology (0417)
igcseSubjects.description: A written paper plus two practical tests on documents, data handling and website authoring, using specific software skills that are examined precisely. It rewards drilled practice more than understanding, which makes it a reliable grade for a disciplined private candidate and a poor one for a student who prepares by reading.

igcseSubjects.name: Geography (0460)
igcseSubjects.description: Written papers plus a geographical skills paper, with case studies the candidate must supply themselves. A student without a class has no shared set of examples, so building a personal case-study file from the first month is the whole difference between a middle grade and a strong one here.

igcseSubjects.name: Accounting (0452)
igcseSubjects.description: Double-entry bookkeeping, financial statements and interpretation, examined on structured questions with no essay writing. It suits a private candidate well because the content is bounded and self-checkable: a trial balance either balances or it does not, and practice on past papers gives immediate feedback without a teacher.

igcseSubjects.name: Arabic First Language (0508)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and writing at native-speaker level in Arabic, and for most students in this province the most secure grade on the certificate. It is examined on structured response and composition rather than on literary criticism, so the preparation is different from Arabic A in the Diploma and should not be assumed to transfer.

buraidah.regionsTitle: Al-Qassim towns we teach into, and what distance actually changes
buraidah.regionsIntro: Distance is the organising fact in this province, not traffic. The towns below sit between twenty minutes and two hours from central Buraidah, and for an international-curriculum student the practical effect is the same everywhere: the nearest person who teaches the syllabus is not within driving range, so the lesson arrives over a connection instead.

regions.name: Central Buraidah
regions.note: The provincial capital and the administrative centre for Al-Qassim, with the widest local choice of private schooling and almost none of it international. Families here have the best access to centres and services in the province and still look outside it for syllabus teaching, which is the whole shape of the local market.

regions.name: Al Mulaida and the Qassim University side
regions.note: The university quarter southwest of the city. A noticeable share of enquiries come from academic households here, often bilingual, often planning an overseas application. These are the families most likely to ask about the Diploma core and about how points map onto an offer abroad rather than about weekly homework.

regions.name: Unaizah
regions.note: The province's second city, roughly half an hour south of Buraidah, with its own long-established schools and a strong commercial base. Students here are typically attached to a centre or an online school for an international curriculum, and the scheduling question is the evening, not the journey.

regions.name: Ar Rass
regions.note: West of Unaizah, further from the provincial centre and from any international cohort. A student working towards IGCSE here is almost always doing so without classmates in the subject, which changes what a tutor has to supply: calibration against other candidates, not just teaching.

regions.name: Al Bukayriyah
regions.note: A sizeable town northwest of Buraidah on the agricultural belt. Families here weigh an international curriculum against a daily commute into the city, and the online route often wins on the arithmetic of the week rather than on any educational preference.

regions.name: Al Mithnab
regions.note: East of Buraidah towards the Riyadh road, far enough that a city-centre evening class is not a weekly proposition. Enquiries tend to be whole-subject rather than top-up, because there is no local class to top up in the first place.

regions.name: Riyadh Al Khabra
regions.note: North of Buraidah, smaller and quieter, with a correspondingly thin local market for anything beyond the national curriculum. A reliable connection and a fixed weekly hour do more for a candidate here than any amount of published material.

regions.name: Uyun Al Jiwa and Al Badayea
regions.note: Towns on the western side of the province, both well outside any reasonable evening commute to Buraidah. For a Diploma or IGCSE student in either, the tutor's time zone matters far more than the tutor's address, which is why slots are agreed on Arabia Standard Time and left there.

schoolClusters.city: Riyadh, where most Al-Qassim boarders and commuters go
schoolClusters.note: The nearest concentration of IB World Schools and Cambridge centres to Al-Qassim sits in the capital, a long road journey southeast. Families who want their child in a Diploma cohort rather than studying it remotely usually end up looking at this list, and weekly boarding or a relocation is the real decision behind it.

The second place Al-Qassim families look, usually when a parent's work takes the household west rather than south. The mix is broader here, with British, IB, American, German and Indian curricula all represented in one city, which makes a mid-course transfer easier to arrange than it is from this province.

buraidah.schoolDisclaimer: These schools are listed purely as context for families comparing options; IB Gram is not connected to any of them and claims no relationship with any school or school group.
buraidah.modesIntro: Support in Al-Qassim divides differently from support in a city with international schools, because more of the teaching load sits outside the classroom. These four patterns cover almost every arrangement, and all of them run live online, one-to-one, on Arabia Standard Time.

modes.title: Whole-syllabus teaching, one subject at a time
modes.description: For a candidate whose school does not run the course at all. The tutor owns the sequence from the first topic to the last, sets interim tests, and keeps a written map of what has been covered against the published syllabus content list. This is slower per topic and cheaper per grade than discovering six months of gaps in the final term.
bullets: A written coverage map against the syllabus content list, updated every month
Interim tests on past-paper questions rather than textbook exercises
Two sessions a week is the usual minimum for a full subject
Mock papers set and marked at the points a school would set them

modes.title: Private-candidate preparation
modes.description: Built around the fact that nobody in the household has done this before. The tutor works to the entry window, the paper combination and the practical route the centre has chosen, and flags what the family must confirm with the centre rather than guessing on their behalf. Private candidate IGCSE entry has administrative edges, and most of the avoidable damage happens there.
bullets: Preparation matched to the exact paper combination on the entry
Clear separation of what the tutor handles and what the centre must confirm
Practical or alternative-to-practical work planned from the first month
A checklist of entry deadlines to take to the centre, not from us

modes.title: Qudurat and Tahsili technique sessions
modes.description: Separate from syllabus teaching, because the tests are different animals. Qudurat rewards practised reasoning under time pressure; Tahsili rewards recognising national-curriculum framing of content the student already knows. Sessions work on question types, pacing and answer format. No score threshold is quoted here, because thresholds differ by university and by programme and belong to the universities.
bullets: Question-type drilling rather than content reteaching
Pacing practice under the real time allowance
Mapping what the student has studied against each Tahsili section
Admission criteria read off the university's own published pages

modes.title: Extended Essay and Internal Assessment feedback
modes.description: Short runs of sessions attached to one piece of assessed work. The tutor reads the student's own draft against the published criteria and returns questions, not corrections. Every change is made by the student. Where a school supervisor exists, their process and their deadlines take precedence over anything agreed here.
bullets: Criterion-by-criterion feedback in the criteria's own language
Research-question and method problems caught in the first fortnight
Referencing taught as a skill before the draft, not patched after it
Nothing written, redrafted or filled in on the student's behalf

sections.heading: What each qualification is actually made of
paragraphs: Begin with the machine that produces the grade. A Cambridge IGCSE subject grade comes from two or three written papers, plus a practical test or an alternative-to-practical paper in the sciences, all marked by the board from scripts sent out of the centre. There is no teacher judgement in the result and, on most syllabuses, no coursework. The tier the candidate was entered for sets the highest grade reachable, which means the entry decision is part of the result and is made months before the papers.

A Diploma subject grade is built differently. Written papers are marked externally, and an internally assessed component, the investigation, exploration, project or oral depending on the subject, is marked by the school and then moderated by the board across the whole cohort. On top of the six subjects sits the core: a Theory of Knowledge exhibition and essay, plus the Extended Essay, whose two grades combine in a published matrix worth up to three points. The ceiling is forty-five, and the Diploma is awarded against a published pass requirement rather than a simple total.

The Middle Years Programme is a third machine again, and the one families understand least. Each subject is marked against four criteria, out of eight apiece, using descriptors rather than marks per question, with some schools adding external eAssessment at the end. A student can hold every fact in the course and sit in the middle band for two years because their answers never addressed the criterion in front of them. Knowing which machine you are feeding is the difference between useful revision and busy revision, and it is the reason this page starts here rather than with a tutor list.

sections.heading: Studying a curriculum the schools around you do not teach
paragraphs: Al-Qassim's private-school sector is almost entirely national curriculum. That is a statement about supply, and it reflects what the overwhelming majority of families in the province want, which the national system provides. It does create a specific position for the minority working towards IGCSE or the Diploma: the student holds an international syllabus without the department, the mock calendar, the laboratory and the internal deadlines that normally come attached to one.

Families solve it in three ways, and the three have different consequences. Some enrol with a school elsewhere in the Kingdom and board or relocate, which buys the full apparatus at the price of the household arrangement. Some enrol with an online or distance school, which supplies the enrolment, the reporting and some teaching, with the depth varying a great deal between providers. Some register the student as a private candidate with a centre that accepts external entries, which is the cheapest route and the one that puts the most work on the family.

The third route is where one-to-one online tuition in Buraidah does the most. A private candidate has nobody setting interim deadlines, nobody marking a mock in January, and no classmates against whom to judge whether an answer is strong. A tutor in that position is supplying three things rather than one: the teaching, the calibration, and the calendar. Ask any prospective tutor how they would handle all three, and treat a vague answer about covering the syllabus as the warning it is.
bullets: Confirm with the centre which paper combination and practical route the entry covers
Ask who is setting mock papers, and when, before the final year begins
Get the syllabus content list and tick it off monthly; memory is not a coverage record
Find out early whether the centre accepts external candidates for every subject you need

sections.heading: The route from Buraidah into a Saudi university
paragraphs: This is the part of the picture that decides what the qualification was for, and it is almost entirely absent from the tutoring pages that rank for these searches. A foreign or international school certificate is not automatically treated as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. Ministry of Education equivalency, the mu'adalah decision, is what establishes that equivalence, and it applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. Families in this province meet it late far more often than early.

Alongside it sit the two Qiyas tests. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the National Center for Assessment within the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, and it examines verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than taught content, in Arabic or in English. Tahsili, the achievement test, covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum. For an international-curriculum student that last point is the whole story: the material is largely familiar and the framing is not.

Universities then publish their own admission criteria, combining the school result with the Qiyas outcomes, and the weightings differ by university and by programme. Competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili. No tutor and no tutoring site should be quoting you a required score, because the figure changes by institution, by programme and by cycle; the only trustworthy source is the university's own published criteria. Some universities also state a maximum age for the secondary certificate they will accept, which quietly rules out a long gap between school and application.

sections.heading: Applying abroad from Al-Qassim, and what changes
paragraphs: An overseas application runs on a different clock and asks for different things. Most systems want a predicted Diploma total or predicted IGCSE and A Level grades, specified grades in named Higher Level subjects, and evidence of English language competence. Some add an admissions test, a written statement or an interview. The deadlines usually fall in the first term of the final school year, which is earlier than families expect and earlier than the Saudi route requires.

Subject prerequisites are where applications from this province most often fall over, because there is no sixth-form counsellor across the corridor to catch it. A degree that asks for Higher Level Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches will not accept Standard Level Applications and Interpretation, and the student making that choice in the first Diploma year rarely knows it yet. The fix is boring and effective: write down the published entry requirements for six target courses before subject choices are locked, and keep the list.

Predicted grades deserve particular attention for a student not attached to a conventional school cohort. A prediction is the school's professional judgement built on mocks and marked work, and a school with little evidence will predict cautiously. That is not unfairness; it is the absence of evidence. A tutor cannot award or raise a prediction, and nobody can promise a place at any university. What a tutor can do is make sure strong marked work exists before the prediction is finalised, which is a question of timing rather than persuasion.

sections.heading: What this costs in the Kingdom, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Rates advertised in this market cover a wide span, and the span is informative once you know what sits behind each end of it. Tutoring platforms list general online tutoring from around SAR 55 an hour, and budget IGCSE platforms advertise one-to-one from around SAR 35. Tutor-marketplace guides put general private tuition in Saudi cities at about SAR 50 for primary and SAR 200 and above for senior-school examined subjects. Tutoring companies advertise IB subject tutoring from around SAR 180, with Higher Level and premium tracks quoted nearer SAR 200 to 220. Some international providers quote in dollars instead.

Every one of those figures is published by a provider as a marketing rate. None is a measured market average, and none is IB Gram's price, which we quote directly when you ask. What is genuinely useful in the spread is the ordering of what moves it. Subject scarcity comes first: a Higher Level Physics or Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches specialist is dearer than a Standard Level mathematics tutor in every market on earth. Then marking or examiner experience. Then level, with Higher Level above Standard Level above Middle Years Programme above IGCSE. Then whether the tutor travels. Then package length.

For Al-Qassim there is a sixth factor that families here should price in deliberately. Teaching a whole syllabus is not the same purchase as supporting a taught class, and it is not comparable on an hourly basis. Two sessions a week across a full course is a different commitment from one session a week topping up a school's teaching, and a quote that looks expensive per hour may be cheaper per grade. Ask what the tutor is actually carrying before comparing two numbers.

sections.heading: When to start, counted by year group rather than by term
paragraphs: For a student without a local class, the start date does more work than the choice of tutor. In Year 9 the task is settling the subject list and the tier intentions, because an IGCSE subject not started is simply not available later in the same window. In Year 10 the task is coverage, at a pace that leaves the final year free for papers. In Year 11 it is papers, mock discipline and the practical component, which cannot be improvised in the last month.

The Diploma has its own shape. The first autumn term decides whether the Higher Level choices were right, and that is still a cheap decision to revisit. The first spring is the Internal Assessment across six subjects at once, which is an organisational problem more than an academic one. The following autumn is predicted grades and applications. The final eight weeks are papers and command terms. A student who starts outside support in the final spring gets technique and little else, and should be told so rather than sold two years of catching up.

There is one window families in Al-Qassim underuse badly: the long summer before the first Diploma year, or before Year 10. For a student with no local cohort, those weeks are the only time the whole week is available, and the right use of them is narrow. Algebra fluency for mathematics and the sciences, written explanation in English, and the habit of reading a mark allocation and answering to it. That is three things, not a syllabus, and it is worth more than the same hours spent in term time.
bullets: Year 9: lock the subject list and the tier intention; an unstarted subject is unavailable later
Year 10: coverage at a pace that leaves Year 11 for papers
Year 11: whole papers, mock discipline, and the practical route confirmed with the centre
DP1 autumn: confirm the Higher Level choices while they are still cheap to change
DP2 autumn: predicted grades, prerequisites and applications, all at once

sections.heading: Where marks go missing when a subject is learned at a distance
paragraphs: A student learning without a class loses marks in places a classroom student does not. The first is calibration. Without classmates there is no sense of what a strong answer looks like, so a student who feels they have written plenty has no way to discover that the mark scheme wanted four separable points rather than one long paragraph. The only cure is marked past-paper work, in volume, early, with the published scheme visible beside the script.

The second is the practical and fieldwork component. An alternative-to-practical paper tests experimental reasoning rather than laboratory technique, which is good news for a candidate without a laboratory, but it still has to be practised on its own terms: identifying variables, reading apparatus, spotting a flawed method. In Geography, fieldwork needs a site and a method chosen months ahead. Nothing here is impossible outside a school, and all of it fails if left until the final term.

The third is simply attention to the examined form. Command terms are instructions with technical meanings: explain wants a mechanism, outline wants brevity, discuss wants both sides and a judgement, evaluate wants weighted criteria, and state wants a single line with nothing added. A distance student often learns the content well and the form not at all, and the form is half the marks. Teaching the command terms as a vocabulary list, with one model answer each, is a short piece of work with a disproportionate effect on the grade. The same applies to the mechanics around the answer: showing working so method marks survive a wrong final figure, labelling a graph's axes, and writing the number of separable points the mark allocation has asked for rather than one continuous paragraph.

sections.heading: The line a tutor does not cross on assessed work
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject carries internally assessed work, and the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the Personal Project sit beside it. All of it must be the student's own, and the school declares it to be so. A tutor may not write, draft or produce any part of it, and nobody working through IB Gram will. For a family in a province where the school has limited capacity to supervise closely, that boundary deserves stating plainly rather than burying in small print.

The permitted work is still substantial, and it is where most of the available marks actually are. A tutor can teach the skills before the task begins: framing a research question that can be answered, choosing a variable that can be measured with the equipment available, structuring an argument, referencing correctly. They can read the student's own draft and report, in criterion language, where the marks are not yet being earned. They can catch a doomed method in week two instead of week ten, which is the single most valuable thing anybody does on assessed work.

There is a simple test a family can apply at the trial lesson. Ask what the tutor does with a first draft. An answer that describes reading it against the criteria and handing back questions is the right one. An answer that offers to tidy it, strengthen it or fill its gaps is a description of malpractice, however pleasantly it is phrased. Feedback that leaves the student with more work to do is the version that is permitted, and it is also the only version that teaches anything.

process.title: Send the syllabus code and the centre, not just the subject
process.description: Chemistry means something different as Cambridge 0620 Extended with an alternative-to-practical entry, as Edexcel International GCSE, and as Diploma Chemistry at Higher Level. Send the code, the tier, the paper combination if you have it, and the name of the centre or school the student is entered through. That single message removes a week of back-and-forth.

process.title: Say whether we are teaching the course or supporting it
process.description: These are different jobs with different weekly loads, and quoting for one while delivering the other is how arrangements fall apart in the spring. If nobody is teaching the subject, say so at the start; the plan, the frequency and the mock schedule all change, and so does the honest answer about how many weeks are needed.

process.title: A free trial lesson that produces a document
process.description: The first session is diagnostic. The tutor works through recent material, marks something the student has already written, and ends by writing down what is actually wrong and in what order to fix it. You keep that whether or not you continue. A diagnosis that amounts to needing more practice is not a diagnosis and should not persuade anybody.

process.title: A coverage map, kept in writing
process.description: For a student without a department, the single most useful artefact is a list of the published syllabus content with dates against what has been taught. It takes minutes a week to maintain and it answers the question families cannot otherwise answer in February: how much of this course has actually been covered, and what is left.

process.title: Mock papers at the points a school would set them
process.description: A private candidate has no mock calendar unless somebody builds one. We set whole papers under timed conditions at the points in the year a school would, mark them against the published scheme, and report the result as a mark rather than an impression. Those marks are also the evidence a prediction can later be built on.

process.title: An honest review each term, including the option to stop
process.description: At the end of a term we look at the marked evidence and decide whether to continue, change tutor, or stop. If the match is wrong after two or three lessons, tell us and we change it. If no specialist is free for the syllabus and slot you need, we say that rather than putting a generalist in front of your child.

whyPoints.title: Built for students whose school runs something else
whyPoints.description: Most tutoring copy assumes a school is teaching the course and a tutor is filling gaps. In Al-Qassim that assumption is often wrong, and a plan built on it fails by the spring. Whole-syllabus teaching, a written coverage map and a mock calendar are different products from weekly top-up, and they are priced and planned as such.

whyPoints.title: The university route treated as part of the teaching
whyPoints.description: Equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili are not a separate topic from tutoring; they decide which subjects and levels are worth holding. We explain each mechanism, say who runs it, and send you to the university's own published criteria for any number. We will not quote a threshold, because thresholds differ by university, by programme and by cycle.

whyPoints.title: Distance treated as a fact, not a complaint
whyPoints.description: The nearest Diploma cohort to Ar Rass or Al Mithnab is a long drive away, and no amount of goodwill shortens it. Live one-to-one video teaching is the arrangement that makes a Higher Level specialist available in a province that does not have one locally, and the slot is pinned to Arabia Standard Time so it does not drift.

whyPoints.title: Rates explained with their source attached
whyPoints.description: Advertised figures in this market run from around SAR 35 an hour on budget platforms to about SAR 220 for premium Higher Level tracks, and all of them are provider marketing rather than measured averages. We name the source of every band on this page and quote our own figure directly instead of asking you to request a callback.

whyPoints.title: A firm boundary on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the Personal Project are read against the criteria and returned with questions. Nothing is written, redrafted or filled in on the student's behalf. That loses us some enquiries from families who wanted the other service, and it is the reason this support is safe for a school to know about.

whyPoints.title: Clear about what we are not
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no accreditation from the Ministry of Education, the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and we are not connected to any school named on this page. There is no office in the Kingdom. No grade, score or university place is promised. What remains is a specialist, a syllabus and a weekly hour that is kept.

faqs.question: Does an equivalency decision work the same way for a student taught a British curriculum at a distance from Buraidah?
faqs.answer: The requirement is the same: the Ministry of Education must decide that the certificate is equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate before a Saudi university treats it as qualifying. What differs for a distance or private candidate is the paperwork trail, because the certificate comes from a board and the schooling record may not come from a single school. Assemble the evidence as you go rather than at the end: enrolment records, transcripts and the board certificate itself. Your centre and the university admissions office are the right places to confirm what each will accept.

faqs.question: Which Tahsili sections overlap least with what an IGCSE student in Al-Qassim has studied?
faqs.answer: The overlap is strongest in mathematics and weakest where the national curriculum sequences topics differently from Cambridge or Edexcel, which most often shows up in the physics and chemistry sections. The content is rarely genuinely new; the ordering, the emphasis and the question style are. Students report recognising the material and not recognising the questions, which is a framing gap rather than a knowledge gap. The practical approach is to work through released question types section by section and list what is unfamiliar, then teach only that.

faqs.question: Is Qudurat worth sitting more than once, and what changes between attempts?
faqs.answer: Candidates commonly sit it more than once, and how a university treats multiple results is set by that university's own published rules, so check them rather than assuming. What changes between attempts is almost entirely technique: pacing, question recognition and not spending four minutes on an item worth the same as one that takes forty seconds. Because Qudurat examines reasoning rather than taught syllabus content, additional revision of school material moves the result very little. Practice under the real time allowance moves it considerably more.

faqs.question: Can a Diploma student from Al-Qassim apply to Qassim University and a university abroad in the same year?
faqs.answer: Yes, and plenty do, but the two routes want different documents at different times. The Saudi route turns on the equivalency decision and the Qiyas results. The overseas route turns on predicted grades, named Higher Level prerequisites and English evidence, with deadlines often falling in the first term of the final school year. The practical risk is a collision between a Qiyas sitting and an overseas deadline. Put both timelines on one page in the autumn of the final year, while the clashes can still be moved.

faqs.question: What does a competitive science programme in the Kingdom weigh most heavily for an international-curriculum applicant?
faqs.answer: Published admission criteria for competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili, with the school result and Qudurat also weighted. The exact combination differs by university and by programme, and it is published by each institution rather than centrally, so the only reliable figure is the one on the university's own admissions page. For an IB or IGCSE student the planning consequence is clear: Tahsili deserves deliberate, separate preparation rather than being treated as a formality that strong school grades will cover.

faqs.question: What evidence of English does a university abroad want from a student schooled in English in Buraidah?
faqs.answer: It varies by country and by institution. Some accept a First Language English or English A result as sufficient evidence; others require a recognised language test regardless of the school's language of instruction, and a few waive the requirement only after a set number of years taught in English. A student from this province schooled partly in Arabic should assume a test will be needed and plan for it, because booking a sitting late is one of the commonest reasons an otherwise strong application misses a deadline.

faqs.question: How do Diploma points translate into an offer from a university outside the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: Most systems convert a Diploma total plus specified Higher Level subject grades into their own entry standard, and the subject grades often matter more than the total. An offer typically names a total and two or three Higher Level grades, so thirty-eight points with a five in the required Higher Level subject can be refused where thirty-five with a six is accepted. This is why the prerequisite list matters more than the headline number, and why it should be written down before subject choices are locked.

faqs.question: When should a Year 9 student in Buraidah commit to an IGCSE subject list?
faqs.answer: Before the Year 10 teaching starts, because a subject not begun is not available in the same window later, and in a province with no local class nobody will be adding a subject mid-course. Settle the number of subjects honestly against the hours a household can actually supervise, and settle the tier intentions in mathematics and the sciences at the same time. A list of eight subjects nobody can teach properly produces worse certificates than a list of six that are taught well.

faqs.question: What does a student in the final IGCSE year need in place before the November series?
faqs.answer: Four things, in order. The entry itself, confirmed with the centre, including the paper combination and whether a practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper applies. Full content coverage, checked against the published syllabus list rather than against memory. At least three whole papers per subject sat under timed conditions and marked to the published scheme. And the command terms learned as a vocabulary list. A candidate holding those four is prepared; a candidate holding only the first and second is hoping.

faqs.question: Is the summer before DP1 worth using for a student in a province with no Diploma school nearby?
faqs.answer: It is the most valuable block of time available, and it is usually wasted on getting ahead in content. Three things repay the hours. Algebra fluency, because it limits mathematics and both the physical sciences for two years. Written explanation in English, because every subject pays for it. And the habit of reading a mark allocation and producing that many separable points. That is a fortnight's focused work, not a syllabus, and a student who arrives holding it starts the Diploma ahead of one who pre-read two textbooks.

faqs.question: What should a Middle Years Programme student in Al-Qassim build before switching to a paper-based course?
faqs.answer: Timed writing against a mark allocation, which criterion-based marking never requires. In the Middle Years Programme a strong answer addresses a descriptor; in IGCSE a strong answer collects discrete marking points inside a fixed time. Students who have only ever been marked against descriptors write fluently and score moderately for a term while they adjust. A short block of past-paper questions with the mark scheme visible closes most of the gap, and mathematics is where the change in style bites first.

faqs.question: What does teaching a whole IGCSE subject from scratch cost compared with topping up a taught course?
faqs.answer: It is not comparable on an hourly basis, which is where families go wrong in the comparison. Topping up a school's teaching is typically one session a week for part of a year. Carrying the subject means roughly double the weekly contact, across the full course, plus mock setting and marking. The hourly figure may be identical; the total is not. The useful question is not what an hour costs but what the grade costs, and on that measure a properly taught single subject often beats three loosely supported ones.

faqs.question: Are advertised SAR rates per hour comparable between platforms and tutoring companies?
faqs.answer: Not directly. A platform rate advertised from around SAR 35 or SAR 55 an hour usually describes a marketplace floor where tutors set their own fees and syllabus knowledge varies widely. A tutoring company quoting from around SAR 180 for IB subjects is describing a specialist with a stated subject and level. Both are published marketing figures rather than measured market averages. Before comparing two numbers, ask which syllabus the tutor has actually taught, at which level, and how many candidates they have prepared for that paper.

faqs.question: Does a free trial lesson tell a Buraidah family anything useful, and what should it produce?
faqs.answer: It is only useful if it produces a document. A trial that is a pleasant conversation about goals tells you the tutor is personable and nothing else. A trial worth having works through material the student has recently studied, marks something they have already written, and ends with a written note of what is wrong, in what order it should be fixed, and roughly how long that takes. Ask for that note. If it says the student needs more practice, you have learned that the tutor did not diagnose anything.

faqs.question: Is a small group ever better value than one-to-one for a student with no classmates in the subject?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and for a specific reason: calibration. A private candidate in Al-Qassim has no way of judging whether their answer is strong, and sitting alongside two other candidates on the same syllabus supplies that comparison cheaply. Where a group fails is pace, since three students with different gaps cannot be taught the same hour efficiently. The arrangement that tends to work is one-to-one teaching with occasional group paper sessions, rather than choosing one format for everything.

faqs.question: Does the hourly rate change for a Tahsili or Qudurat technique session rather than a syllabus lesson?
faqs.answer: It can, in either direction, and the reason is scarcity rather than difficulty. A tutor who knows the national-curriculum framing of the Tahsili science sections and can map it onto what an IGCSE or Diploma student already holds is a narrower specialism than Higher Level Chemistry, so availability drives the figure more than content does. Ask directly what the tutor has prepared candidates for and how recently, and treat the price as a question about scarcity rather than about the subject's level.

buraidah.closingHeading: Where an Al-Qassim family should begin
buraidah.closingBody: Send three things and we can answer properly: the syllabus code and tier, who is currently teaching the course if anybody is, and the hour that works on a weekday evening in Buraidah. We will say whether a specialist in that exact paper is free in that window, and if none is, we will tell you rather than offering a generalist. The first lesson is free and diagnostic, and it ends with a written account of what is actually wrong and in what order to fix it. Everything is taught live online, one-to-one, on Arabia Standard Time.

cambridge-checkpoint-tutor.tutorsIntro: The teachers listed here have taught the Cambridge curriculum framework at Stages 6 to 9 and carried the same students into IGCSE. A Checkpoint match is made on the strand your report flags, not on the subject label: a student losing marks in geometry and measure does not need the same teacher as one losing them in statistics.

intro.heading: The report comes first, the tutoring comes second
paragraphs: Most families searching for a Cambridge Checkpoint tutor in Saudi Arabia are holding a piece of paper. It arrived from school with a scale score for English, Mathematics or Science, a statement of achievement, and a feedback table that nobody sat down and explained. The score lands somewhere between 0.0 and 6.0. The feedback table splits the subject into strands and shows, strand by strand, how the student performed against the Cambridge curriculum framework. That table is the most useful single document a Cambridge family receives before IGCSE, and it is routinely filed in a drawer and forgotten.

This page is built on that report. Cambridge Primary Checkpoint sits at the end of Stage 6, around age eleven. Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint sits at the end of Stage 9, around age fourteen. Both are set and marked by Cambridge International and administered by the school, and neither one is a qualification. There is no graded certificate, no tier ruling, no entry that follows a student onto a university file. What there is, is externally marked evidence that does not depend on one teacher's view of one class in one building. Read properly, it names the two or three things worth paying a specialist to fix.

The money question follows from that, not the other way round. Advertised one-to-one rates in the Kingdom run from around SAR 35 an hour on budget online platforms to SAR 200 and above for senior examination subjects in Riyadh, according to tutoring-platform listings and tutor-marketplace guides. Those are figures providers publish about themselves. They are not a market average, and none of them is what IB Gram charges. A Checkpoint subject sits towards the lower half of that spread, because the pool of teachers who can teach Stage 7 to Stage 9 mathematics properly is far wider than the pool who can teach Mathematics AA at Higher Level.

Lessons for families in the Kingdom are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. That is the honest argument rather than a workaround. A family in Yanbu or Jazan gets the same Checkpoint science specialist a family in north Riyadh gets, on the same Sunday-to-Thursday evening slot, with no travel loading priced into the rate and no forty-minute drive across town deciding whether the lesson happens at all.

What follows works backwards from evidence to plan to price. First, how to read the Checkpoint report. Then how to turn its strands into a shortlist short enough to act on. Then what the Kingdom's market charges, what actually moves that number, and the cases where a group class beats one-to-one. Then the IGCSE tier decision the report quietly feeds, the Sunday-to-Thursday week a weekly slot has to survive, and the Ministry of Education equivalency step that sits years away but shapes subject choices now.

cambridge-checkpoint-tutor.programmesIntro: Checkpoint is a staging post inside a longer Cambridge pathway, and the stage a student is at changes what a tutor should be doing with them. These are the four programme contexts Checkpoint families in the Kingdom ask about most.

programmes.name: Cambridge Primary
programmes.description: Cambridge Primary runs from Stage 1 to Stage 6 and ends, in schools that choose to enter candidates, with Cambridge Primary Checkpoint in English, English as a Second Language, Mathematics and Science. The tests are set and marked by Cambridge International. At this stage the useful work is almost never content coverage. It is arithmetic fluency, reading stamina and the habit of writing an answer that matches what the question asked for.
programmes.countryNote: In the Kingdom, Cambridge Primary is where a family relocating from a national-curriculum or American-curriculum school first meets an externally marked test. Advertised rates for primary private tuition in Riyadh sit around SAR 50 an hour according to tutor-marketplace guides, well below the senior-subject bands, and a Stage 6 student rarely needs more than one weekly hour pointed at a named strand.

programmes.name: Cambridge Lower Secondary
programmes.description: Cambridge Lower Secondary covers Stages 7 to 9 and ends with Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint in the same four subjects. This is the stage where a gap stops being cosmetic. Algebraic manipulation, the particle model in chemistry, and the difference between describing and explaining in a written answer all get laid down here, and all three are examined much harder at IGCSE than at Stage 9.
programmes.countryNote: Stage 9 is the single most common point at which a Saudi family first hires outside help, because the Checkpoint report arrives at the same moment the school is deciding IGCSE subject sets and tiers. A Stage 9 student in Dhahran or Jubail whose school runs one combined science class has a different problem from one in north Riyadh choosing between three separate sciences.

programmes.name: Cambridge Upper Secondary and IGCSE
programmes.description: Cambridge IGCSE is the qualification the Checkpoint pathway feeds into, and it is where tiering starts to matter. Many Cambridge IGCSE subjects are tiered: Core is graded C to G, Extended is graded A* to E. A student entered for Core cannot be awarded above a C however well the papers go. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades 9 to 1 and is structured differently.
programmes.countryNote: The tier decision is made by the school, usually inside the first year of the course, and it is reversible only before the entry deadline. A Checkpoint strand report is the clearest piece of evidence a parent can bring to that conversation, which is why the report is worth reading in the week it arrives rather than the term before entries close.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme is the other route a student of Checkpoint age may be on, and families comparing schools in the Kingdom often hold offers from both. MYP assesses against published criteria rather than terminal papers, builds the Personal Project in the final year, and is marked internally with external moderation available. It produces different evidence from a Checkpoint scale score.
programmes.countryNote: Some schools in Riyadh and Jeddah run the Middle Years Programme and then the Diploma; others run Cambridge Lower Secondary and then IGCSE. A family moving between the two mid-stage should expect the command vocabulary to change more than the content does, and that is usually what a transfer student needs teaching first.

cambridge-checkpoint-tutor.subjectsIntro: Checkpoint covers four subjects, but a report does not. It reports strands inside those subjects, and the strand is what a tutor is actually hired for. These are the areas Saudi families most often arrive with, written as the report writes them.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Number
subjects.description: Fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio, standard form and index laws. A weakness here is the one that quietly follows a student all the way to IGCSE, because every later topic assumes it. Most Stage 9 marks lost on the non-calculator paper trace back to number, not to the topic the question appeared to be about.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Algebra
subjects.description: Expressions, equations, sequences, inequalities and the beginnings of graphing. This strand is the strongest single predictor of how an IGCSE mathematics course will go. A student who cannot rearrange reliably at Stage 9 will meet the same difficulty again in physics, in chemistry calculations and in every IGCSE mathematics paper.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Geometry and Measure
subjects.description: Angle reasoning, properties of shapes, Pythagoras, area, volume, bearings and scale drawing. Marks here are lost to unstated reasons rather than wrong answers: the student knows the angle but does not name the rule, and the mark scheme pays for the rule. It responds quickly to teaching because the fix is a habit.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Statistics and Probability
subjects.description: Averages from tables, data representation, comparing distributions and simple probability. The weakest area is almost always interpretation rather than calculation. A student computes the mean correctly and then writes a comparison sentence that earns nothing because it quotes a number without saying what the number means.

subjects.name: Science: Biology strand
subjects.description: Cells, human and plant systems, ecosystems, variation and inheritance. The content is largely recall at this stage, which makes it look easy and makes it easy to lose marks on. Definitions are examined strictly, and a student who writes a loose version of a definition learned once in Stage 7 will be marked down.

subjects.name: Science: Chemistry strand
subjects.description: States of matter, the particle model, elements and compounds, reactions, acids and the reactivity series. The particle model is the hinge: a student who cannot explain a change of state in terms of particles will struggle with every IGCSE chemistry explanation question, because they are all built on it.

subjects.name: Science: Physics strand
subjects.description: Forces and motion, energy, electricity, light, sound and space. Physics is the strand where mathematics weakness surfaces first. A student fine on recall and poor on rearranging a formula loses marks in physics long before the mathematics report says anything is wrong.

subjects.name: Science: Thinking and Working Scientifically
subjects.description: Planning an investigation, identifying variables, drawing and reading graphs, evaluating a method and spotting anomalous results. This strand is assessed inside the subject papers rather than separately, and it is the one most often untaught because it is nobody's topic. It carries real marks at Stage 9 and far more at IGCSE.

subjects.name: English: Reading
subjects.description: Retrieval, inference, and commenting on how a writer uses language and structure. The jump that catches students is from what the text says to how the writer achieves an effect. Marks go on quoting at length without analysis, or on analysing a device without connecting it to meaning.

subjects.name: English: Writing
subjects.description: Composition for a stated purpose and audience, with accuracy in sentence structure, punctuation and spelling. Two students can lose the same number of marks for opposite reasons, one for a thin plan and one for sentences that never vary. The report usually shows which, and the teaching differs completely.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Reading, writing, listening and speaking assessed for learners whose first language is not English. For many families in the Kingdom this is the entry route rather than first-language English, and the strand profile looks different: strong accuracy, narrower range, and marks lost on idiom and on inference rather than on grammar.

subjects.name: Mathematics: non-calculator technique
subjects.description: Written method, estimation, and knowing which operations to do mentally. Checkpoint mathematics is typically split between a paper taken without a calculator and one taken with it, so a student fluent only with a calculator loses marks on one whole paper. Confirm the component list for your child's entry with the school in writing.

cambridge-checkpoint-tutor.igcseSubjectsIntro: A Checkpoint report is read by schools as evidence for the IGCSE sets a student will be placed in. These are the courses Stage 9 Checkpoint most directly feeds, with the strand that tends to decide how each one goes.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics
igcseSubjects.description: Extended is graded A* to E and Core C to G, so the tier decision caps the grade before the course starts. The Checkpoint algebra and number strands are what a head of department looks at when placing a student, far more than the headline scale score.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Combined or Coordinated Sciences
igcseSubjects.description: One or two awards covering biology, chemistry and physics. Schools in smaller Saudi cities often run this instead of three separate sciences because of staffing, and a strong Checkpoint science profile is the argument a family makes for the separate route where it exists.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Biology
igcseSubjects.description: Separate-science biology rewards precise definitions and structured explanation. The Stage 9 biology strand transfers almost directly, but the volume roughly doubles and the marking gets stricter about using the correct term rather than a near-synonym.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry
igcseSubjects.description: Moles, bonding and energetics are where Stage 9 chemistry stops being enough. A student whose Checkpoint chemistry strand was carried by recall rather than by the particle model usually hits this in the first term of the course.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics
igcseSubjects.description: The most mathematical of the three separate sciences, and the one where a Checkpoint algebra weakness shows up as a physics problem. Rearranging, units and significant figures account for a steady stream of avoidable marks.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and directed writing assessed against published criteria. The Checkpoint English reading strand predicts this better than the writing strand does, because the reading questions at IGCSE demand the same move from retrieval to analysis, only on harder texts.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language
igcseSubjects.description: A different course from First Language English with a different mark scheme, and the one many Kingdom families are entered for. Checkpoint ESL strand data is the fairest evidence for which of the two a student should sit, and the decision is the school's.

igcseSubjects.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
igcseSubjects.description: Some schools in the Kingdom run Edexcel rather than Cambridge, with a different grade scale and a different paper structure for the same subject. A Checkpoint report still reads as evidence, but the tier and component vocabulary changes and parents should ask the school which board each subject sits with.

cambridge-checkpoint-tutor.regionsTitle: Where Checkpoint candidates we support are studying
cambridge-checkpoint-tutor.regionsIntro: Cambridge Lower Secondary is taught across the Kingdom, but the reason a family wants outside help changes with the city. In Riyadh it is usually set placement; in the smaller cities it is that the school runs one class per stage and no specialist for the strand in question.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The deepest concentration of Cambridge and IB schools in the Kingdom, and the city where Checkpoint reports most often feed a genuine choice between separate sciences and a combined award. The city is roughly an hour across in traffic, which is why evening online slots fill between five and eight.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur, with British-curriculum and Cambridge schools spread along it. Families here commonly hold a Checkpoint report from one school and an offer from another, and want the strand data read independently before they choose.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One school and labour market in practice: families live in one of the three and attend school in another. Checkpoint demand here clusters around science strands, because several campuses run coordinated rather than separate sciences at IGCSE.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: An industrial city with a small international school population, where a Stage 9 cohort may be a single class. When that class has no mathematics specialist free for a strand repair, there is no second class to move into, and an online specialist is the only option available.

regions.name: Makkah and Madinah
regions.note: Makkah sits roughly 80km east of Jeddah, and families in both cities often choose a school in the other. Checkpoint support here is mostly English and English as a Second Language, and lesson timing bends around Hajj and Umrah seasons.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Two cities about 25km apart at altitude in 'Asir, sharing one catchment. International-curriculum provision is thin, so a Checkpoint family here is usually looking for a subject the local school cannot staff rather than for extra practice in one it can.

regions.name: Yanbu and Ras Tanura

sections.heading: What a Cambridge Checkpoint report actually tells you
paragraphs: Checkpoint produces two things. The first is a statement of achievement, confirming that the student sat the tests and in which subjects. The second, and the one that matters, is a feedback report. Cambridge International sets and marks the tests; the school administers them and passes the results back. Because the marking sits outside the building, the feedback is the only academic evidence a Cambridge family holds before IGCSE that is not a judgement made by the student's own teacher about the student's own class.

The headline figure for each subject is a scale score reported between 0.0 and 6.0. On its own it is close to useless to a parent, because it compresses a whole subject into one number and gives no clue where the marks went. The part worth reading is the breakdown underneath, which splits the subject into strands drawn from the Cambridge curriculum framework and shows performance against each. That is the layer that converts into a plan, because a strand is small enough to teach in a handful of lessons and specific enough to test afterwards.

The report also has clear limits, and it is worth knowing them before anybody acts on it. It is not a prediction of an IGCSE grade. It does not decide a tier, and it does not bind the school to anything. It cannot tell you why a strand went wrong, only that it did; a low geometry strand can come from not knowing the content, from not stating reasons in the answer, or from running out of time on the paper, and the teaching for those three is entirely different. The report tells you where to look. Somebody then has to look, and that is the work the first lesson should do.

sections.heading: Turning a strand breakdown into a shortlist you can afford
paragraphs: A Checkpoint report typically flags more than a family can sensibly buy. The discipline is to pick two strands, not five, and to pick them by what they block rather than by how low they look. In mathematics that almost always means number and algebra first. Geometry sits on top of them, physics calculations sit on top of them, and every IGCSE mathematics paper assumes them. A student with a weak algebra strand and a weak statistics strand should be taught algebra, because fixing it moves statistics as a side effect and the reverse is not true.

Science reads differently. The report splits into biology, chemistry and physics strands plus thinking and working scientifically, and the last one is the one nobody owns. It covers planning an investigation, naming variables, drawing and reading graphs and evaluating a method, and it is assessed inside the subject papers rather than as a separate test. Because it is not a topic in anybody's scheme of work, it is the strand most often left untaught, and it carries marks at Stage 9 and considerably more at IGCSE. If a student's three content strands are fine and the overall science score is not, this is usually why.

English splits into reading and writing, and a low overall score can come from either for opposite reasons. A thin reading strand usually means the student retrieves well and analyses badly: they quote at length and never say what the writer achieved by writing it that way. A thin writing strand can mean a weak plan or it can mean monotonous sentence construction, and those two need different lessons entirely. For a student entered for English as a Second Language the profile shifts again, with accuracy often strong and range and inference carrying the losses. One look at the strand data separates these cases in about five minutes, which is why the first lesson should spend time on the report rather than on teaching.

sections.heading: What a Cambridge Checkpoint tutor costs in the Kingdom
paragraphs: Saudi providers are unusually coy about rates, and most of the pages ranking for this search hide the number behind a contact form. The figures below are advertised rates, published by tutoring platforms, tutoring companies and tutor-marketplace guides about their own services. They are a map of what the market asks, not a market average, and none of them is what IB Gram charges. We quote per match, because a Stage 6 number strand and a Stage 9 chemistry strand do not need the same teacher and should not cost the same.

Read the table by tier rather than by headline price. The lowest advertised numbers come from large online platforms with wide tutor pools, where the rate buys availability rather than syllabus depth. The highest come from senior examination work, Diploma and Advanced Placement teaching, where scarcity sets the price. Checkpoint sits below both of those extremes for a straightforward reason: the teaching is foundational, the pool of people who can do it well is wide, and no part of it requires examiner experience in a scarce Higher Level subject.

Two practical warnings. A figure quoted in dollars has to be converted before it can be compared, and it moves with the exchange rate rather than with the quality of the teaching. And an hourly rate is not the whole cost: ask whether marking between lessons, past papers, mark schemes and a written progress note are inside the rate or billed on top. A lower rate with nothing marked between sessions is usually the more expensive arrangement by the end of a term, because the student practises their mistakes for six days and gets them corrected on the seventh.

sections.heading: What moves the rate for a Checkpoint subject, and what should not
paragraphs: Subject scarcity is the heaviest driver of price everywhere, and it is the main reason Checkpoint teaching is cheaper than Diploma teaching. A teacher who can take a Stage 8 student through index laws is not rare. A teacher who has marked Higher Level physics for a board is. Families sometimes read a low Checkpoint quote as a signal of low quality when it is simply a signal of a wide supply pool, and they overpay for a Diploma specialist who will teach Stage 9 competently but no better than a good lower-secondary teacher would.

Marking and examiner experience is worth paying a premium for at IGCSE and above, where the difference between knowing content and being paid for it on a mark scheme decides whole grades. At Checkpoint it matters less, because Checkpoint is diagnostic rather than terminal and the marks are not being banked towards a certificate. What does matter at this stage is whether the teacher has carried students from Stage 9 into IGCSE and knows which Stage 9 habits survive the transition and which collapse.

Travel is the driver that disappears entirely online. In-home tuition in the Kingdom carries a travel loading, and agencies price the tutor's time in the car into the hour; it is one of the reasons Riyadh senior-subject rates are quoted at SAR 200 and above. It also silently restricts the pool to whoever lives within a sensible drive, which in Jubail or Khamis Mushait can mean nobody with the right specialism at all. Package length is the last driver, and the one to be most careful with: a discount for a long commitment is only a saving if the match is right, which is the argument for a trial lesson and a short block before anything longer.

sections.heading: One-to-one, a group class, or the school's own intervention
paragraphs: One-to-one is not automatically the right purchase at Checkpoint level, and a page that pretends otherwise is selling rather than advising. Schools in the Kingdom frequently run their own intervention groups for Stage 9, free, staffed by the teacher who will write the IGCSE set recommendation. That is the first thing to use. It is poorly suited to a single-student strand problem, because the group moves at the pace of its weakest common weakness, but it costs nothing and it keeps the school engaged with the student's progress.

Commercial group revision classes occupy a narrow but real niche. They work when the content is genuinely missing across a whole topic and the student is otherwise functioning, because content delivery scales reasonably well. They do not work for technique, for timing, or for a student who has stopped asking questions, since all three require somebody to watch one student work and intervene at the moment the error happens. A group of eight students and one teacher cannot do that, whatever the marketing says.

One-to-one earns its price in exactly the cases a group cannot cover: a named strand against an otherwise sound profile, a technique problem where the student knows the content and loses the marks anyway, or a mid-stage arrival who needs the Cambridge framework caught up rather than revised. The honest version of the recommendation is a short block, a written diagnosis, and a decision afterwards. If the diagnosis says the school's own group is enough, that is a real outcome and it costs a family three lessons instead of a term.

sections.heading: From the Checkpoint report to the IGCSE tier decision
paragraphs: The decision a Checkpoint report feeds most directly is tiering, and it is the decision parents in the Kingdom understand least. Many Cambridge IGCSE subjects are tiered. Core is graded C to G; Extended is graded A* to E. A student entered for Core cannot be awarded above a C however well the papers go on the day. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades 9 to 1 with a different structure, and some schools in the Kingdom run Edexcel for one subject and Cambridge for another in the same building.

Tier entry is a school decision, made on the school's reading of the evidence it holds, and it is reversible only before the entry deadline. After that the ceiling is fixed. This is the single most consequential academic decision taken about a student between Stage 9 and the end of IGCSE, and it is frequently taken without the parent realising a decision was made. A Checkpoint strand report is the clearest independent evidence a family can bring to that conversation, which is why it is worth reading in the week it arrives rather than the term entries close.

Entries themselves are made by the school, not the family, and the windows close several months ahead of the papers. Your school's examinations officer holds the exact dates. Cambridge and Pearson both run a June series, which is the main one for schools in the Kingdom, and a November series used for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge's February/March series is an India-only arrangement, so a candidate in the Kingdom sits June or November and any advice built on a February entry is advice written for a different country.
