sections.heading: Experience that transfers, and experience that does not
paragraphs: A great deal of teaching experience does not cross over, and the mismatches follow a pattern. A long A Level career transfers well to Diploma Higher Level content and badly to the internally assessed component, because A Level coursework, where it exists at all, is assessed on different criteria and supervised under different rules. The content lessons will be strong and the internal assessment supervision will be guesswork, which matters because that component is often the difference between a five and a six.

Advanced Placement experience transfers in the opposite direction. The content depth is there, particularly in the sciences and in calculus, but the Diploma's command terms, its data-booklet conventions and its insistence on evaluating rather than describing are unfamiliar. Students taught by an ex-Advanced Placement teacher often know more than their classmates and score less, which is a specific, diagnosable problem and a quick one to fix once somebody names it.

Inside the IB itself, the transfer between programmes is weaker than families assume. An experienced MYP teacher works with four criteria scored out of eight; a Diploma teacher works with markbands and a seven-point scale built on published boundaries. A strong MYP teacher moving a Year 11 student into the first Diploma year will often under-prepare them for how little credit the Diploma gives for effort shown. And IGCSE experience, which is genuinely close to MYP in content, is a long way from it in assessment style.

The sharpest mismatch is Mathematics. Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are different courses with different papers, and a teacher fluent in one is not automatically fluent in the other: the statistics reach of Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level defeats plenty of excellent pure mathematicians. When a family asks for a maths tutor, the first thing we establish is which of the two courses the student is entered for, and the second is whether the tutor has taken a cohort through that exact one.

sections.heading: Experience goes stale, and the subject guide is where it shows
paragraphs: Experience has a shelf life, and nobody in this market mentions it. Subject guides are revised on a cycle. When a new guide is published there is a first-teaching cohort and then a first-assessment series, and in between the two a teacher who is not actively teaching the course can miss the change entirely. Topics are removed, assessment outlines are rebalanced, the number and length of papers can change, and option units are reorganised. A tutor who left the classroom before the current guide was introduced is experienced at a course your child is not sitting.

The same applies on the Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel side, where syllabus codes are reissued and component structures adjusted. Two students in the same Riyadh classroom can be entered for different codes if the school changed board between year groups, and the alternative-to-practical arrangements in the sciences differ in ways that decide how a student should revise. This is not an exotic risk: it is the most common quiet failure in paid tutoring, because content teaching still looks and feels productive while being aimed at the wrong paper.

The fix is cheap and it belongs in the trial lesson. Ask what changed in the current guide or syllabus for this subject, and listen for specifics: a dropped topic, a restructured paper, a different weighting, a renamed assessment objective. Ask which code the student is entered for, and whether the tutor has taught that code rather than its predecessor. Then ask the school's examinations officer to confirm the code and the component list in writing, because tier and component decisions are the school's to make and are reversible only before the entry deadline.

An experienced tutor welcomes those questions, because they are the questions that distinguish them from the profile sitting next to theirs. A tutor who treats them as an interrogation has told you something useful for free. We ask them ourselves before a tutor takes a subject, and we re-ask when a family's school changes board or when a student moves school mid-course, which in the Kingdom happens more often than it does in most markets.

sections.heading: What an experienced tutor's hour costs in this market
paragraphs: Money in this market is discussed directly, and vagueness reads as evasion, so here are the figures that are actually published. Everything in the table below is an advertised rate taken from vendor listings, platform marketing pages and tutor-marketplace guides aimed at Saudi families. They are what providers say they charge. They are not a market average, they are not verified by us, and none of them is IB Gram's price: your own quote depends on the subject, the level and the individual tutor, and you are told it before a paid lesson, after the free trial.

Read down the table and the pattern is obvious. The cheap end is general tutoring with no subject specialism named, and the figures rise sharply once a listing commits to a named Diploma subject at a named level. The premium attached to Higher Level and to marking experience is the single largest jump in the whole market, and it is the one families most often pay without asking what it buys. Travel is the other loading: an in-home tutor prices the drive into the hour, and in Riyadh or along the Jeddah coast that drive is not short.

What moves a number, in order of weight: scarcity of the subject at the level entered, then marking or cohort experience, then level itself, then whether anybody travels, then the length of the package. A Higher Level Physics or Mathematics Analysis and Approaches specialist costs more than a Standard Level mathematics tutor everywhere in the world, and the Kingdom is no exception. A longer block usually lowers the hourly figure and raises the total, which is worth saying out loud before a family commits.

The honest comparison is per useful hour rather than per hour. An in-home tutor at a lower hourly rate who arrives late through Riyadh traffic, teaches a subject adjacent to the one entered, and cannot make the following week delivers fewer useful hours than a specialist on video at a higher rate who never misses. That is the actual argument for online delivery here, and it is an argument about arithmetic rather than about technology.

sections.heading: What a parent actually sees in an online lesson
paragraphs: Lessons run over live video with a shared whiteboard, and the mechanics matter more than the software. The student needs a laptop rather than a phone, a headset, and a way to show handwritten working: either a cheap document camera, a second device propped over the page, or a photograph taken at the end of each problem and dropped into the shared board. Diploma mathematics and the sciences are written subjects, and a lesson where the tutor can see only a face is a conversation rather than a lesson.

The working session itself usually looks like a marked script on screen. The tutor annotates the student's own photographed work, or a past paper, line by line, with the published mark scheme open beside it. That is the single most useful thing video does better than a kitchen table: both people see the same page at the same magnification, the annotation is saved, and the student has it afterwards instead of a memory of being told. Over a term those annotated pages become a record of exactly which marks the student keeps dropping.

On recordings, connection and privacy, the policy should be stated rather than assumed. Ask whether lessons are recorded, who holds the recording, how long it is kept and who inside the family may watch it. Ask what happens when the connection drops: a lesson should continue on audio while the student photographs their working, and lost minutes should be made up rather than quietly absorbed. Household bandwidth in the Kingdom is generally good, but the evening peak is real, and a wired connection or a sat-near-the-router habit removes most of the problem.

A parent is entitled to a short written note after each session: what was taught, what was set, and what the tutor thinks the next obstacle is. That note is also how you audit the tutoring without sitting in the room. Parents are welcome in a lesson, and in practice the most useful arrangement is the parent present for the first fifteen minutes of the first session and then out of it, because a fourteen-year-old performs for an audience rather than admitting what they do not understand.

sections.heading: The university endgame, and where a subject tutor's experience stops
paragraphs: A Diploma earned in the Kingdom does not automatically function as a Saudi secondary certificate. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, the mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent, and this applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. Families discover this late, often in the final school year, and it is paperwork rather than teaching: start by asking the school's own counsellor which documents they issue and in what form.

Alongside it sit the Qiyas tests. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, and it tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, with Arabic and English options. Tahsili, the achievement test, covers science-stream subjects including mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum. That last point is the one that catches international-curriculum students: the material overlaps with what they have studied, but the framing, the ordering and the expected notation do not.

This is where a subject tutor's experience genuinely stops, and saying so is more useful than pretending otherwise. An experienced Diploma Chemistry teacher is not automatically a Tahsili tutor, because Tahsili is examining a different syllabus in a different style, sometimes in a different language of instruction. The right move for a family is to treat them as two separate briefs with two separate people, and to start the Qiyas preparation earlier than feels necessary, since it competes directly with the final Diploma term.

Universities publish their own admission criteria combining school grades with the Qiyas results, and the weightings differ by university and by programme, with the most competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes leaning hardest on Tahsili. We do not publish those formulas or any threshold, because third-party sites disagree with each other and a wrong number here is a decision a family acts on. Read the criteria on the university's own site, note that some set a maximum age for the certificate they will accept, and no honest provider will promise you an outcome from any of it.

sections.heading: Starting, including what happens when nobody experienced is free
paragraphs: The sequence is short. You tell us the subject, the level, the board and the exact hours that work in Arabia Standard Time, and we ask for two documents: the most recent school report and, if there is one, a marked piece of work with the teacher's comments on it. Those two things tell a specialist more in five minutes than a parent can in half an hour, because they show whether the problem is content, technique or pace. Then you get two or three names, each with their base, their working pattern and the units of experience set out above.

The trial lesson is free and it is a diagnostic, not a sales call. The tutor works through something real, usually a past paper question in the student's weakest area, and afterwards you get a plain statement of where the student is, what is fixable in a term, and what is not. If the student does not want to continue with that person, say so and we match again; the fit between a sixteen-year-old and a tutor is not something a profile predicts.

Sometimes the honest answer is no. The four-hour evening window is narrow, and for a scarce brief such as Higher Level Physics at eighteen hundred on a Sunday, the specialist you want may already be teaching somebody else at that hour. When that happens we say it rather than putting a generalist in the slot. The options we then offer are real ones: a different hour with the specialist, a Friday morning block, a fortnightly pattern while a slot opens, or a wait with a date attached. No tutor, however experienced, can guarantee a grade, and no provider should promise a slot that does not exist.

After the first month there is a review, and it has a decision in it. We look at the school's own assessments, at the marked work from the lessons, and at whether the weekly slot actually held without being moved. Continue, change tutor, change pattern, or stop: all four are on the table, and stopping is sometimes the right call. A family that has been told honestly to stop is a family that comes back when the need is real.

process.title: Tell us the week before the subject
process.description: We start with the hours that genuinely work in Arabia Standard Time, the school's finish time and the door-to-door school run. That narrows the pool honestly before anybody gets attached to a profile, and it stops a match failing in week three over logistics that were knowable in week one.

process.title: Send the report and one marked piece of work
process.description: A recent school report and a marked script with the teacher's comments tell a subject specialist whether this is a content gap, a technique problem or a pace problem. Those three need different tutors and different lesson patterns, so getting it right at the start saves a term.

process.title: Two or three names, with base and hours stated
process.description: You get a shortlist, not a single take-it-or-leave-it suggestion, and each name comes with the tutor's base, their working pattern, the cohorts they have taught in that subject at that level, and any series they have marked. Everything on it is a claim you can test in conversation.

process.title: A free trial lesson in the slot you actually want
process.description: The trial runs at the real proposed time, so you learn whether that hour works for your child as well as on paper. The tutor teaches something real rather than selling, and afterwards you get a written view of what is fixable this term and what is not.

process.title: A plan, weekly notes, and a review at four weeks
process.description: The plan names the components being targeted and the evidence that will show movement. Short notes arrive after each lesson. At four weeks we review against the school's own assessments and decide to continue, change the tutor, change the pattern, or stop.

whyPoints.title: Availability is checked before credentials
whyPoints.description: A tutor who cannot hold your hour every week for a term is not offered to you, however strong their record. The Saudi evening window is four hours wide and shared by every family in the country, so we filter on reachable hours first and subject expertise second, which is the opposite of how most shortlists are built.

whyPoints.title: Slots are pinned to Arabia Standard Time
whyPoints.description: The Kingdom does not change its clocks and most tutor countries do. Every slot is written in Arabia Standard Time, and when a tutor's own clock moves it is their side of the arrangement that adjusts. That removes the twice-yearly silent failure where one person logs on and the other does not.

whyPoints.title: One subject, one level, one specialist
whyPoints.description: A student carrying Higher Level Chemistry and Standard Level Economics is matched with two people, not with one tutor stretched across both. The cost of stretching a tutor is invisible for a month and then shows up as confident teaching aimed at the wrong paper.

whyPoints.title: Feedback on your child's own work only
whyPoints.description: A tutor here teaches, questions and gives feedback on the student's own internal assessment, Extended Essay or Personal Project. None of them will draft, complete or rewrite assessed work, because the IB treats authenticity as a condition of the award and because a family paying for that is buying a risk, not a grade.

whyPoints.title: We say so when nobody suitable is free
whyPoints.description: For a scarce brief at a popular hour, the specialist may be taken. We tell you, and offer a different hour, a Friday block, a fortnightly pattern or a wait with a date on it. Putting a generalist into a Higher Level slot to fill it would cost you a term to discover.

faqs.question: Why does an experienced IB tutor charge more per hour than a newly qualified one in this market?
faqs.answer: Because scarcity and marking history are what the premium is actually priced on. Vendor listings aimed at Saudi families advertise general tutoring from around SAR 55 an hour and named IB subject tutoring from around SAR 180, with Higher Level and premium tracks advertised at roughly SAR 200 to 220. Those are advertised rates published by providers, not a market average and not our price. What sits behind the gap is a teacher who has taken complete cohorts through the same paper, has marked for a board, and can tell your child why a fluent paragraph scored two marks out of four rather than three.

faqs.question: Do we pay per lesson or per block when the tutor is an experienced Higher Level specialist?
faqs.answer: Both arrangements exist in this market and they behave differently. A per-lesson arrangement keeps you free to stop after any session, which matters most in the first month while the fit is still being tested. A block lowers the hourly figure, raises the committed total, and buys something real in return: the specialist reserves your hour for the whole term, which for a scarce Higher Level brief at a popular Saudi evening time is the actual constraint. Ask before you commit what happens to an unused lesson, how much notice a cancellation needs, and whether an unused hour expires at the end of the block.

faqs.question: Is a small group with an experienced tutor better value than one-to-one with a less experienced one?
faqs.answer: It depends on what is wrong. If the student has a content gap in one topic and can follow a taught explanation, a small group with a strong teacher is good value and the discussion helps. If the problem is technique, command terms or internal assessment work, the group format removes the only thing that fixes it: somebody watching this student write, line by line, and stopping them at the point the marks leak. Groups also fix the pace to the middle of the room, which is the wrong pace for both the strongest and the weakest student in it.

faqs.question: Does the hourly rate for an experienced tutor rise in the weeks before the May session?
faqs.answer: Advertised rates do not usually change, but availability does, and in practice that costs more. In the final term before the May session the specialists with the strongest records are already committed to students they have taught all year, so what is left at a popular Saudi evening hour is thinner. Families who arrive then often end up paying for an intensive block of two or three sessions a week, which is the most expensive way to buy support per week and the least effective way to close a content gap. Booking the same hour in the autumn term costs less and achieves more.

faqs.question: What happens to our fee and our slot if we change tutor after the first two paid lessons?
faqs.answer: Changing tutor early is common and should not cost you the term. Ask any provider three things in writing before you start: whether unused paid lessons transfer to a new tutor, whether your weekly hour is held while a new match is made, and how long the rematch takes. At IB Gram the hour stays reserved while we match again, because the slot is the scarce thing in the Kingdom, not the willingness to teach. Say plainly what did not work, since the second match is only better if the first failure is described accurately.

faqs.question: Does an IB Diploma earned at a Saudi international school need Ministry of Education equivalency before a local university will accept it?
faqs.answer: Yes. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, known as the mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. The same applies to A Levels and to an American high school diploma. It is an administrative process rather than an academic one, so start by asking your school's counsellor which documents they issue, in what language, and how they are attested. Leave time for it: families routinely discover the requirement in the final school year, when it competes with examinations.

faqs.question: Can an experienced Diploma subject tutor also prepare a student for Tahsili?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and a tutor who says otherwise without qualification is overselling. Tahsili covers science-stream subjects including mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum rather than the IB guide. An experienced Diploma Chemistry teacher knows the chemistry, but the framing, the ordering of topics and the expected notation differ, and the test may be sat in a different language of instruction from the one the student learned in. Treat it as a second brief with a second specialist, and start it earlier than feels necessary.

faqs.question: Is Qudurat sat in Arabic or in English, and does an international-curriculum student have a choice?
faqs.answer: Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is offered in Arabic and in English, and it is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment. It tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, so a student taught entirely in English is not automatically disadvantaged on the reasoning itself. The language decision should be made on where the student reads fastest under time pressure, not on sentiment. Check the current registration options and sitting arrangements on the National Center for Assessment's own site, because these are administered centrally and do change.

faqs.question: Which part of an overseas university offer do Saudi IB families most often misread?
faqs.answer: Overseas universities set their own conditions, and they are usually expressed as a total point score plus named Higher Level subjects at a stated grade. The Higher Level requirement is the part families underestimate: an engineering course asking for Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level will not accept Applications and Interpretation, however high the total. Read the course page on the university's own site rather than an aggregator, note that some require specific subjects at Higher Level rather than at any level, and make the Higher Level choices with those requirements already on the table.

faqs.question: What platform do lessons run on, and does anything need installing on a family laptop?
faqs.answer: Lessons run over live video with a shared whiteboard in the browser, so in most cases nothing needs installing. What matters more than the software is the hardware around it: a laptop rather than a phone, a wired headset, and a way to show handwritten working, which can be a cheap document camera, a second device propped over the page, or a photograph dropped into the shared board. Test the setup once before the first paid lesson rather than in it, and sit the student near the router if the household connection dips in the evening peak.

faqs.question: Are lessons recorded, and who in the family can watch a recording afterwards?
faqs.answer: Ask for the policy in writing before you start, because practice varies across this market. A reasonable arrangement is that lessons are recorded only with the family's agreement, the recording is held by the provider rather than by the individual tutor, the retention period is stated, and access is limited to the student and the parent who booked. Recordings are genuinely useful for a dense Higher Level mathematics session the student will want to replay. They are much less useful than the annotated script, which is the thing worth asking for after every lesson.

faqs.question: What happens when the connection drops in the middle of a Higher Level lesson?
faqs.answer: The lesson should continue rather than end. In practice the pair move to audio while the student keeps writing and photographs their working, or the tutor sends the next question by message and they talk it through. Lost minutes should be made up in the same week or added to the next session, and a reasonable provider states that rather than quietly absorbing them. If the drop is persistent, the fix is usually at the household end: a wired connection, a different room, or a slot outside the evening peak.

faqs.question: How does an experienced tutor mark a handwritten script that the student photographs at home?
faqs.answer: The photograph goes into the shared board or the lesson folder, and the tutor annotates it directly against the published mark scheme, marking method lines rather than only the final answer. The student gets the annotated page back, so the record is a page of their own working with the lost marks circled rather than a list of topics to revise. Over a term those pages are the most useful evidence a family has, because the same two or three leaks recur and become visible even to a parent who does not know the subject.

faqs.question: Can a parent sit in on a lesson with an experienced tutor without changing how the lesson goes?
faqs.answer: A parent is welcome, but the honest answer is that it does change the lesson. A fourteen-year-old with an audience performs rather than admits what they do not understand, and admitting it is the whole mechanism of one-to-one teaching. The arrangement that works is being present for the first fifteen minutes of the first session, then leaving. After that, audit the tutoring through the written note after each lesson and through the annotated scripts, which show you more than sitting in the room would.

faqs.question: How does a tutor share past papers and mark schemes during an online session?
faqs.answer: Papers are opened in the shared workspace so both people see the same page at the same magnification, and the mark scheme is kept beside it rather than quoted from memory. Copies your school has given the student are used where possible, since schools hold the proper licensed versions, and anything the tutor supplies should be properly sourced rather than a scan of unknown origin. Ask that the annotated versions stay in the shared folder after each lesson, because the value is in the accumulated record rather than in the individual paper.

faqs.question: What should a family expect to pay for a single intensive block before a Cambridge June series?
faqs.answer: Providers in this market advertise intensive work at the top of their published bands, and the arithmetic is simply more hours in fewer weeks: two or three sessions a week instead of one. The figures advertised for senior examination subjects in Riyadh start at SAR 200 and above per hour in tutor-marketplace guides, which makes a short block a significant commitment. Before you buy one, ask what it is for. An intensive block is good at timing, question choice and command terms, and poor at building a foundation that was never there.

experienced-ib-tutor.closingHeading: Start from the hour, then find the experience
experienced-ib-tutor.closingBody: If you take one thing from this page, make it the order of operations. Work out the two or three hours in the Saudi week that genuinely work for your child, write them down in Arabia Standard Time, and only then start asking about cohorts, series marked and the current subject guide. A tutor who is available and specific beats a more decorated one who has to move the lesson every third week. Tell us the subject, the level, the board and those hours; send a recent report and one marked script; and take the free trial lesson in the slot you actually want, so you find out whether the hour works before anybody is paid for it.

It also explains why the pool of genuinely experienced specialists inside the Kingdom is thin, which follows from how schools here are licensed, evaluated and staffed. experienced-igcse-tutor.tutorsIntro: Each specialist below is described by the kind of experience they hold rather than by a slogan: the board and specification taught, the component marked, the years in a senior department, the curricula they have moved students between. Ask for the part that matters to your child's entry and ignore the rest.

intro.heading: The decision is not whether to get help, it is which kind of experience to buy
paragraphs: By the time a family in the Kingdom searches for an experienced IGCSE tutor, the decision to buy help has already been made. What is still open is harder and rarely discussed: experience in what, exactly? The word is applied to at least five different people. A current classroom teacher in a senior department. A former head of department now tutoring full time. Somebody who has marked a component for a board. A graduate with several thousand hours of tutoring behind them. And a very capable teacher whose experience is on a different curriculum from the one your child is entered for. All five are experienced. Only two or three of them are experienced at the thing your child needs.

The second thing nobody says out loud is that no authority anywhere licenses private tutors. Schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which also operates approval services for international accreditation bodies. None of that machinery touches tutoring. There is no register to check, no inspection report, no renewal cycle. Which means that when a provider writes experienced, there is no body standing behind the word. The only defence a family has is knowing which claims could be confirmed by somebody, and by whom.

That regulatory gap also explains why the local pool is thinner than families expect. Licensing shapes which schools exist and where, and the senior end of an international school is small by design. A department may carry two teachers across three sciences, with one of them covering a subject outside their specialism because there is nobody else to do it. Add expatriate staff turnover and the practical result is that experience in one specific specification, at one specific tier, is scarce even in Riyadh, and scarcer in Buraidah, Najran or Jazan where a student may be the only candidate in their year for a subject.

So the recommendation this page arrives at is narrow. Buy experience in the specification your child is entered against, confirmed by something checkable, and ignore every other kind of experience on offer. A tutor who has taught the component, read its mark schemes repeatedly and seen how this cohort loses marks is worth paying for. A tutor whose experience is impressive but adjacent is not, however good they are, because the gap between a syllabus and its near neighbour is exactly where the marks go.

Delivery for Saudi families is online. Lessons run over live video, one to one, scheduled against Arabia Standard Time and the Sunday-to-Thursday school week. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; in-home visiting is a service we offer only in India. That is not a limitation in this market so much as the mechanism that solves the scarcity problem described above: the question stops being who lives nearby and becomes who has taught this specification, which is a much better question for a family in Tabuk or Al Ahsa to be asking.

experienced-igcse-tutor.programmesIntro: A family weighing experience is usually weighing it across two or three programmes at once: the one the child is on now, the one they came from, and the one they are heading towards. Each demands a different kind of experienced teacher, and the differences are concrete.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Individual subjects, each with a four-digit syllabus code and its own numbered components. Many subjects tier into Core and Extended with separate papers and separate grade ranges, and the sciences add either a laboratory practical or a written alternative. Experience here means knowing one syllabus version in detail, because the component list changes when Cambridge revises it.
programmes.countryNote: The most commonly entered international route in the Kingdom, and the one most often delivered by departments too small to specialise. That is why the useful question to a prospective tutor is which code and which tier they have taught most recently, rather than how many years they have taught the subject in general.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Graded 9 to 1, with Foundation and Higher tiers where a subject tiers, and identified by specification codes rather than syllabus codes. Mathematics A 4MA1 runs two calculator papers, so a tutor whose experience is entirely on a board with a non-calculator component will plan preparation differently from how this board examines.
programmes.countryNote: Board choice varies school by school and sometimes department by department inside one school, so a family moving between cities in the Kingdom can find the specification changes under them. Experience in both boards is useful for exactly that situation and much less relevant for a settled candidate.

programmes.name: The Saudi national curriculum
programmes.description: Taught in public schools licensed by the Ministry of Education, on a two-semester year that opens in late August and closes in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. Assessment, medium of instruction and subject sequencing all differ from an international programme.
programmes.countryNote: Students moving from a national-curriculum school into IGCSE are the group where experience of both systems genuinely matters. The content overlap is real; the framing, the technical vocabulary in English and the examination conventions are the parts that need rebuilding, and a tutor who has only taught one side tends to underestimate how long that takes.

programmes.name: A Level and the IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two routes an IGCSE record feeds into. A Level departments set specific IGCSE grades as conditions for their own courses; Diploma Programme departments read them when arguing Higher Level against Standard Level. Both assume Extended mathematics and the separate sciences as prior knowledge rather than revisiting them.
programmes.countryNote: The equivalency decision a Saudi university relies on is taken by the Ministry of Education on the final secondary certificate, not on the IGCSE statement of results. A tutor experienced with Saudi-domiciled families will know to raise that early; one experienced only with overseas applications usually will not.

experienced-igcse-tutor.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are listed with the thing that makes experienced cover hard to find in each one. In almost every case the shortage is not of good teachers but of teachers who have taught that specific component recently enough to know how it is currently examined.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: The clearest staffing shortage in the Kingdom. It needs somebody comfortable with calculus, series and trigonometric identities beyond the standard syllabus, and schools offer it unevenly for that reason. Families frequently buy the whole course from outside rather than topping up a taught one.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625)
subjects.description: Commonly taught at the senior end by a teacher whose own specialism is chemistry or mathematics. They teach the content perfectly well; the gap shows on the suggest and explain questions, where marks depend on examiner conventions a non-specialist has not absorbed.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
subjects.description: The experienced-teacher premium here is almost entirely about equation and state-symbol conventions, and about the alternative-to-practical paper. A tutor who has marked that component knows what the scheme will and will not accept for an improvement or a source of error.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610)
subjects.description: Easier to staff than physics, harder to examine well. Definitions are marked strictly and paraphrase earns nothing, so experience means knowing the published wording rather than the concept. A teacher new to the specification tends to accept answers the scheme rejects.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 and Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.description: The best-staffed subject in most schools, which makes the tier decision the place experience earns its money. An experienced teacher argues a tier from evidence before the entry deadline; an inexperienced one accepts the set the student was placed in and discovers the grade ceiling afterwards.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500)
subjects.description: Often taught by a teacher experienced in a national-curriculum English course, which is a different subject with different marking. Reading and directed writing fail for opposite reasons here, and knowing which of the two a student is losing marks on takes familiarity with the components themselves.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
subjects.description: Misplacement between this course and First Language English is one of the more expensive mistakes in the senior school, and it is usually invisible until mock results. An experienced tutor identifies it in one diagnostic session by looking at the writing rather than at the grade.

subjects.name: Economics (0455) and Business Studies (0450)
subjects.description: Frequently covered by a teacher from a humanities or commerce background without specific examination experience. Both subjects turn on data response rather than theory, and knowing how many marks hang on quoting figures from the stem is the experience a family is buying.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478)
subjects.description: Small cohorts mean many schools run it with one teacher and no second opinion. Theory rewards precise terminology; the programming element rewards legible pseudocode and documented design, and students who code informally lose marks because the structure is not visible to a marker.

subjects.name: Geography (0460) and History (0470)
subjects.description: Both examine source and case-study handling as skills in their own right. Experience shows in how a tutor handles the longer questions: narrating instead of answering is the standard failure in history, and describing a pattern without quoting figures is the standard one in geography.

experienced-igcse-tutor.regionsTitle: The school-system picture, region by region
experienced-igcse-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives changes which kinds of provision exist and therefore which kinds of experience are locally available. The notes below describe the school picture rather than the districts, because that is what decides whether the local market can answer the question at all.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The broadest mix of Cambridge, Pearson and IB provision in the Kingdom, with long-established international schools alongside newer bilingual campuses. Even here, senior sets in the scarcer subjects are small, and a department that teaches a subject well may still have nobody who has recently taught its hardest tier.

regions.name: Jeddah and Thuwal
regions.note: Provision runs along the coastal spine north from the historic centre, with a research-campus school at Thuwal serving a very different community from a city school. Cambridge and IB both have deep roots here, so families more often compare programmes than search for any provision at all.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: A single school market spread across three cities, with group-operated campuses and British-curriculum schools side by side and the Diploma Programme at some campuses but not all. Board allegiance varies by campus, which is why experience claims here have to be matched to a specification rather than to a city.

regions.name: Jubail and Ras Tanura
regions.note: Industrial and camp communities with small schools and smaller senior departments. A subject may be covered by a capable non-specialist simply because no alternative exists on site, and the family discovers it from mock marks rather than from anything the school says.

regions.name: Al Ahsa and Qatif
regions.note: Roughly an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster. Candidates are more often entered through examination centres than through a large international department, which changes who holds the specification knowledge and who a family should be asking about the entry.

regions.name: Makkah, Madinah and Taif
regions.note: Smaller international cohorts, with Cambridge entries more common than Diploma ones, and seasonal rhythms around the Hajj and Umrah periods that shape the school year in Makkah in particular. Specialist cover for Extended sciences is thin and families often need full-course teaching from outside.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: Communities in the north-west where the school picture is still forming and families arrive part-way through a course more often than anywhere else. The most valuable experience here is in mapping one specification against another, because a mid-course arrival is a comparison problem before it is a teaching problem.

regions.name: Abha, Khamis Mushait and Jazan
regions.note: The southern cities, with Abha and Khamis Mushait about 25km apart sharing a catchment at altitude. Distance rules out a visiting specialist for most subjects, so the honest local comparison is between a general tutor nearby and a specialist reachable only online.

regions.name: Buraidah, Ha'il and Najran
regions.note: Regional centres with very small international cohorts. A student may be the only candidate in their year for Additional Mathematics or Computer Science, which means no class, no departmental past-paper culture and no colleague for the teacher to check a judgement against.

Cambridge and IB provision both long established along the Jeddah coast, with a school on the research campus at Thuwal north of the city serving a community with its own calendar and its own mobility pattern. Named here as context, with no affiliation implied.

A group operator runs several campuses across the conurbation and at Jubail, with the Diploma Programme available at some and British or Cambridge provision at others. Families here compare campuses within one market rather than choosing between cities.

sections.heading: Five kinds of experienced person, and what each one is actually good for
paragraphs: The word experienced covers at least five distinct backgrounds, and a family choosing between them is making a real decision rather than a cosmetic one. A current classroom teacher in a senior department knows how a cohort behaves and how a school's scheme of work runs, and is often unavailable at the hours a Saudi evening needs. A former head of department has judgement about pacing and tier decisions that nobody else has. A board marker knows what a scheme will accept, which is a different and narrower kind of knowledge, and an extremely valuable one.

Then there are the two that families most often buy by accident. A graduate with several thousand tutoring hours has real skill at explaining and at managing a reluctant teenager, and may never have read the specification your child is entered against. And a genuinely excellent teacher whose experience sits on another curriculum, a national system, an American high school programme or a different board, will teach the content well and misjudge the conventions. Both are experienced. Neither is experienced at the thing being bought.

The practical move is to decide which of these you need before looking at anybody. A student with a content gap and low confidence needs the explainer. A student scoring below their understanding needs the marker. A student in the term before an entry decision needs the head of department. Most families need the second of those and buy the first, because the first is easier to find, cheaper and more pleasant to interview.

sections.heading: Nobody licenses a tutor, so check who could confirm the claim instead
paragraphs: Schools in the Kingdom sit inside a regulatory structure. Private and international schools hold licences from the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which also operates services for approving international accreditation bodies. Private tutoring sits outside all of it. There is no register of tutors, no inspection, no renewal and no complaints route. Any provider describing itself as accredited in this market should be read carefully, because there is no body in the Kingdom that accredits tutors.

That sounds like a reason to despair and is actually a reason to be systematic. Most experience claims have somebody behind them who could in principle confirm them, and the useful question is simply who. A teaching qualification was issued by a named jurisdiction and carries a number. An examining role was an appointment by a board for a named component and a named series. Employment at a school is a fact the school holds. A degree is on a transcript. Each of those is a different kind of evidence with a different owner.

The claims with nobody behind them are the ones to discount entirely. Accredited tutor. Certified coach. A results percentage with no sample size, no date and no method. A rating out of five from an unnamed population. None of these can be checked by anyone, which does not make the person dishonest but does make the claim worthless as information. Ask instead for the two or three things that have an owner, and judge the rest on the trial lesson.

sections.heading: Why the experienced pool inside the Kingdom is thinner than families expect
paragraphs: This is the part that makes the rest of the page make sense. The senior end of an international school is small, and licensing and demand together decide where those schools exist. In a city with three or four international schools, a subject like Additional Mathematics might have one set across the whole city, taught by one person. In a camp or industrial community the senior department may be two or three teachers covering everything between them. Nobody is doing anything wrong in either case; that is simply what a small cohort produces.

Staff mobility compounds it. International-school teaching in the region runs on contracts, and a department can lose the one person who had taught a specification for years at the end of a contract cycle. The replacement may be stronger overall and still be new to that syllabus version, which is invisible to a parent until marks come back from a mock. Families reading a school's evaluation outcome should also understand what it measures: evaluation looks at the school, not at whether one department has recent experience of one component.

Distance finishes the job. In Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province conurbation a family can at least shop around locally. In Al Ahsa, Najran, Ha'il or Jazan there may be no second opinion within an hour and a half's drive. Saying that plainly is more useful than pretending the local market can always answer the question, and it is the honest basis for teaching online: the constraint being removed is not convenience, it is the size of the pool a family can reach at all.

sections.heading: Switching into IGCSE part-way through, and what experience is worth there
paragraphs: Mid-course arrivals are common across the Kingdom and especially in the north-west, where communities are growing quickly. A student joining an IGCSE year from elsewhere is not primarily a teaching problem; they are a comparison problem. Somebody has to work out what the previous course covered, what the new entry demands, where the two genuinely differ and where they only appear to. That is the work a tutor experienced in both systems can do in two sessions and an inexperienced one cannot do at all.

The commonest misdiagnosis is treating a vocabulary gap as a content gap. A student from a national-curriculum school may understand electrolysis perfectly and not know the English terms the mark scheme requires, which looks identical to not knowing the topic and takes a tenth of the time to fix. The reverse error also happens: a student from an American high school programme who has met a topic briefly is assumed to have covered it, and the shortfall only appears in the Extended paper. Reading marked work rather than a transcript is the only way to tell.

What is realistic in one term depends mostly on which subject. English and the humanities absorb a mid-year arrival reasonably well. Mathematics at Extended tier and the separate sciences are the hardest to pick up late, because each depends on a sequence built earlier. The honest conversation sets out what can be recovered before the series, what should be deferred, and whether a November entry for one component is the better plan than forcing all of them into June.

sections.heading: Two calendars in one city, and when support should actually start
paragraphs: Two school years run side by side in every Saudi city and they do not line up. Public schools licensed by the Ministry of Education run a two-semester year that opens in late August and closes in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, with dates that differ school by school inside the same city. Two neighbours can therefore be on holiday in different weeks.

This matters for support because the sensible starting point is defined by distance from the examination series, not by a month. On a three-term calendar the natural moment to begin content work is early in the year with two terms still ahead, which leaves the tier conversation comfortably before the entry deadline. On a two-semester calendar the same distance falls at a different point in the household's year, and families who synchronise with a neighbour's school rather than with their own lose several weeks.

The practical instruction is short. Read your own school's published calendar, not a general one, and count backwards from the series rather than forwards from the first day of term. Then agree in advance what happens to a weekly slot during each break, because an abandoned slot gets filled and a paused one with an agreed restart date does not. During Ramadan school days shorten and household routines move later, so it is worth agreeing a different weekly time for that period in advance rather than cancelling.

sections.heading: The evening slot, the clock, and the week an arrangement has to survive
paragraphs: The school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. Pages written for other markets inherit a Monday-to-Friday assumption and get this wrong, which matters because it changes which evenings are usable. Sunday carries the restart of the week and is the worst evening for demanding technique work. Wednesday and Thursday sit against the weekend, which makes them the best slots when a session sets written work to be completed before the next one.

Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks. A tutor based in a country that does will drift by an hour twice a year unless the slot is pinned to Saudi local time in writing at the outset. That one sentence in the arrangement prevents the most common scheduling failure in cross-border tutoring. The arithmetic also tells you which tutors can realistically hold a slot over a whole year: a six o'clock Saudi evening is an ordinary working afternoon in Europe and a late evening in India, and the difference shows up in month four rather than week one.

Experience matters here in a mundane way. A tutor who has taught Saudi families before will propose a slot that survives a school run, a shortened Ramadan day and a three-week break. A tutor who has not will propose one that works in their own week and will keep asking to move it. Ask directly how many Saudi-based students they currently teach and at what times, and ask what they do about the long summer break. The answers are concrete and they predict the next twelve months better than a credential does.

sections.heading: What the school owns, what you own, and where a tutor fits
paragraphs: Confusion about responsibility causes more damage in this market than weak teaching does. The school makes the entry, chooses the tier, marks and submits any school-assessed component, and runs its own supervision of that work. The board owns the syllabus, sets and marks the papers, moderates school marking and issues the certificate. The family owns the decision to buy outside help and the record of what that help consisted of. A tutor has no standing in any of it, which is exactly why the honesty line has to be explicit.

A tutor may teach the content, explain how published criteria work, work through a comparable task that is not the assessed one, read a draft the student has written and give written feedback on it. A tutor may not supply sentences, dictate a structure paragraph by paragraph, provide data the student did not gather, or improve a draft to the point where the improvement is theirs rather than the candidate's. Several providers competing for these searches will offer to do exactly those things. The penalty for accepting falls on the student: a component mark can be withheld, and in serious cases a grade or a certificate is affected.

The protective habit is a record, and it costs a family a few minutes a week. Dated session notes. The written feedback as it was sent. The student's own drafts in sequence. If a school ever asks how a piece of work developed, that trail answers the question. Nobody's assurance substitutes for having it, and an experienced tutor will suggest keeping it before being asked, because they have seen what happens when a question is raised and nothing has been kept.

sections.heading: From the certificate to a university decision: equivalency and the Qiyas tests
paragraphs: The document a Saudi university acts on is not the IGCSE statement of results. Equivalency, or mu'adalah, is a Ministry of Education decision taken on the final secondary certificate, and it applies in the same way to an IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma. IGCSE grades sit beneath that, as the conditions a post-16 department sets for its own courses and as the evidence a school reads when arguing Higher Level against Standard Level. Families should work from the Ministry's own published requirements rather than from a summary written by anybody else.

Alongside equivalency sit the Qiyas tests, run by the National Center for Assessment under the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, examines verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than taught content and may be sat in Arabic or in English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects and follows the Saudi national curriculum. That last fact is the one worth telling an international-curriculum family early: the overlap with an IGCSE or Diploma course is partial, and the framing is unfamiliar even where the material is not.

No page should publish a threshold or a weighting formula for either test, because institutions set their own and they differ by university and by programme. Competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili, and some institutions state a maximum age for the secondary certificate they will accept. The only durable advice is to read the receiving university's own published admission criteria, and to read them a year before the application rather than during it.

sections.heading: The recommendation, stated plainly
paragraphs: Having laid out the options, here is the view. Buy experience in the specification your child is entered against, confirmed by something with an owner, and treat every other kind of experience as a tie-breaker rather than a reason. For most families that means a specialist who has taught the code and tier recently and can produce a marked past-paper answer to show how they work. It does not mean the person with the longest list of years, and it does not mean the most expensive hour available.

Sequence the decision rather than making it all at once. Get the entry line from the school in writing. Send recent marked work. Take the free trial lesson with the person who would actually teach, and judge it on whether the session worked from the script in front of them. Agree the plan, the slot and the reporting in writing, with the slot pinned to Saudi local time. Then read the written notes after each session, and review at the end of a block against marked work from before and after.

What should stop you is also simple. No evidence of specification knowledge after two sessions. No written notes. A recommendation of many weekly hours before anybody has seen marked work. An offer to help produce assessed work, which is a reason to end the conversation rather than negotiate it. Experience that cannot show its workings is indistinguishable from confidence, and at this level the difference between those two things is measured in marks.

process.title: Get the entry line in writing
process.description: Subject, syllabus or specification code, tier, component numbers and variant, as the school holds it. The examinations officer will provide this on request. Matching an experience claim to anything less specific than that line is guesswork, and it is the step families most often skip.

process.title: Decide which kind of experience you need
process.description: A content gap, a technique problem and an imminent tier decision call for three different backgrounds. Deciding this before looking at anybody stops the choice being made by whoever interviews best. The first section of this page sets out which background suits which situation.

process.title: Ask for the one checkable thing
process.description: A marked past-paper answer, an annotated specification page, or the component and series of an examining appointment. One piece of evidence with an owner behind it is worth more than a page of claims, and a specialist produces it without preparation.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: One session with the person who would teach, at no cost and with no commitment. Judge it on whether it worked from your child's marked script rather than from a textbook, and on whether anything was written down at the end. Those two things predict the term ahead.

process.title: Fix the slot and the reporting
process.description: Agree the weekly time against Arabia Standard Time rather than the tutor's clock, agree what happens during school breaks and during Ramadan, and agree what will be reported and when. Writing it down at the start prevents almost every scheduling dispute that follows.

process.title: Review against marked work
process.description: At the end of a block, compare marked attempts at the same component before and after, under the same conditions. Continue, change tutor, change component or stop. A good arrangement makes that review easy because the evidence already exists in writing.

whyPoints.title: Experience described, not asserted
whyPoints.description: Each specialist is introduced by what they have actually taught and marked: the board, the code, the tier, the component. Where a claim has an owner we say who it is. Where it has none, we do not make it, which is why no results percentages appear anywhere on this page.

whyPoints.title: The pool is national, not local
whyPoints.description: Because lessons run online, a family in Najran or Al Ahsa reaches the same specialists as a family in Riyadh. That matters most in the subjects a small senior department cannot staff, where the local alternative is a capable generalist rather than somebody who has taught the component.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the entry, not the subject
whyPoints.description: We ask for the code, the tier and the component list before matching, because those four facts decide which experience is relevant. A request for help with physics can be answered by almost anyone; a request for Extended 0625 Paper 4 cannot.

whyPoints.title: Built for the Saudi week
whyPoints.description: Sunday to Thursday, Arabia Standard Time, slots pinned to Saudi local time so a clock change abroad does not move them. Breaks and Ramadan are planned for in advance. These are small operational things that decide whether a weekly arrangement survives a full year.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, explain criteria and give written feedback on drafts the student has written. They do not supply sentences, structures or data. We state this because the opposite is openly sold in this market and the consequence falls on the candidate, not on the seller.

whyPoints.title: Free trial before any commitment
whyPoints.description: One session with the specialist who would teach the course, not with a sales contact and not with a different tutor. If the match is wrong, saying so at that point costs nothing, which is the only honest way to sell an arrangement that depends on fit.

faqs.question: How much English technical vocabulary does a student from a Saudi national-curriculum school have to build in their first IGCSE term?
faqs.answer: More than families expect and less than it first appears. The concepts usually transfer: a student who has studied electrolysis understands electrolysis. What has to be built is the specific English wording a mark scheme credits, subject by subject, which is perhaps a few hundred terms across three sciences and mathematics. It looks exactly like a content gap in a mock paper and takes a fraction of the time to repair. A tutor experienced in both systems identifies which it is by reading the marked script rather than the grade.

faqs.question: We are moving from an American high school into an IGCSE Year 11, so is one year enough?
faqs.answer: For English and the humanities, usually yes. For Extended mathematics and the separate sciences it depends entirely on how much depth the previous course carried, because those subjects build in sequence and a topic met briefly is not the same as a topic covered. The honest approach is to map the previous course against the new specification before committing, then decide subject by subject. Entering one component in a November series rather than forcing everything into June is often the better plan than compressing all of it.

faqs.question: Does an experienced tutor need to know the curriculum my child is leaving, or only the one they are joining?
faqs.answer: For a settled student, only the one they are joining. For a mid-course arrival, both, because the first job is comparison rather than teaching. Somebody has to establish what was covered, what the new entry demands, and where the two differ genuinely rather than only in vocabulary. A tutor who knows just the destination specification will treat every gap as new content and over-estimate the hours needed, which is expensive and demoralising for the student.

faqs.question: If we change board part-way through, who decides whether work already completed counts?
faqs.answer: The receiving school, within the rules of the board it enters candidates with. A school-assessed component completed for one specification generally cannot be carried across to another, because the criteria and the moderation differ. Ask the new school in writing what it will accept and what has to be redone, before the student starts. A tutor can tell you what the two specifications require and how large the gap is, but has no standing to decide what transfers.

faqs.question: Is it realistic to move from IGCSE into the Diploma Programme after relocating to another Saudi city?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, provided the subject choices line up and the move happens before the Diploma teaching is far along. The practical obstacles are whether the receiving school runs the Higher Level subjects the student needs, and whether the IGCSE tiers sat support them: Extended mathematics and the separate sciences are treated as assumed knowledge rather than revisited. Ask the receiving school which Higher Level sets are actually running this year, because a programme listed in a prospectus is not always staffed.

faqs.question: Why does a school in the Kingdom sometimes enter a subject through an examination centre instead of teaching it?
faqs.answer: Because the cohort is too small to justify a set, or because no suitable teacher is available. It is a legitimate arrangement and it means the student is examined without being taught by the school. Families often do not realise this has happened until they ask who teaches the subject and discover nobody does. If that is your situation, the outside tutor is not topping up a taught course; they are delivering the whole specification, which is a different brief and a different number of hours.

faqs.question: What should I ask a prospective Saudi school about who actually teaches the senior IGCSE sets?
faqs.answer: Four questions. Which subjects are taught by a specialist in that subject at the senior end. Which are covered by a teacher whose specialism is something else. Which are entered through an examination centre rather than taught. And how long the current teacher has taught this specification. Schools answer these when asked directly, and the answers tell a family far more about the next two years than any general description of the programme does.

faqs.question: What does a school evaluation outcome tell me about one IGCSE department?
faqs.answer: Very little, and this is worth knowing before putting weight on it. Evaluation looks at the school: leadership, safeguarding, provision, outcomes at the institutional level. It is not designed to report whether the chemistry department currently has somebody who has taught Extended 0620 recently, and that is the fact a family buying subject support actually needs. Read the evaluation for what it covers, then ask the department-level questions separately, because nothing in the published outcome answers them.

faqs.question: Our school's senior department has two teachers covering three sciences, so what does that mean in practice?
faqs.answer: It means at least one subject is being taught by somebody whose own specialism is a different science. They will teach the content competently. What tends to be missing is the examiner-level knowledge: which phrases a mark scheme accepts, how the alternative-to-practical paper is marked, where this cohort reliably loses marks. The symptom is a student who understands the subject and scores below that understanding, and it is repairable with a small number of hours aimed at conventions rather than content.

faqs.question: Why does a department that teaches a subject well still struggle to staff its hardest set?
faqs.answer: Because the hardest set needs somebody comfortable above the standard syllabus, and that is a narrower pool than the subject itself. Additional Mathematics is the clearest case in the Kingdom: it asks for calculus, series and identities that most IGCSE teachers do not use. Contract cycles make it worse, since a department can lose its one specialist at the end of a contract and replace them with somebody stronger overall but new to that course. Neither situation reflects badly on the school.

faqs.question: Which evening of the Sunday-to-Thursday week is the worst one to book a demanding session?
faqs.answer: Sunday. The week has just restarted after the Friday and Saturday weekend, the household is resetting and attention is at its lowest, so a timed paper or new technique work lands badly. Use Sunday for light review and for planning what written work the week will produce. Wednesday and Thursday are the strongest slots, because both sit against the weekend, which gives a student time to complete work the session sets and a tutor time to mark it.

faqs.question: The Kingdom does not change its clocks, so what breaks when the tutor's country does?
faqs.answer: The slot moves by an hour, twice a year, in opposite directions, and nobody notices until somebody misses a session. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 all year. The fix is one sentence agreed at the start: the lesson is at a fixed Saudi local time, and the tutor's local time is whatever that happens to be. Written down, the problem never occurs. Left implicit, it produces two confused weeks every year and usually a lost session.

faqs.question: How should a weekly slot be handled during Ramadan so that it is not lost?
faqs.answer: Agree a replacement time in advance rather than cancelling week by week. School days shorten and household routines move later, so the regular slot often stops working, and a slot that is simply dropped gets filled by somebody else. Families who agree a later weekly time for the period, and a date to return to the usual one, keep both the tutor and the rhythm. It is a two-minute conversation held several weeks early rather than a problem solved during.

faqs.question: Our school runs three terms and a colleague's runs two semesters, so why does that change when we start?
faqs.answer: Because the right starting point is a distance from the examination series, not a date on a calendar. Public schools licensed by the Ministry of Education run a two-semester year; most international and British-curriculum schools run three terms with dates they set themselves. The same distance from the June papers therefore falls at different points in two households in the same city. Count backwards from the series using your own school's published calendar, and ignore what the neighbours are doing.

faqs.question: Can a family hold a weekly slot through a long summer break without paying for it?
faqs.answer: Ask at the point of agreeing the arrangement, because practice varies and an assumption made in silence usually goes against the family. What works is an explicit pause with a restart date, agreed in writing, so the tutor knows the slot returns and does not fill it. Some families keep a reduced frequency through the break instead, which holds the slot and keeps a difficult subject warm. What rarely works is stopping without a plan and expecting the same time to be available.

faqs.question: How much notice is needed to move a regular weekly time once a term has started?
faqs.answer: Expect to give a couple of weeks for a permanent change and to accept that the new time may not exist. Evening slots between five and seven o'clock Saudi time are the most contested hours in the week, because they suit both the student and tutors across several time zones. A one-off reschedule for a school trip or an internal examination is a different matter and is normally straightforward with a few days' notice. Agree both rules at the start rather than negotiating them under pressure.

experienced-igcse-tutor.closingHeading: Buy the experience that matches the entry
experienced-igcse-tutor.closingBody: Ask your school for the entry line in writing: subject, code, tier, components and variant. Decide from this page which kind of experience your child's situation actually calls for. Then ask one prospective tutor for one piece of evidence with an owner behind it, and take the free trial lesson with the person who would teach. Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video, on Arabia Standard Time and against the Sunday-to-Thursday week, which is what makes a specification specialist reachable from Najran, Jubail or Tabuk rather than only from the three largest cities in the Kingdom.

intro.heading: Expert is a word; a subject guide is a document
paragraphs: Every tutoring site in this market calls its tutors expert. The word costs nothing to print, which is why it tells you nothing. What a Saudi family is actually trying to establish is narrower and completely checkable: does this person teach the subject at the level my child sits, against the current subject guide, and can they say where the marks go? That question has an answer. The word does not. Asked in the first ten minutes of a trial lesson, it separates a specialist from a generalist faster than any profile page.

The second thing a family is trying to establish is who is responsible for what. A school in the Kingdom sits inside a regulated system: private and international schools are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, ETEC. That system governs the institution. It does not reach down to whether the teacher taking Higher Level Physics this year has taught Higher Level Physics before. That gap is where an outside specialist earns a place.

This page is built as a decision rather than a pitch. There are four kinds of help available to a family in Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province, and they are not interchangeable: the school's own support, a group revision centre, an in-home tutor from your district, and a one-to-one online subject specialist. Each fixes a different problem. Buying the wrong one is the most common and most expensive mistake in this market, and it usually happens because nobody laid the four out side by side.

IB Gram matches students to one-to-one tutors and lessons are delivered online, over live video, timed to Arabia Standard Time. No tutor is sent to a Saudi address; home visits are a service offered only in India. That is stated before anything else because the phrase families search for says home, and a page that lets the ambiguity stand is selling something it does not have. The argument for online teaching is made below on cost, pool size and scheduling rather than asserted.

What follows is the system a Saudi family works inside: what a school licence covers, how to test an expertise claim in one question, how the assessment actually pays out marks, what changes year group by year group from the Middle Years Programme to DP2, and the university endgame of Ministry of Education equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili. Advertised SAR rates are quoted where they help, always as what other providers publish rather than as a market average or as a price here. Where a figure cannot be verified, this page describes the mechanism and leaves the number out, which is the honest way to write about money in a market this opaque.
