hail.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach to a mark scheme rather than to a textbook. They cover Diploma Programme subjects at both levels, Middle Years Programme courses, and Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE papers, and they work with Ha'il students in the evening on Saudi local time. Matching is by board, syllabus code and level.

intro.heading: Find the leak before buying the hours
paragraphs: A student who is two grades short is rarely two grades short of knowing things. Look at a marked script and the shortfall almost always resolves into four or five repeating faults: an explain question answered as a description, a correct number with no working a marker can credit, a units slip in the final line, a last question left blank because the first three took too long, and an investigation whose research question was never answerable with the data collected. Each of those is a separate, teachable fault. Together they routinely account for the gap between a five and a seven, and none of them is fixed by covering the syllabus again.

This matters more in Ha'il than in Riyadh or Dhahran, because a student here has fewer places to notice the problem. In a large Diploma cohort a weak paper technique shows up against thirty classmates sitting the same mock. In a city where Diploma-level international provision is not established locally, a student may be the only person in their year sitting that course, or taking it through a school in another city entirely. There is no local distribution to be ranked against, so a comfortable internal grade can sit above what an external paper would actually pay.

Ha'il's geography then decides when any of this can be worked on. The city sits on the plain between the Aja range to the west and the Salma hills to the south-east, and it is a long drive or a short domestic flight from Riyadh. Inside the city journeys are short by Gulf standards, but the day still fills from both ends: school finishes in the early afternoon, the heat pushes activity into the evening, and the usable teaching window is a block in the middle of the evening rather than a flexible afternoon. A plan that ignores that produces a timetable nobody keeps.

IB Gram teaches Ha'il students one-to-one over live video. There are no home visits in Ha'il or anywhere in the Kingdom — in-home teaching is something we offer only in India — and for a northern city that is the point rather than a compromise. The number of people within driving distance of Ha'il who have taught Physics HL or Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry to examination standard is very small. Over video, the question stops being who lives near you and becomes who knows the paper your child is sitting.

What follows is ordered the way a diagnosis runs. First the specific marks a student here tends to lose and why. Then command terms, which are the largest single fixable fault in both the IB and International GCSE systems. Then the hours the school run leaves, and the routes available when a school cannot offer the qualification a destination university wants. Then the first month, what it has to prove, and what it costs. The money is near the end because it is the least informative number on this page until the rest is settled.
bullets: Four or five repeating faults, not general weakness, explain most of a two-grade gap
A student with no local cohort has no external benchmark, so internal grades can flatter
The usable lesson window in Ha'il is a mid-evening block, not a flexible afternoon
The IB Diploma is taken through an IB World School; Cambridge and Edexcel allow private candidates
Diagnosis starts from a marked script and a timed paper, never from a report card

hail.programmesIntro: Four qualifications cover almost every request from Ha'il, and the first question for each is not what it contains but how a student in this province can actually access and sit it. That access question is answered differently by the IB and by the two International GCSE boards.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, with no external papers and no grades in the familiar sense. Progress is reported against learning outcomes and the programme closes with the Exhibition. Because nothing is externally marked, weakness is easy to miss: a child can be described as engaged and curious and still be unable to write a paragraph that holds together or recall a times table without counting.
programmes.countryNote: Very few Ha'il families meet this programme locally, and most of those who ask about it are planning a move or comparing it with a national-curriculum primary school. The practical advice is the same either way: measure reading age and written output directly rather than relying on a narrative report, because those two things predict the next five years more reliably than anything else at this stage.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Each subject is marked against four criteria, each out of 8, which are then converted to a grade from 1 to 7. The criteria reward investigating, communicating and reflecting as much as knowing, so presentation of thinking is assessed directly. The Personal Project in the final year is assessed on process — the journal matters as much as the artefact.
programmes.countryNote: A Ha'il student in this programme is usually enrolled with a school elsewhere, sometimes online. The gap that opens is examination stamina: the Middle Years criteria do not require a student to sit a long timed paper, so a student can arrive at International GCSE or Diploma level articulate, reflective and completely unpractised at answering twenty questions in ninety minutes.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. The core adds up to three points on top of 42 from subjects. There are also failing conditions beyond the points total — too many low grades, a failed core component — which catch students who focus only on the arithmetic. Internal Assessment is marked in school and moderated externally.
programmes.countryNote: There is no private-candidate route into the Diploma. A student has to be enrolled with an IB World School, which for a Ha'il family means relocating, boarding, or enrolling with a school that teaches the programme online and supervises the Internal Assessment itself. That decision belongs before any tutoring conversation, because it determines who holds the deadlines.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Both boards run a June series and a November series. Cambridge splits several subjects into Core and Extended tiers, and the Core tier limits the top grade available; Edexcel generally runs one tier per subject. The syllabus code on the entry list, not the subject title, tells you which papers a student will actually sit and which formula sheets they can expect.
programmes.countryNote: This is the realistic route for a Ha'il student whose school does not offer an international qualification, because both boards accept private candidates. The family has to find an examination centre that takes them, and the entry window closes months before the June series. Teaching can be arranged online; the centre and the entry cannot be improvised late.

hail.subjectsIntro: Below are the Diploma subjects Ha'il families most often need teaching for, each described by where the marks go rather than by what the course contains. A syllabus list tells a parent nothing useful. A loss point tells them what the next eight weeks should be spent on.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Method is the mark. Students who learned to compute mentally lose the argument marks that a written solution earns, and the Higher Level proof topics punish that habit hardest. Induction, complex numbers and vectors are where students without a disciplined layout stall, usually several months after the content was first taught.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The calculator does the arithmetic, so the marks sit in the interpretation. A regression line computed correctly and then left uncommented scores the first marks and not the last. Higher Level adds a substantial statistics and probability load, and the common failure is confusing a correlation result with a claim about cause.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Three reliable leaks: definitions given in loose words where the mark scheme expects precise ones, graph gradients read without checking what each axis actually plots, and unit or power-of-ten slips in the final line. Higher Level adds topics with no Standard Level equivalent, so a student cannot revise from Standard Level notes.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Equations lose marks before concepts do: missing state symbols, unbalanced charges, incomplete ionic equations. Energetics and equilibrium then separate grades at Higher Level, and the data booklet only helps a student who has practised finding things in it under time rather than reading it afterwards.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The highest-volume content in the group, and the subject where command terms matter most. Outline, describe, explain, evaluate and discuss each want a different structure, and a student who writes everything they know about respiration is paid for a fraction of it. Precision in definitions is examined strictly.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Four skills assessed, and text type is where marks are quietly lost. A blog, a formal letter, a speech and a report are each marked partly on register and convention, so a linguistically strong answer in the wrong form is capped. Higher Level expects a sustained argument rather than competent description.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysis in Arabic of both literary and non-literary texts, with the same assessment architecture as the English A courses. Fluent speakers often assume the course is straightforward and then lose marks on structured analysis and on the global-issue link in the individual oral, neither of which fluency supplies on its own.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams carry marks that prose cannot recover, and the common failure is a diagram drawn correctly but shifted in the wrong direction or left unlabelled. Higher Level adds quantitative questions. Internal Assessment commentaries need articles with enough detail to apply a named concept to, which is a selection problem before it is a writing one.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Case studies are the currency. A student who can name a place, a figure and a date for each process earns the application marks; one who argues in generalities does not. Map, graph and data-response skills are assessed throughout, and the Higher Level extension expects synthesis across topics rather than more detail within one.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Studies have to be used, not just recalled. Marks come from selecting a relevant study and explaining precisely how it supports the point, and the research-methods strand catches students who learned conclusions without the design behind them. Higher Level adds extensions to each approach, examined with the same evidence discipline.

hail.igcseSubjectsIntro: International GCSE is the practical route for most Ha'il students, including those entering as private candidates. The codes below are the ones to confirm against a centre's entry list before any teaching is booked, because a syllabus title is shared across boards and a code is not.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics
igcseSubjects.description: Tier choice is the first decision and the most consequential. A student entered on the Cambridge Core tier cannot reach the top grades however well they perform, and moving tier is an entry-deadline matter rather than a teaching one. Edexcel Mathematics A runs Foundation and Higher papers with the same logic.

igcseSubjects.name: Additional Mathematics
igcseSubjects.description: Worth considering for a student heading towards Mathematics AA HL or A Level Mathematics, because it introduces calculus and more formal algebra a year early. It is demanding and only sensible alongside a secure grade in the main mathematics course, not as a substitute for fixing one.

igcseSubjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences
igcseSubjects.description: Biology, chemistry and physics assessed as a double award rather than three separate subjects. It suits a student whose destination does not demand three separate science grades, and it reduces examination load considerably. Check against the entry requirements of the course the student eventually wants before choosing it.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics
igcseSubjects.description: Formula recall differs between the boards, which is the first thing to establish for a student who has changed board or centre. Both reward practical reasoning assessed through written questions: identifying a control variable, spotting the source of an anomalous reading, explaining why a method improves precision.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language
igcseSubjects.description: A different qualification from First Language English, and the choice between them should be made on a timed writing sample rather than on confidence in conversation. Reading comprehension under time and the directed-writing task are where marks concentrate, and both respond quickly to structured practice.

igcseSubjects.name: Geography
igcseSubjects.description: Skills questions — maps, cross-sections, graph reading, data interpretation — are the most reliably learnable marks on the paper and the ones students prepare least. Case-study recall then carries the extended questions, and a student needs specific named examples rather than general description.

igcseSubjects.name: History
igcseSubjects.description: Source questions follow a fixed logic: provenance, purpose, and what the source can and cannot be used to show. Students who narrate the events score below students who answer the question asked about them. Essay structure is a technical skill here and improves faster than content knowledge.

igcseSubjects.name: Information and Communication Technology
igcseSubjects.description: Often confused with Computer Science, which is a separate qualification assessing algorithms and data representation. ICT includes practical components, so a student needs access to the required software and time on it. Confirm with the centre which papers and practical sessions a private candidate can sit.

hail.regionsTitle: Ha'il city and province: where students join from
hail.regionsIntro: Distance to a tutor is irrelevant when lessons run over video. Distance to a school, a prayer time and a family evening is not, and in Ha'il the pattern differs between the central quarters, the newer edges and the towns out in the province. These notes are about what the day leaves free.

regions.name: Barzan
regions.note: The historic core, anchored by the old market area. Journeys from here are short in distance and slow at the end of the working day, so an evening slot set after the traffic has cleared holds far better than one set to a predicted gap.

regions.name: Samah
regions.note: Established central-north residential streets with a settled routine. Families here tend to want a fixed weekday hour repeated every week rather than a rotating slot, which also suits a scarce-subject tutor who is holding the hour open.

regions.name: Al Nuqrah
regions.note: A large residential district where the school run is short but the evening is busy. A shorter session twice a week is usually easier to hold here than one long session, particularly for a student carrying two weak subjects at once.

regions.name: Aja
regions.note: On the western side, towards the Aja range that gives the district its name. Lower density, longer internal journeys, and families who are often the most willing to use the Friday or Saturday daytime for an intensive block before a series.

regions.name: Al Khuzama
regions.note: Newer housing on the city's expanding edge, with a younger demographic and a lot of primary and lower-secondary enquiries. The common request here is foundation work in English writing and arithmetic before an international course begins.

regions.name: The university quarter
regions.note: The area around the University of Ha'il, where academic households are concentrated. Parents here usually arrive with a clear view of the destination degree, which makes the subject-prerequisite conversation shorter and the Higher Level choices more deliberate.

regions.name: Baqa'a
regions.note: A town out in the province to the north of the city. Schooling is local and international provision is not, so students here are the clearest case for online teaching: the alternative is a daily drive that no study week survives.

regions.name: Al Ghazalah
regions.note: South-east of Ha'il on the route towards Qassim. Families here often weigh boarding in a larger city against staying put and taking an international qualification as a private candidate, and that choice sets everything else about the plan.

schoolClusters.city: Riyadh — the nearest concentration of Diploma Programme provision
schoolClusters.note: For a Ha'il family considering relocation or boarding, Riyadh is the first place they look, because the Diploma is offered at several schools there. Students we support attend schools of this kind. Admission timelines and subject availability vary campus by campus, so the question to ask is which Higher Level subjects will actually run.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah and the Eastern Province — the other two established clusters
schoolClusters.note: Families with work ties to the coast or to the industrial east consider these instead. The Diploma is offered at a limited number of campuses, and British-curriculum provision is wider than IB provision in both places. Neither cluster is reachable daily from Ha'il, which is why the online route exists.

hail.schoolDisclaimer: These schools are named only to describe where international provision in the Kingdom is concentrated; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them and claims no endorsement from any school or group.
hail.modesIntro: Ha'il requests fall into four shapes, and they are genuinely different jobs rather than different package names. All are taught one-to-one over live video in a slot fixed to Saudi local time.

modes.title: Fault-fixing weekly sessions
modes.description: The default. One hour a week aimed at the specific loss points a marked script showed, with the school's current topic kept in view. The work is narrow on purpose: one fault at a time, re-tested two weeks later under the same conditions to check the fix held without prompting.

modes.title: Full-course teaching for a subject the school does not run
modes.description: Where a Ha'il school cannot offer a subject at all, a tutor teaches the whole specification rather than supplementing a class. This is a larger commitment — usually two sessions a week across the course — and it only works with the entry route settled first, because the teaching has to be aimed at a specific board, code and series.

modes.title: Private-candidate preparation and entry planning
modes.description: For students sitting Cambridge or Edexcel papers outside their own school. Alongside the teaching, this covers the parts families get wrong: which centre will accept the entry, when its window closes, which papers and practical components apply, and what the student has to bring. The entry itself remains the family's to make.

modes.description: A short, bounded piece of work for families who are not yet sure tutoring is the answer. Two or three sessions: a timed paper, a marked analysis of where the marks went, and a written view of what would need to change and roughly how long it would take. Families regularly use this and then do nothing for a term, which is a legitimate outcome.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go in a Ha'il student's script
paragraphs: Ask for the script, not the report. A school report says a student is capable but inconsistent, which is a description of the symptom. A marked paper with the mark scheme beside it says exactly which marks were available and which were taken, and the pattern is almost always narrower than a parent expects. Across hundreds of Diploma and International GCSE scripts the same six faults recur, and the first four of them are technique rather than knowledge.

The largest is command-term misreading. A question that says explain wants a causal chain; a student who describes what happens has answered a different question accurately and earned part of the mark. The second is unshown method, which is a habit built by years of being praised for fast mental arithmetic and then penalised by a mark scheme that pays for a visible argument. The third is the units and significant-figures line, which students treat as tidiness and examiners treat as a mark. The fourth is the time budget: a student who has revised thoroughly but never sat a whole paper against the clock will produce a strong first half and an empty last page.

Two faults are structural rather than habitual. Internal Assessment scope is one: a research question chosen because it sounded interesting, then pursued with data that cannot answer it, caps the mark at the planning criterion regardless of how good the write-up is. Technical English is the other, and it is more common in a city where subject content has been learned partly in one language and is assessed entirely in another. A student can hold the right idea and express it in a form the mark scheme cannot credit, which reads on a report as weak understanding and is not.

Each of those has a specific fix and a measurable test for whether the fix held. That is why the first month of any plan here is built around a timed paper and a re-test rather than around content coverage. The table names each fault, what it looks like in a script, and what actually closes it.

sections.heading: Command terms are the largest single fixable fault
paragraphs: Both the IB and the International GCSE boards publish their command terms, and both expect students to treat them as instructions with a defined shape. State wants a fact with no justification. Describe wants the features, in order, without explanation. Explain wants a causal chain in which each link is stated. Compare wants both similarities and differences, in parallel. Evaluate and discuss want a weighed judgement with the judgement actually made. Suggest accepts a reasoned possibility rather than the single right answer. None of that is secret, and almost no student is taught it as a separate skill.

The consequence is visible in any marked script. A six-mark explain question answered with six accurate descriptive statements earns two or three marks, and the student reads the result as not knowing enough biology. They then revise more biology, sit another paper, and lose the marks again in the same place. This is the single most common reason tutoring that consists of re-teaching content produces no movement: the content was never the fault.

The fix is mechanical and fast. Take questions the student has already answered and already knows the content of, and rewrite them to the term. Keep the topic constant so the only variable is the shape of the answer. Then test it cold two weeks later on an unseen question with the same term. Most students need four to six weeks of this before the habit holds without prompting, and the gain appears across every subject at once, which is why it is worth doing first rather than alongside everything else.

Mark allocations deserve the same treatment. A two-mark question wants two creditable points and nothing more; a student writing a paragraph for it is spending minutes they will need for the eight-mark question later. Reading the mark allocation as a word budget is a learnable habit, and in a city where a student may not have a large cohort to compare pace against, it is one of the few technique disciplines that can be built entirely from past papers and a clock.

sections.heading: The school run, and the hours a lesson can realistically occupy
paragraphs: The Saudi school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. That alone rules out most of the scheduling advice written for this market, which is routinely adapted from British or Indian pages and offers a Saturday morning as the obvious slot. In Ha'il, Saturday is the second weekend day and Sunday morning is a school morning. Weekday evenings are the working currency, and Friday and Saturday daytime are available for intensive blocks rather than for routine weekly teaching.

Within a weekday the shape is tighter than in a bigger city, not looser. Ha'il journeys are short, so a family does not lose ninety minutes to a commute the way a Dammam or Riyadh family might. But school finishes in the early afternoon, the middle of the day is not usable for concentrated work, and the evening carries prayer times, family time and homework. What survives is a block in the middle of the evening. Families who try to start a demanding Higher Level session straight after the school return almost always find it is the first commitment to slip, because the student is not ready to work and nobody wants to say so.

Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, applies with no seasonal change anywhere in the Kingdom. A tutor in a country that does change its clocks will see an agreed time drift twice a year unless the slot is written down in Saudi local time, and a drift of an hour is enough to move a session into a school night. We fix slots in Saudi local time for that reason. A tutor based in India sits two and a half hours ahead, which makes a mid-evening Ha'il lesson a late-evening one for them: workable midweek, tiring as a long double session.

School calendars add the last constraint. Public schools in the Kingdom run two semesters from late August to late June with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, which differ between schools in the same city. Ramadan shortens the school day and reshapes the evening, and most families either move the session later or pause for the month. The table below is the hour-by-hour version of a Ha'il school night.

sections.heading: Studying for a qualification your school does not run
paragraphs: This is the position most Ha'il families who contact us are in. The student is at a good local school, the destination is a university that wants an international qualification, and the school does not offer one at the level required. There are four real routes, and they differ in cost, disruption and how much the family has to arrange themselves. Choosing between them is a decision that should be made before any teaching starts, because each route sets a different board, a different deadline and a different examination venue.

The two International GCSE boards both accept private candidates, which makes them the flexible option. A student stays at their school, is taught the specification separately, and sits the papers at a centre that accepts external entries. The teaching can be online; the entry cannot be arranged late. Entry windows close months before the June series, centres differ in which subjects and which practical components they will take, and a family that leaves this until the spring term has usually lost a year. Ask a centre directly, early, and get the answer in writing.

The Diploma works differently and the difference matters. There is no private-candidate entry for the IB Diploma. A student must be enrolled with an IB World School, which means relocating to Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province, boarding, or enrolling with a school that delivers the programme online and supervises the Internal Assessment itself. That last option is real and it is how a number of students in smaller Saudi cities take the Diploma, but the school — not the tutor — owns the deadlines, the coursework supervision and the examination arrangements.

A Level as a private or school candidate is the fourth route, and for a student aiming at a British or Commonwealth university it is often the most efficient. Fewer subjects, deeper specialisation, and subject prerequisites that map directly onto what the destination course asks for. The trade is breadth: a student who may still change direction keeps more doors open with the Diploma, and one who is certain about engineering or medicine usually loses nothing by narrowing.

sections.heading: Switching into an international curriculum from a Ha'il school
paragraphs: A student moving from a national-curriculum school into Cambridge or Edexcel International GCSE carries over far more than families expect. The mathematics and science content overlaps heavily, and at Year 10 almost nothing of substance is missing. What does not carry over is the assessment culture, and that is where the first term goes. Marks are awarded for applying content to unfamiliar material rather than for reproducing it accurately, and extended-response questions want a position taken and defended rather than a complete account given.

Technical English is the second gap, and it is narrower and more fixable than it looks. A student may be conversationally fluent and still not know that describe, explain and evaluate are paid differently, or that a six-mark answer in biology has an expected shape. This is vocabulary and structure rather than language: forty or fifty standard explanatory sentences per science subject, practised until they are automatic, cover most of what the mark schemes credit. It responds to drilling in a way that general language study does not.

Timing the switch matters more than the switch itself. The start of Year 10 is clean, because the two-year International GCSE course begins there. A move part-way through Year 11 is difficult but survivable if the board is the same and the entry can still be made. A move into the final year of the Diploma is the hardest case in the system, because Internal Assessment work is already underway in six subjects and does not transfer cleanly between schools. Anybody who promises an easy version of that is not describing the Diploma.

Direction of travel changes the diagnosis too. A British-curriculum student entering the Diploma has the content and has to learn criterion-referenced marking and the core. An American-curriculum student usually has breadth and needs depth, and the gap appears at Higher Level in the sciences and in Mathematics AA. A national-curriculum student has the content and needs the assessment language. Each is a bounded, identifiable job, and each is best measured against a past paper in the first week rather than guessed at from a transcript.

sections.heading: The first month, and what it has to prove
paragraphs: Tutoring that cannot show its working is indistinguishable from tutoring that is not working. The first month exists to produce evidence, and the evidence is the student's own marked script rather than anybody's impression. The structure we use is the same regardless of subject: a trial lesson built around one real question, a baseline paper sat under time, teaching aimed at the largest single loss point, a re-test of exactly that loss point, and then a plan written against four weeks of actual data.

The baseline matters because it is the only honest benchmark a Ha'il student may have. Where a school has no established international cohort, internal grades carry no external calibration, and a student can be the strongest in a small group while sitting several grades below what an external paper would award. A full component sat under real conditions in week one removes that ambiguity. It is uncomfortable and it is cheaper than discovering the same thing in a mock eighteen months later.

Reporting is deliberately short and specific. After each session a parent receives a note naming what was covered, what was set, and what was weak — not a grade and not an encouragement. After four weeks the note becomes a plan: the ranked fault list, what has already moved, a realistic range rather than a target grade, and the number of sessions a week that range assumes. Where the honest answer is that the student needs a different subject supported, or no tutoring at all this term, the plan says so.

There is also a defined answer to the match being wrong. If a student and a tutor are not working after two or three sessions, the match changes and the next tutor starts from the same written diagnosis rather than from scratch. That happens often enough to be a normal part of the process rather than a failure, and a provider who treats it as an awkward exception is a provider who will leave a teenager with a tutor they have stopped listening to.

sections.heading: Preparing for a university abroad from Ha'il Province
paragraphs: Most families here who choose an international qualification are choosing it because of where the student is going next, and the destination sets the requirements rather than the other way round. A British or Commonwealth university will ask for A Level grades or a Diploma point total, with named subjects at Higher Level or A Level for anything technical. North American admissions look at the whole school record, standardised testing where it is still asked for, and evidence of activity outside the classroom. A European programme taught in English will usually ask for a Diploma total plus specific subjects and a language certificate.

The practical consequence is that Higher Level and A Level choices have to be made against a shortlist, not against preference. Engineering generally wants Mathematics AA at Higher Level rather than Applications and Interpretation, and will often specify Physics. Medicine wants chemistry and usually biology. Economics at competitive universities frequently specifies mathematics. A student who selects subjects in the first Diploma year without checking those prerequisites can close a destination without realising it, and the correction costs a year.

English language evidence is the step most often left late. Universities differ on whether a Diploma or International GCSE in English satisfies their requirement or whether a separate test is needed, and the answer differs by university and by programme. It is a question with a definite answer available in advance on each institution's own admissions pages, and it should be settled in the term before applications rather than in the month they are due.

A student who returns to study in the Kingdom afterwards, or who applies to a Saudi university alongside overseas options, needs the equivalency step as well: a foreign certificate requires an equivalency decision from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equal to the Saudi secondary certificate, and the Qiyas tests sit alongside it. Universities publish their own admission criteria per programme, and that is where a family should read rather than relying on a summary written by anyone else, including us.

sections.heading: What this costs from Ha'il, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Advertised rates for one-to-one tuition in the Kingdom span a wide band, and the band is informative once you know what each end represents. Tutoring platforms list general, non-specialist online tutoring from around SAR 55 an hour, and budget platforms advertise International GCSE one-to-one from around SAR 35. Tutor-marketplace guides put general private tuition for primary around SAR 50 and senior-school examination subjects in Riyadh at SAR 200 and above. Tutoring companies list IB subject tutoring from around SAR 180, with Higher Level and Advanced Placement tracks around SAR 200 to SAR 220, and international providers quoting in dollars sit near sixty dollars an hour. Those are advertised figures published by those vendors, not a market average, and none of them is our price.

Four variables move the number, and only one of them is negotiable. Subject scarcity is the largest: a Mathematics AA HL or Physics HL specialist costs more everywhere because there are fewer of them, and no amount of searching changes that. Level is next, with Higher Level above Standard Level and Diploma above International GCSE. Examining or marking experience is third, and it is worth paying for in the final year specifically, because what it buys is knowledge of what a script is paid for rather than what a textbook contains. Travel is fourth, and it is the one a Ha'il family escapes entirely by teaching over video, since an in-home tutor prices the drive into the hour.

The variable a family does control is timing. Weekly support started early enough is cheaper per grade than an intensive block bought under pressure, because demand concentrates before a series and the specialists fill first. A full-course arrangement for a subject a school does not offer costs more than supplementary support, simply because it is more hours; that is a volume difference rather than a premium. Pausing in a long break and holding a scarce slot are both reasonable, and the second one costs something because the tutor is turning other work away.

A blunt note on the cheap end of the range. For a Year 10 student two grades below target in a well-staffed subject, a capable non-specialist working from past papers can genuinely be enough. For a Higher Level student in the final Diploma year, or for a private candidate whose teaching has to cover a whole specification and aim at a specific paper, it is not, and families who try it generally pay twice. We quote per student after a trial lesson rather than publishing a rate, because the honest number depends on the subject, the level and how many weeks are left.

process.title: Send us the marked work, not the report
process.description: One recent marked paper or piece of coursework tells us more than a term of school reports. With the board, the syllabus code and the level we can name likely loss points before the first session, which means the trial lesson can go straight at the real problem instead of spending itself on introductions.

process.title: Settle the entry route before booking teaching
process.description: If the school does not enter the qualification, the centre and the entry window decide the teaching plan. Cambridge and Edexcel take private candidates; the Diploma does not. Getting this wrong is the one mistake on this page that cannot be fixed by working harder later.

process.title: A free trial lesson on one real question
process.description: An hour with the tutor we think fits, spent on an actual past-paper question rather than a conversation about goals. You find out whether the student will work with this person, and we find out whether the fault is content, technique or confidence. No charge and no commitment.

process.title: A baseline paper in the first week
process.description: A full component sat under real time pressure, marked against the published scheme. For a student with no large local cohort this is the only external calibration available, and it converts a vague sense of underperformance into a ranked list of where the marks went.

process.title: Four weeks, then a written plan and a decision
process.description: Teaching aimed at the largest fault, a cold re-test of it, and then a plan written against the evidence rather than against hope: a realistic range, the weekly commitment it assumes, and a clear recommendation. Continuing, changing subject, and stopping are all acceptable answers.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before hours
whyPoints.description: We will not quote a number of sessions before seeing a marked script and a timed paper. Most shortfalls turn out to be four or five repeating technique faults rather than missing content, and a plan built on that assumption costs a family less than one built on re-teaching a syllabus nobody had forgotten.

whyPoints.title: Distance is the honest argument here
whyPoints.description: There is no large pool of Diploma Higher Level specialists within reach of Ha'il, and pretending otherwise would be the easiest way to mis-sell this. Teaching over live video replaces the question of who lives nearby with the question of who knows the paper, which is the only one that affects a grade.

whyPoints.title: The entry route is treated as part of the job
whyPoints.description: For a private candidate the centre, the window and the component list matter as much as the teaching. We map them backwards from the series and tell a family plainly what they have to arrange themselves, because a brilliantly taught student with no valid entry has nothing to show for it.

whyPoints.title: Assessed work is questioned, not written
whyPoints.description: On an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a Personal Project, a tutor reads the student's draft, interrogates the method and names the criterion it does not yet meet. The student writes it. The school supervisor signs it off. We state this before anyone asks, because the alternative creates a malpractice risk the student carries.

whyPoints.title: Rates are attributed and claims are not made
whyPoints.description: Every figure on this page is an advertised rate published by a named type of source, with no market average implied. We publish no success percentages, no star ratings and no Qudurat or Tahsili thresholds, because those numbers move, differ by institution, and belong to whoever actually publishes them.

faqs.question: How late can a lesson start for a Ha'il student on a school night?
faqs.answer: Most families settle on a mid-evening hour, after the main meal and after homework has begun. Starting straight after the school return looks efficient and is reliably the first commitment to slip, because the student is not ready to work. Late-evening slots are workable close to a series but tend to cost the next school day, so we would rather hold a slightly earlier hour that survives a whole term. The slot is written down in Saudi local time, which means it does not move when a tutor's own country changes its clocks.

faqs.question: Can a Ha'il student take lessons on Friday or Saturday instead of a weekday evening?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for some students it is better. Friday and Saturday are the weekend in the Kingdom, so those are the only long, unbroken windows in the week. They suit intensive work: a whole past paper sat under time, then marked and discussed in the same session, which is hard to fit into a school-night hour. The usual pattern is a weekday evening for routine teaching and a weekend daytime block in the weeks before a series. Weekend-only arrangements work less well for a subject needing steady weekly contact.

faqs.question: Our tutor is in India — does the two-and-a-half-hour difference make an evening lesson in Ha'il workable?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, with one caveat. India sits two and a half hours ahead of Arabia Standard Time, so a mid-evening Ha'il lesson lands in the late evening for the tutor. That is sustainable as a weekly hour and tiring as a long double session, so for intensive work before a series it is worth moving to a Friday or Saturday daytime slot that falls in their afternoon. India also keeps a single time zone with no seasonal change, as the Kingdom does, so this particular pairing never drifts.

faqs.question: How do the autumn and midyear breaks in a Ha'il school affect a weekly tutoring slot?
faqs.answer: Public schools in the Kingdom run two semesters with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break; international and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, which differ school by school. For a short break, most families keep the slot and reduce the frequency. For the midyear break, a focused block on one weak topic often does more than routine lessons. The slot itself is worth holding in a scarce subject, because releasing a Higher Level mathematics or physics hour and expecting it back is optimistic.

faqs.question: How long should a session be for a Year 10 student in Ha'il, and why that length?
faqs.answer: An hour, in most cases. That is long enough to mark a piece of work, teach one thing properly and set the next task, and short enough that a fourteen-year-old at the end of a school day is still thinking. Two shorter sessions a week beat one long one for a student carrying two weak subjects, because the gap between contact points is what causes forgetting. Ninety minutes only earns its length in the final Diploma year or during a timed-paper block, where the paper itself takes most of the time.

faqs.question: What does a Ha'il student give up by moving from a national-curriculum school into Cambridge IGCSE in Year 10?
faqs.answer: Less than families fear in content and more than they expect in familiarity. The mathematics and science material overlaps substantially at this level, so very little knowledge is lost. What goes is the assessment culture the student has learned to succeed in: accurate, complete recall against a defined syllabus is replaced by applying content to unfamiliar material and taking a defensible position in extended answers. The first term should be spent on that shift, using past papers and mark schemes, rather than on revisiting content the student already holds.

faqs.question: Can a student in Ha'il start the IB Diploma if no school in the city runs it?
faqs.answer: Only through a school, because there is no private-candidate entry for the Diploma. The realistic options are relocating or boarding in Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province, or enrolling with a school that delivers the programme online and supervises the Internal Assessment itself. In the online case that school holds the deadlines, the coursework supervision and the examination arrangements, and an outside tutor works inside its structure. Families wanting a qualification they can sit independently from Ha'il should look at International GCSE and A Level, which both accept private candidates.

faqs.question: Which subjects are hardest for a Ha'il student to pick up late in an international course?
faqs.answer: The ones that build vertically. Mathematics at Higher Level is the hardest, because every later topic assumes fluency in an earlier one and gaps compound rather than sit still. Physics is next for the same reason, with the added problem that its mathematics is assumed rather than taught. Chemistry is more modular and recovers faster. Biology is content-heavy but shallow in dependency, so a determined late start can work. Subjects with coursework components are limited less by difficulty than by deadline: the time to complete the work may simply not exist.

faqs.question: How long does it take a student in Ha'il to adjust to IB command terms?
faqs.answer: Four to six weeks of deliberate practice for the habit to hold without prompting, and the practice is narrow. Take questions the student has already answered on topics they already know, and rewrite the answers to the term rather than to the content, so the only thing changing is the shape. Then test cold on an unseen question using the same term a fortnight later. The improvement shows across every subject at once, which is why it is worth doing before anything else rather than alongside a full revision programme.

faqs.question: What does the first diagnostic session cover for a Ha'il student?
faqs.answer: One real past-paper question, worked out loud. The tutor watches how the student reads the command term, whether they plan before writing, how they lay out method, whether they check units and the final line, and how long they take against the marks available. That hour usually identifies the two faults costing the most marks. It does not cover goals, motivation or study habits, which parents often expect: those conversations are useful later and tell us nothing measurable in the first hour.

faqs.question: What does the first month of tutoring look like for a student in Ha'il?
faqs.answer: A trial lesson on one question, then a full component sat under time in week one so there is a real baseline rather than a school grade. Week two teaches the single largest loss point. Week three re-tests exactly that point cold, under the same conditions, to see whether the fix held unprompted. Week four produces a written plan built on four weeks of evidence: a ranked fault list, what has already moved, a realistic range, and the weekly commitment that range assumes. The plan can legitimately recommend stopping.

faqs.question: How is progress reported to a parent in Ha'il, and how often?
faqs.answer: A short note after every session naming what was covered, what was set and what was weak — not a grade and not encouragement. A longer written review after the first month and then at the end of each term, built on the student's own marked work rather than on impressions. Where a parent wants to see the evidence directly, the marked scripts and the mark schemes are the report. We avoid progress percentages because there is no honest way to calculate one over a few weeks.

faqs.question: What happens if the first tutor is not the right fit for our child in Ha'il?
faqs.answer: The match changes, and the next tutor starts from the written diagnosis rather than from nothing. This happens often enough to be a normal part of the process: a teenager who has stopped listening will not learn from the most qualified person available, and a tutor who cannot find the student's way in is not going to find it in week six. Two or three sessions is usually enough to know. Say so early rather than waiting for a term to prove it, because the lost time is the real cost.

faqs.question: How do we decide after one term whether to carry on?
faqs.answer: Compare marked scripts, not feelings. If the fault identified in week one is no longer costing marks on a comparable paper, the teaching is working and the question becomes which fault is next. If the same marks are going in the same place after a term, something is wrong with the diagnosis or the match, and more of the same will not fix it. The third honest outcome is that the student has what they need and should stop, which is the recommendation we make least often and the one families trust most.

faqs.question: What should a parent in Ha'il do between lessons?
faqs.answer: Protect the slot and check that the set work was done, and little else. Marking it, re-teaching it or sitting through the session usually makes a teenager less willing to be wrong in front of a tutor, and being wrong out loud is where most of the learning happens. The one genuinely useful intervention is logistical: keeping the hour clear, making sure the device and connection work, and making sure the student is not starting a demanding session immediately after a school day with no break.

faqs.question: How is a target grade set honestly for a student with no local Diploma cohort to compare against?
faqs.answer: From a timed paper marked against the published scheme, not from an internal grade. Where a school has no established international cohort, internal marks carry no external calibration, and a student can be the strongest in a small group while sitting several grades below what an external paper would award. We state a range rather than a grade, say what weekly commitment the range assumes, and revise it against each subsequent timed paper. Nobody can promise a specific grade, and a provider who does is describing a hope.

hail.closingBody: If you have a recent marked script, that is the whole of what we need to begin. Send it with the board, the syllabus code and the level, and we will name the likely loss points before the first session rather than spending the first session finding them. The trial lesson is free, it is built around a real past-paper question, and it ends with a short written view of where the marks are going. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time, in a mid-evening slot that fits a Ha'il school night, and the entry route gets settled before anybody books a term of hours.

ib-classes.heroEyebrow: EVIDENCE FIRST, THEN THE PLAN, THEN THE FORMAT
ib-classes.heroSubtitle: IB classes in Saudi Arabia are sold by the hour and judged by feel, which is why families rarely find out whether the money worked. This page starts from the other end. It sets out what counts as evidence that a student is improving, how often that evidence can honestly be collected, and then works backwards to the weekly plan and the format that produce it. Teaching is delivered one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time, and the page is direct about where a group class is the better buy and where it is not.

ib-classes.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach named Diploma and Middle Years Programme courses and report progress the same way: marked written work, scored by question type, against a baseline written at the start. That is the only evidence a family can actually audit, and it is what the sessions are designed to produce.

intro.heading: Start with the evidence, because everything else follows from it
paragraphs: Ask a family three months into paid classes how it is going and the answer is usually 'better, I think'. Ask what has moved and the answer runs out. That is not the family's failure. It is a design failure in how classes are sold: an hour is the unit of sale, attendance is the unit of delivery, and nothing in the arrangement obliges anybody to produce a number. A student can attend thirty pleasant hours and arrive at the May session exactly where they started, and nobody will have noticed in time to change course.

So begin with the question that should come first. What would count as evidence that this is working? There is a short, honest list. Marks on a specific question type, collected weekly from marked work. A full paper under timed conditions every three to four weeks, which tests pacing rather than knowledge. An annotated Internal Assessment draft, which tells you which criterion band the work currently sits in. A topic checklist against the subject guide, which tells you about coverage and nothing about security. School mocks, once or twice a year, which tell you the school's view of the student against its own cohort.

Everything else is impression. Impression is not worthless; a teacher's sense that a student has stopped guessing is real information. It is just not information a decision can be built on, and it is available constantly, which makes it the easiest thing to mistake for progress. The practical consequence is that a class without marked work coming out of it cannot be evaluated at all, at any price, however good the teaching inside the hour happens to be.

Working backwards from that list produces a plan rather than a timetable. If the evidence you want is marks by question type, then written work has to be set, collected and marked against the published scheme between sessions, and the next session has to be built from what the marking showed. If the evidence you want includes pacing, a full paper has to be sat under timed conditions on a known cadence rather than when somebody remembers. The sessions are the consequence of the measurement, not the other way round.

Format follows last, and this is where the word 'classes' gets slippery in this market. Four different products are sold under it: one-to-one teaching, a small group on a shared gap, a large online cohort, and a recorded course with a question bank. They differ enormously in what they can measure. A large cohort class can deliver excellent exposition and cannot mark thirty students' individual answers weekly, so it cannot produce the evidence above. That is not a criticism of the format; it is a limit on what it can be used to prove.

Our own teaching is one-to-one, over live video, with the tutor's screen shared so papers and mark schemes are visible on both sides. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in Saudi Arabia; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Sessions are written in Arabia Standard Time and fitted to the Sunday-to-Thursday school week. Where a family's problem is genuinely a shared gap rather than an individual one, we will say that a group format or the school's own free revision club is the better use of the money, because a page arguing that one-to-one is always the answer would be arguing against the evidence.

ib-classes.programmesIntro: The evidence that counts differs by programme, because the assessment does. These four stages are where families in the Kingdom ask about classes, and the note under each says what you can actually measure at that stage rather than what the programme is designed to achieve.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core. The measurement here is the richest of any stage: published mark schemes, past papers by question type, internally assessed components with criterion bands, and the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix contributing points of its own. A Diploma student is the easiest case in which to prove or disprove that classes are working, and the hardest in which to ignore the answer.
programmes.countryNote: Families in the Kingdom also carry equivalency and the Qiyas tests in the background of these two years, and neither produces evidence a subject class can show you. Keep them as separate lines in the plan. A Diploma student whose subject marks are moving and whose Tahsili preparation has never started is still behind on the thing that decides a Saudi university application, and the subject evidence will not reveal it.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed against published criteria rather than terminal papers, finishing with the Personal Project. The evidence is criterion bands over time, and it is genuinely useful once a family learns to read a descriptor. The common misreading is to treat a mid-band score as a mark out of eight; it is a description of what the work did and did not do, and the descriptor names the missing behaviour directly.
programmes.countryNote: Mobility makes baselines matter more here than anywhere. Families in the Kingdom move between Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province cluster mid-course, and two campuses running the same programme can be a term apart in coverage. A topic and criterion baseline at the point of a move is worth more than a term of classes bought on the assumption that the new school's sequence matches the old one's.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary teaching with no external examination, ending in the exhibition. Evidence at this stage is narrower and slower: reading fluency measured over months, number facts under a time limit, a piece of writing compared with one from a term earlier. None of it comes from a paper, so a family buying classes here should agree what will be compared and when before anything starts.
programmes.countryNote: Primary enquiries in the Kingdom are mostly about an imminent transition rather than a present difficulty. A family moving into an international-curriculum school, or relocating to a city with different provision, wants written English and number fluency in place before the move. Light, regular sessions across a term produce comparable evidence; an intensive block before a start date produces a feeling of readiness and little that can be measured.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: An IB route combining Diploma Programme courses with a career-related study and a core of its own, including a reflective project. The measurement is mixed: Diploma-course evidence works as it does anywhere, while the career-related component and the reflective project are assessed differently and need their own criterion-based feedback rather than paper practice.
programmes.countryNote: Provision for this route in the Kingdom is limited and uneven, and the IB's own school directory is the place to check which campuses offer it rather than any third-party list. Where a family is considering it, the question worth asking a school is which Diploma courses it will actually staff alongside the career-related study, because that is what determines whether the combination is deliverable next year.

ib-classes.subjectsIntro: Progress looks different in each subject, so the note under each one names the thing you can actually watch move. A subject where the gains show up weekly needs a different plan, and a different budget, from one where the first honest measurement is a full paper a month away.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The fastest subject in which to show movement, because the losses are concentrated in long-answer technique. Score the six-mark questions separately from the rest and the number moves within a handful of sessions as a student learns to answer the command term. Content coverage is the slow half and should be tracked on a checklist, not confused with the technique score.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Two separately measurable things sit inside this subject: definition and recall accuracy, which can be scored weekly and improves quickly, and multi-step calculation under time pressure, which does not. Track them apart. A student whose recall score has doubled while their calculation score is flat has made real progress that a single overall mark would hide.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The subject where a full timed paper tells you most, because the losses are usually about time and sequence rather than topic. Score the extended responses, the graph questions and the unit errors as three separate lines. Higher Level extension topics should be on a coverage checklist because they arrive late in most schemes of work and are easy to leave unmeasured.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Measure method marks, not answers. A weekly count of questions where the student reached a wrong answer with no visible working is the single most actionable number in this subject, and it falls fast once it is being watched. At Higher Level the third paper needs its own score line, since performance there rarely tracks performance on the first two.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The marks here sit disproportionately in written justification rather than calculation, so the useful measurement is the score on the explain-and-justify parts taken alone. Students often look stronger than they are on an overall mark because the calculation parts carry them, and the gap only becomes visible when the two are scored separately.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Score diagrams as their own line. Unlabelled axes and curves shifted the wrong way are a discrete, countable error that disappears within two or three sessions once it is being counted. Evaluation is the slow measurement and the Higher Level dividing line, and it needs marked writing over weeks rather than a technique fix.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The slowest subject to evidence and the one families most often abandon early. Progress shows in the structure of an analysis, not in its vocabulary, so compare a piece of writing against one from a month earlier rather than looking for a weekly number. Oral components need recording and reviewing, which almost nobody does until it is late.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Unusually responsive to measurement because the gap between recall and application is so visible. Score application separately: how many points were tied to the organisation in the paper rather than left generic. That number typically moves two bands within a few well-marked sessions, which makes this subject a poor candidate for a long block bought up front.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Frequently taught in schools by a non-specialist, which pushes it into outside classes more than its difficulty warrants. The measurable thing is use of studies as evidence inside an argument, not how many studies a student can name. A student who can list twelve studies and deploy none has a flat score that recall practice will not move.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Two score lines that diverge sharply: working code, and written explanation of that code. Most students are strong on the first and weak on the second, and the written paper marks the second. Trace tables and pseudocode discipline produce visible weekly movement; the abstract data structures at Higher Level do not and belong on a coverage checklist.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Measured by criterion band on the student's own drafts and nothing else, which means evidence arrives a handful of times rather than weekly. Agree at the outset how many drafts will be reviewed and when, because the single most common failure in the core is a timetable nobody set. A tutor gives feedback on the student's own writing and never supplies the text.

ib-classes.regionsIntro: Whether a group class is even formable depends on how many students in one city are sitting the same course at the same level in the same year. That number is small almost everywhere in the Kingdom outside the largest clusters, which is the practical reason one-to-one dominates here rather than a philosophical one.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The one market in the Kingdom where a genuine group class in a mainstream Diploma subject is sometimes formable, because the cohort exists. Even here the city is roughly an hour across in traffic, so a group has to agree one hour that survives several different school runs, and that is usually what kills it.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north towards Obhur. Cohorts exist for the common subjects, but a shared slot has to work for families spread along that axis, and one incident on the main road removes several students from a group session at once rather than one.

regions.name: Dammam
regions.note: Part of a conurbation that behaves as one school market with Al Khobar and Dhahran, so a cohort assembled across the three cities is larger than any single city's. Scheduling is the limit rather than numbers, since families routinely live in one of the three and attend school in another.

regions.name: Dhahran
regions.note: Compound and camp living produces an unusual pattern: a fairly dense cohort in a small area, with the IB Diploma offered at some campuses and not others. Where a shared gap is genuinely shared across a campus, this is one of the few places in the Kingdom a small group is the right answer.

regions.name: Al Khobar
regions.note: Families here compare provision across the King Fahd Causeway as well as locally, which widens what they consider and narrows what they can schedule. An online slot priced in SAR and pinned to Arabia Standard Time removes the crossing from the arithmetic entirely.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: Parental rotation rosters rather than traffic decide what a schedule can hold, and a group class is the first thing a roster breaks. One student's shift change moves a session for everybody, which is why industrial-city families almost always end up with an individual slot.

regions.name: Al Ahsa
regions.note: About ninety minutes inland from the Eastern Province cluster. The cohort for any given Diploma subject at a given level is too small for a group to form, so the real question is whether the subject can be taught at all rather than in what format.

regions.name: Madinah
regions.note: A school calendar that bends around the Hajj and Umrah seasons in ways a published term list does not fully capture. Blocks agreed for the quieter weeks of a term survive; group sessions scheduled across those weeks tend to lose half their attendance and then dissolve.

regions.name: Thuwal
regions.note: The KAUST School serves the university campus community north of Jeddah, with a highly mobile cohort. Students arrive and leave mid-course, so the useful measurement at the start is always a coverage checklist against the subject guide rather than a mark, because the gap is usually topics rather than technique.

schoolClusters.note: Students we support attend schools along this coast, and The KAUST School serves the university campus community at Thuwal. The British International School of Jeddah is both an IB World School and a Cambridge school. What matters for a class decision is cohort size in one subject at one level, which a school can tell you if you ask precisely.

The broadest IB provision in the Kingdom and the only market where a group class in a mainstream Diploma subject is reliably formable. Ask a school how many students are taking a subject at Higher Level this year, not how many take the subject, because the level is where a cohort splits in half.

The IB Diploma is offered at the American School of Dhahran and at ISG Jubail rather than across every campus in the region, while British School Dhahran and Multinational School Dhahran follow British and Cambridge curricula. A compound cohort is dense enough that a shared gap really can be shared, which is rare in the Kingdom.

ib-classes.modesIntro: Four formats, chosen by what the evidence says the problem is rather than by what is cheapest per head. Everything we deliver runs one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time; where a group or a free school club is the better answer, this page says so and names the condition.

modes.title: One-to-one, which is what most classes become
modes.description: A fixed weekly slot with written work set, marked between sessions and used as the agenda for the next one. This is the only format that can produce marks by question type for an individual student every week, which is why it dominates in this market despite costing more per hour than any group alternative.

modes.title: A small group on one genuinely shared gap
modes.description: Two to five students who were all taught the same topic badly, or who all need the same examination-technique teaching. The condition is that the gap is identical, which is rarer than it sounds: three students failing the same paper usually fail it in three different ways. Where it does hold, this is better value than one-to-one and we will say so.

modes.title: Paper clinics under timed conditions
modes.description: A two-hour block, usually on the Kingdom's Friday or Saturday weekend, in which a full paper is sat under timed conditions and then marked against the published scheme in the same session. This is the measurement that a weekday evening cannot produce, and it is the only reliable way to see pacing rather than knowledge.

modes.title: A measured eight-week run before the series
modes.description: A compressed block before the May session in which measurement, not content, drives every decision. A timed paper at the start rewrites the plan, two question types are drilled, a second timed paper checks the effect, and the final fortnight introduces nothing new. The shape is fixed because the evidence arrives on a known cadence.

sections.heading: What measurable progress in an IB subject actually looks like
paragraphs: There are six things a family can look at and only four of them are worth making decisions on. Marks on a specific question type, collected weekly from marked written work, are the primary evidence: they are granular, they move quickly where the problem is technique, and they are hard to fake. A full paper under timed conditions, sat every three to four weeks, measures something different and equally important, which is whether a gain survives the clock and the mark tariff.

An annotated Internal Assessment draft is the third, and it is the only honest evidence for the internally assessed components. It tells you which criterion band the work currently sits in and why, which is a far more useful statement than any grade estimate. The fourth is a topic checklist against the subject guide. It shows coverage, which matters enormously after a relocation or a change of school, and it shows nothing at all about whether covered content is secure.

The two weaker sources are the ones families rely on most. School mock results arrive once or twice a year, reflect the school's own cohort and marking, and cannot tell you anything about a single question type. And a teacher's or tutor's impression is available constantly, which is exactly what makes it dangerous: it fills the space where a number should be. A student can feel more confident and be losing the same marks for the same reason, and the impression will not catch it.

The reason to be strict about this is financial as much as academic. Paid teaching with no marked output cannot be evaluated, so a family cannot tell in November whether the money spent since the autumn term moved anything. By the time a school mock answers the question it is usually too late in the second Diploma year to change the plan. The table below is the whole of the evidence base, with what each item cannot show written down next to it.

sections.heading: Working backwards from the evidence to a weekly plan
paragraphs: Once the evidence is agreed, the plan writes itself and stops being a matter of taste. If the primary measurement is marks by question type collected weekly, then written work has to be set at the end of every session, collected before the next one, and marked against the published scheme rather than ticked. The marking is not an extra. It is the thing that generates the number, and a session structure that leaves no time for it has quietly removed the measurement.

The next session then has one job: address what the marking showed, in order of marks available. This is where most plans fail, because it requires the tutor to abandon what they intended to teach. A student who lost eleven marks on command-term handling and four on a topic gets a command-term session, even if the topic was next on the scheme of work. Teaching in the order of the syllabus is comfortable and it is not what the evidence asked for.

The timed paper cadence has to be set in advance or it never happens. Every three to four weeks, a full paper under timed conditions, scored by question type and compared with the last one. Families resist this because it eats a session and produces a demoralising number early. Both objections are correct and both are worth accepting: the number is the point, and a demoralising score in the autumn term is far cheaper than a demoralising one in the spring.

Finally, the plan has to name a decision date. At the end of each block there is a review against the baseline, and the review has three possible outcomes rather than one: continue, change the plan, or stop. A review that can only produce 'continue' is a renewal notice. Writing the alternatives down at the start is what makes it an honest measurement rather than a sales step, and it is the reason we agree the review date before the first session rather than after the last.

sections.heading: What 'IB classes' means in this market, and the four things it can mean
paragraphs: The word covers four products that behave completely differently, and families comparing prices across them are usually comparing things that are not alternatives. One-to-one teaching is the only format that can produce individual marked evidence weekly. A small group can teach a shared gap and deliver technique well, and cannot mark five students' individual answers to a weekly cadence. A large online cohort class can deliver excellent exposition to twenty or forty students and can do nothing individual at all. A recorded course with a question bank can provide coverage and practice and cannot diagnose anything.

None of that makes three of them bad. It makes them useful for different problems. A student who was never taught a topic properly and needs it explained clearly has a problem a cohort class solves cheaply. A student who needs volume practice with answers to check against has a problem a question bank solves cheaply. A student losing marks for reasons specific to the way they personally write answers has a problem only individual marking solves, and buying any of the other three for it wastes the money entirely.

There is a fifth option this market rarely mentions because nobody profits from it: the school's own revision club or clinic, which is usually free and usually the right first thing to try. A teacher running a revision set for a cohort cannot address individual weaknesses, but they know the scheme of work, they know the class, and they cost nothing. A family who has not used that before buying classes is often buying the cheaper half of what they need at the dearer price.

The right-hand column of the table gives the advertised positions in this market, with the kind of source attached. Budget online platforms advertise from about SAR 35 per head, IB subject tuition is advertised from about SAR 180 on tutoring-company listings, and Higher Level or Advanced Placement routes are published at roughly SAR 200 to 220. Those are provider-published figures rather than a market average, and none of them is our price. The point of putting them beside the formats is that a per-head figure and a one-to-one figure are not comparable numbers.
