sections.heading: Choosing a coach: the questions that separate a specialist from a generalist
paragraphs: No credential in this market is regulated, so verification falls to the parent. Six questions do most of the work and they are all answerable in a sentence. Ask them before a trial session rather than after, and ask them of us as readily as of anybody else, because a provider who is uncomfortable with them has told you something.

Which subject and level have you taught, and in which of the last two cohorts? What are the assessment components for that subject, and what does each carry? Where do students most often lose marks on the paper that decides this grade — a good answer is specific and unglamorous, naming command terms or uncertainties or timing, while a weak one is about confidence and revision habits. What do you decline to teach? Everybody has a boundary and a coach claiming three sciences and two mathematics routes is covering, not specialising. On examining: which board, which paper, in what capacity. And what will you put in writing after each session, with what marking turnaround?

Two further questions are specific to the Diploma and almost never asked. First, what do you need to know about my child's school scheme of work, and will you read it? A coach working alongside a school produces better results than one working around it, and a coach who does not want to see the school's sequence is planning to teach their own. Second, what is your line on internally assessed work? The only acceptable answer is that they will read, question and give feedback on the student's own writing and put nothing into the document.

On results claims, one rule covers everything: no statistic without a number of students, a date and a method. A success percentage, a star rating or a tutor headcount with none of those attached carries no information. What an honest provider offers instead is an explanation of how they work and a free first session you can judge for yourself, which is a weaker-sounding promise than most of this market makes and a considerably more checkable one.
bullets: Ask which cohort, not just which subject — recency matters at Diploma level
A specific answer about where marks leak is the strongest signal available
Ask whether the coach will read the school's scheme of work; the answer is revealing
Treat any rate, rating or headcount without n, date and method as no information

process.title: Tell us the subject, the level and your evening ceiling
process.description: 'Chemistry HL, the investigation and Paper 2' tells us what to match. 'Two weekday evenings maximum, nothing before 6.30pm, Riyadh school run' tells us whether a match is possible at all. Families give us the first and almost never the second, and the second is what decides whether the arrangement survives a full Diploma year.

process.title: We match on the syllabus, then on the coach's own week
process.description: A specialist in that subject and level first, then a check on when their school day ends, which days are their weekend, and whether your most valuable slot sits inside it. A coach who agrees to work inside their own weekend in the autumn term often resents it by the spring, so we ask before offering rather than afterwards.

process.title: A free first session, used as a diagnostic
process.description: The coach works on real material — a past paper, a returned assessment, a live coursework draft — and ends with a written read: which of the common losses apply, in what order to address them, and roughly how long each takes. You keep that document whether or not you continue, and it is useful even if you choose another provider.

process.title: Pin the slot in Arabia Standard Time, in writing
process.description: The slot is recorded in Saudi local time so the drift lands on the coach when their country changes its clocks. We also agree the attachments now: marking turnaround in days, who supplies past papers, the note you receive after each session, and what happens to a cancelled lesson.

process.title: A two-year arc, reviewed each term
process.description: Teaching and foundations in the first Diploma year, coursework in the middle, timed papers and technique in the last. Each term we compare marked work against the component list we started from, and the plan changes if it has not moved. The mix of teaching to coaching is meant to shift across the course rather than stay fixed.

process.title: Say stop when it is time to stop
process.description: Sessions are per lesson or per agreed block rather than an open subscription, so ending needs no negotiation and a pause costs nothing. When a student no longer needs the hour, we will say so rather than keep billing a slot that has done its job. Slots can be held through breaks if you give us the dates early.

whyPoints.title: The clock is checked before the match is offered
whyPoints.description: A coach's own working week — their school day, their weekend, their time zone — decides whether a weekly hour survives two years. We ask about it first, because a mismatch there ends arrangements faster than any disagreement about teaching, and almost nobody in this market checks it in advance.

whyPoints.title: Slots written in Saudi local time
whyPoints.description: Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom never changes its clocks. Most countries our coaches live in do. Recording the slot in Saudi time means their clock moves and your evening does not, which is a thirty-second administrative act that prevents two confusing weeks every year.

whyPoints.title: Designed for a Sunday-to-Thursday week
whyPoints.description: Sunday evening here carries the weight a Monday night carries elsewhere, and Thursday evening carries none. The weekly pattern is designed against that, with Friday and Saturday mornings used deliberately to reach specialists whose own week cannot touch a Saudi school night.

whyPoints.title: The core is planned, not conceded
whyPoints.description: Three points sit in the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix and are the most commonly surrendered points in the Diploma, because no subject teacher owns them. We treat the core as scheduled work with its own sessions, and we test an Extended Essay research question for answerability before any writing begins.

whyPoints.title: A stated line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Feedback on the student's own drafts against the published criteria, with a record of what was discussed. No drafting, no rewriting, no model answer on the student's own title, and nothing a coach produces ever enters the document. A parent can ask us that question in one sentence and get one word back.

whyPoints.title: No accreditation claimed, no statistic unevidenced
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no accreditation from the IB and says so on the page rather than in small print. There are no success percentages, star ratings or headcounts here, because none of them would carry a number of students, a date and a method. What we offer is a free first session you can judge yourself.

faqs.question: How does a coach work through a Mathematics AA HL Paper 3 question on a shared screen?
faqs.answer: The paper is loaded as a document and annotated live while both sides write on a shared whiteboard, so the student's working and the coach's appear on the same page. Paper 3 questions are long and sequential, so the method is to stop at each part and ask what the question has just given you and what it is setting up, rather than producing a worked solution. The student writes with a stylus, a mouse, or on paper held to the camera. Typing mathematical working is avoided because it is slow enough to change how a student reasons.

faqs.question: Can a parent in the Kingdom sit in on an IB session, and should they?
faqs.answer: Yes to the first, and mostly for the first session only. A parent watching the opening session learns what the coach is actually doing and whether the diagnosis is specific, which is worth an hour. After that, presence tends to make a teenager perform rather than struggle, and visible struggling is the point of the hour. The written note after each session replaces the need to attend: it names the component worked on, what went wrong and what has been set, which is more useful than having watched.

faqs.question: What is shared with us after each IB session, and how is progress tracked across two years?
faqs.answer: A short note after every session: the component worked on, the specific errors, and what has been set before the next one. Across two years those notes become the record that matters, because they show whether the same weakness keeps reappearing. At each term review we compare marked work against the component list agreed at the start — not the student's confidence, and not the coach's impression. If nothing has moved on paper after a term, the plan changes or the coach does.

faqs.question: How does an online session handle a Theory of Knowledge essay draft?
faqs.answer: The student's draft is read against the prescribed title and the assessment criteria, and the session is spent on questions rather than corrections: what is the knowledge claim here, which area of knowledge does this example actually belong to, where is the counter-argument handled rather than mentioned. The coach names where the argument fails to do what the title asks. The student then rewrites it themselves. Nothing the coach produces goes into the document, and a record of the exchange exists so the school can see the support was legitimate.

faqs.question: Does online coaching work for a Diploma subject with a practical component like Physics HL?
faqs.answer: For the written papers and the data analysis, yes, and often better than in-person work because annotated papers and a shared whiteboard are exactly what those components need. For the practical work itself, the student is in their school laboratory with their own teacher, and that does not change. What a coach contributes is the part students lose marks on: research question feasibility, control of variables, uncertainty treatment, and evaluation written in the vocabulary the criteria reward. The experiment is the school's; the thinking around it is coachable.

faqs.question: What does a year of weekly coaching in one Higher Level subject actually commit us to?
faqs.answer: One evening a week in term time, around thirty sessions across a school year, plus written work between them. Price it per term rather than per hour, because that is the decision you are actually making. The commitment is real and worth comparing against two alternatives: a study-leave intensive, which costs far less and does far less, and the school's own subject clinics, which cost nothing and are routinely unasked for. Sessions are per lesson or per agreed block, so the year is not locked in at the start.

faqs.question: Why does a Mathematics AA HL coach cost more than a Mathematics AI SL one in the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: Scarcity, and it is the dominant driver everywhere. The pool of coaches who can teach Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level to examination standard — including Paper 3, which rewards unfamiliar extended problems — is far smaller than the pool who can teach Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level. Level adds to it, and examining experience adds again. None of this means the Higher Level coach is a better teacher; it means you are buying a scarcer specialism, and the comparison worth making is against other Higher Level mathematics rates rather than across routes.

faqs.question: Is an intensive block before the May session better value than weekly sessions all year?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on whether the problem is technique or content. For a student whose knowledge is adequate and whose answers are not, a study-leave block of timed papers marked against the published scheme is the highest-return money in the Diploma year, and it costs a fraction of a year's weekly support. For a student with real content gaps it is close to useless, because you cannot teach two years of a Higher Level subject in a fortnight. The diagnostic session tells you which case you are in, and we will say so plainly.

faqs.question: Are there costs beyond the hourly rate for IB coaching — past papers, reports, materials?
faqs.answer: There should not be, and this is worth settling in writing before the first paid session, because practice varies wildly across this market. Ask who supplies past papers and mark schemes, whether marking of written work between sessions is included and with what turnaround in days, whether the note to the parent is included, and what happens to a lesson cancelled with short notice. At the bottom of the advertised range those items are usually absent rather than charged, which is how the price gets there.

faqs.question: Why do some providers quote in US dollars, and what does that mean for a Saudi budget?
faqs.answer: International providers often price in dollars because their coaches are spread across many countries, and rates near sixty dollars an hour are advertised. For a Saudi family the practical effect is on a long commitment rather than on a single lesson: the riyal's relationship to the dollar is stable, but any provider quoting in a third currency introduces a variable you do not control. Ask for the rate in SAR for the term, and ask whether it is fixed for the duration or reviewed, before committing to a full Diploma year.

faqs.question: What should an IB coach know about my child's school scheme of work?
faqs.answer: Enough to work alongside the school rather than across it: the order topics are being taught in, when the school's internal deadlines for assessed work fall, which optional topics have been chosen, and when mock examinations are set. A coach who asks for this is planning to reinforce what the classroom is doing. A coach who does not want it is planning to teach their own sequence, which produces a student holding two incompatible versions of a course. Ask the question in the first session and listen to the answer.

faqs.question: Is a coach who has marked for the IB better than one who has taught the course for years?
faqs.answer: They are different purchases. Somebody who has marked under an awarding body's standardisation process knows what the scheme pays for in a way reading it does not teach, which is most valuable for paper technique in the final year. Somebody teaching the course now knows how it is being delivered in schools, has seen internal moderation, and is better placed on coursework supervision. For a technique problem the marking background usually wins; for an internally assessed piece, current classroom experience often does.

faqs.question: Can we choose the coach's gender, and how does that work for one-to-one online sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes. You state the preference and we match to it, with no explanation required. One of the practical advantages of one-to-one video teaching is that a family's choice on this is straightforward rather than constrained by who happens to be available locally, and in the Kingdom that matters to a good number of families. The same applies to a preference for a coach who speaks Arabic alongside the subject, which can help in explanation even when the examination itself is sat in English.

faqs.question: What happens if our coach becomes unavailable part-way through DP2?
faqs.answer: We rematch, and the handover is the part that matters. The new coach receives the component list, the session notes and the marked work, so they start from where the student actually is rather than from a fresh diagnostic that wastes two weeks of a final year. Where we can see a change coming — a relocation, a contract ending — we overlap the two coaches for a session. A mid-DP2 change is disruptive and manageable; it is one reason the written record after each session exists at all.

ib-coaching.closingHeading: Give us the subject and the evening you can actually spend
ib-coaching.closingBody: Tell us the subject and level and the honest ceiling on your week — two evenings, nothing before 6.30pm, a Riyadh school run — and we will match a specialist whose own working week can hold that slot for two years, then write it down in Arabia Standard Time. The first session is free and runs as a diagnostic: it names which components are weak, in what order to fix them, and how long each should take, and you keep that read in writing either way. Lessons are one-to-one over live video. If the school's own subject clinic covers what you need, we will tell you that instead.

ib-crash-course.tutorsIntro: These are the tutors families ask for when a block has to start quickly: Diploma subject specialists who can carry three or four sessions a week, and who already know the paper the student is about to sit.

intro.heading: An IB crash course is a block of hours, not a shorter year
paragraphs: A crash course is a fixed quantity of one-to-one teaching bought inside a fixed window. Three numbers define it: total hours, the span in weeks, and how many components it is aimed at. Twelve hours across four weeks pointed at one paper is a completely different purchase from thirty hours across eight weeks spread over two Higher Level subjects. Providers sell both under the same two words, which is why families end up comparing quotes that are not comparable with each other at all. Settle the three numbers first, and only then ask anybody for a price.

Saudi families usually arrive at this search after an event rather than on a plan. Mock scripts came back well below the school's predicted grade. A relocation dropped a student into the Diploma part-way through the first year, with an internal assessment already running. A Higher Level option was taught by a non-specialist for a term, and the gap only showed up under timed conditions. Or the final stretch before the May session has started and one subject is still unreliable. Each of those needs a different block, bought against the marked evidence rather than against a feeling.

The constraint that actually decides whether a block works is the week. Schools in the Kingdom run Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. A block that needs four sessions a week is asking for four of the five school evenings, on top of the homework the school still expects to receive, and that is a very different ask from one weekly lesson. Families who plan the hours without planning the week tend to cancel a third of the block and pay for the rest, which is the most common way this purchase goes wrong.

The second constraint is the tutor. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks, so a slot agreed with someone in a country that does will drift twice a year unless it is written down in Saudi local time. Beyond the clock, every tutor has their own working week, and most good subject specialists are teaching somewhere during it. Carrying four sessions a week for eight weeks is a real commitment, and the pool of specialists who can genuinely sustain that is much smaller than the pool who can take one lesson.

What follows is the logistics first and the teaching second, because in this market the logistics are what fail. The four shapes a block can take and what each can reach. The density a Sunday-to-Thursday week will actually hold. What the clock does to a four-session week, read from the tutor's side. Then the teaching itself: command terms, the long answer, the marked work between sessions, the line a tutor does not cross on assessed work, and the university steps that a block aimed at the papers leaves completely untouched.

ib-crash-course.programmesIntro: Crash blocks make sense at some stages and not at others. Intensity repairs technique quickly and content slowly, so the earlier the stage, the weaker the case for buying a block at all.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary learning with no external papers, so there is no examination technique for a block to compress.
programmes.countryNote: Riyadh and Jeddah families often ask about a holiday block here. Steady weekly reading and number work does more at this stage, for less.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme

programmes.countryNote: A useful block targets one criterion the student keeps losing marks on across subjects, rather than a whole subject. The Personal Project stays theirs.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and an internally assessed component in each subject.
programmes.countryNote: Almost every Saudi IB school sits the written papers in the May session, and this is where blocks earn their money: timed rehearsal and marked homework.

ib-crash-course.subjectsIntro: A block is only worth buying if the hours point at something nameable. These are the Diploma subjects Saudi families most often book intensive work in, with what a short block can move.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus depth and the optional Paper 3 investigation. Blocks buy structured working and fluency with the formula booklet.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics carry the grade. Blocks pay off on interpreting calculator output in words a mark scheme accepts.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Marks go missing in explanation chains and uncertainty treatment rather than in the algebra itself.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics are the usual repair jobs. The data booklet has to be fluent, not merely available.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume hides the real problem, which is command terms. A block separating state, outline, explain and evaluate finds known marks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams must be labelled to a standard and evaluation has to be earned. The commentaries stay the student's own work.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study response is technique, not knowledge. Blocks work best on reading the stimulus and answering the question set.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis under time pressure is what a block can rehearse. The oral belongs to the student and the school.

ib-crash-course.regionsIntro: Where a family lives changes the start time of a block more than it changes the teaching. These are the patterns that come up when a Kingdom-wide block is timetabled.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: Roughly an hour across in traffic at the wrong time. A seven o'clock start survives the school run; five o'clock usually does not.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine running north to Obhur. Families at opposite ends attend the same schools and need different session times.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran

regions.name: Thuwal and KAUST
regions.note: A campus community with its own term calendar, so blocks here are often planned around campus dates rather than school holidays.

regions.name: Makkah and Taif
regions.note: Makkah sits about 80km east of Jeddah. Hajj and Umrah seasons change traffic and school hours, so spare weeks matter.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: About 25km apart at altitude, sharing one catchment. The local specialist pool is thin, which is the honest argument for online hours.

ib-crash-course.modesIntro: A block is a shape, not only a number of hours. These three patterns survive a Saudi school week, and most families use two of them together.

modes.title: Four sessions a week, Sunday to Thursday
modes.description: The densest pattern a school week will take. It holds for four to six weeks and then starts to cost homework time, so it suits one subject rather than two.

One session each week kept for marked written work

sections.heading: Four block shapes, and what each one can realistically reach
paragraphs: Ask three providers for a crash course and you will be sold three different things. The variable that matters is not the hourly rate but the shape: how many hours, over how many weeks, pointed at how many components. A clinic of five hours aimed at one paper has a decent chance of changing something measurable. Thirty hours spread thinly across four subjects in six weeks almost never does, because nothing in it gets enough repetition to survive the pressure of a timed paper.

What a block can reach is narrow and worth stating plainly. It can rehearse a question type until the student recognises it on sight. It can repair one or two topics that were taught badly or missed outright. It can make timing automatic, which is where a large share of lost marks actually sits. What it cannot reach is two years of content that was never learned, or a Higher Level option topic nobody has taught. Buying hours against that gap is buying disappointment at a premium rate.

Choose the shape from marked evidence rather than from a conversation. Mock scripts, the subject teacher's written comments, the internal assessment criterion letters already awarded, and any question the student left blank are the four inputs that matter here. A tutor who asks to see those before quoting is doing the job properly. One who quotes a package length before seeing anything is selling a shape off a shelf, and the shape on that shelf may not be yours.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week decides how many sessions a block can hold
paragraphs: Schools in the Kingdom run Sunday to Thursday, and Friday and Saturday are the weekend. That single fact sets the ceiling on block density, and most tutoring copy written for a Monday-to-Friday country gets it wrong. Four sessions a week means four of five school evenings. Five means every one of them, which no student sustains for eight weeks alongside internal assessment deadlines and the ordinary homework their school still expects to receive on time.

The school run sets the earliest workable start. In Riyadh a family on one side of the city and a family on the other have very different journeys to the same school, so an afternoon slot that works in one district collapses in another. Across the Kingdom, a start between six and eight in the evening is what survives contact with reality. Sessions beginning earlier get cancelled; sessions beginning after nine on a school night buy an hour of a tired student and little else.

Thursday evening is the most reliable slot in the week and the most under-used. Nothing is due the next morning, so a longer session is possible and a student will tolerate a full timed paper rather than a fragment. Sunday evening is the second most reliable, because it sets up the week ahead. The middle of the week is where cancellations cluster, so a block that loads its heaviest work there quietly loses hours the family has already paid for.

sections.heading: Arabia Standard Time, and the tutor's own working week
paragraphs: The Kingdom runs on Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, and does not observe daylight saving. Tutors in countries that do will see their offset change twice a year. If the agreement says eight in the evening without saying whose eight, the slot silently moves by an hour and a family spends a week arguing about it. Write the time into the block plan as Saudi local time, and let the tutor's own clock be the thing that moves around it.

The offset is only half the question. The other half is the tutor's working week, because most good subject specialists are also teaching somewhere during theirs. A teacher in the United Kingdom finishes their school day in the early afternoon their time, which lands neatly in the Saudi evening, so four sessions a week is genuinely possible for them. A tutor in Singapore would be teaching at one in the morning, and no amount of goodwill makes that sustainable across an eight-week block.

This is why a block narrows the pool of real specialists far more than a single weekly lesson does. A family can usually find someone excellent for one hour a week in almost any time zone on the map. Finding someone excellent who can hold four Saudi evenings for two months is a different search entirely, and it is worth asking that question directly before the first lesson rather than discovering the answer in week three of the block.

sections.heading: Three crash courses that share a name and nothing else
paragraphs: The block a student needs at the end of the first Diploma year is not the block they need eight weeks before the papers. At the end of the first year the job is to stop a weakness compounding, because Higher Level content in the second year assumes the first year is secure. Those hours go on foundations: algebraic fluency, the mechanisms, the definitions that later questions are built on. It is unglamorous work and it is the cheapest point in the Diploma to do it.

After the second-year mocks, the job changes. The student usually knows more than the script shows, and the gap is between knowing and being paid for knowing. Hours go on marked timed questions, on command terms, and on the difference between an answer that is correct and an answer that scores. Published rates give the range families are quoting against: a tutoring-company listing advertises IB subject tutoring in Riyadh from around SAR 180 an hour, with Higher Level premium tracks listed at roughly SAR 200 to 220, while a tutor-marketplace guide puts senior-school examination subjects at SAR 200 and above. Those are other providers' advertised rates rather than ours, and they are not a market average.

In the final weeks before the May session the block has to get narrow or it is wasted. Two subjects at most, one question type at a time, and no new content unless a specific topic is genuinely missing. This is also the point to stop adding hours. A student in four sessions a week who still has school mock feedback to act on will simply stop doing the written work, and the written work is where the marks were coming from in the first place.

sections.heading: A block buys mark-scheme technique before it buys more content
paragraphs: Command terms are the most reliable place to find marks inside a short block. State, outline, describe, explain, compare, evaluate and justify each ask for a different structure, and an examiner pays for the structure the term demands. A student who writes a thoughtful paragraph where the paper asked them to state three things has lost marks on material they knew. Teaching that distinction takes a few hours and transfers across every paper in the subject, which is exactly what a compressed block needs.

The second place is the long answer. A six-mark question is not a short essay; it is six specific things the mark scheme is willing to pay for, usually signposted by the wording of the question itself. Working through published mark schemes alongside the student's own attempts shows them what was being counted and what was simply ignored. Most students are surprised by how mechanical it turns out to be, and that surprise is the point at which their scripts start changing.

Neither of those sticks without written work between sessions. The session is where technique is taught; the marks come from what the student produces alone afterwards, under time, and then has marked against the published criteria. A block with no homework cycle is a block of conversation. Four hours a week of teaching plus two timed questions marked and returned does considerably more than six hours of teaching with nothing written in between them.

sections.heading: The core, and the line a tutor does not cross
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and the internally assessed component in each subject are supervised by the school, and the school has to declare that the work is the student's own. A crash block can sit alongside that, but it cannot take it over. The useful work is teaching the skill the component assesses: how a knowledge question is framed, how a research question gets narrow enough to answer, how a method section earns the marks the criteria actually describe.

What a tutor may do is bounded, and worth saying out loud because this market contains people who will offer otherwise. A tutor may teach the criteria, ask questions about a draft the student wrote, point at a paragraph that does not do what the criterion asks, and model the technique on a different question entirely. No tutor should ever produce the text that gets submitted, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, or supply an argument for the student to adopt as their own. That is malpractice, and the consequence lands on the student rather than on the tutor.

Keep the record simple. Drafts stay in the student's own files with their own version history, feedback is kept as comments and questions rather than as replacement text, and the school's supervisor stays the primary authority on what each component needs. If a provider offers to deliver a finished internal assessment inside a crash course, that is not a shortcut; it is the moment to leave the conversation and find a different provider.

sections.heading: Equivalency and the Qiyas tests: what a May-session block leaves untouched
paragraphs: A crash course aimed at Diploma papers does nothing about the step that comes after them. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. That applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. It is a paperwork process with its own requirements, and families who plan only for the examinations tend to meet it far too late.

Alongside equivalency sit the Qiyas tests. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, and tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content. It can be sat in Arabic or in English. Because it is a reasoning test, preparation for it looks nothing like Diploma revision, and putting both inside one short block usually means neither of them gets enough repetition to matter.

Tahsili is the one that catches international-curriculum students. It covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum, so the material overlaps an IB course while the framing does not. Universities publish their own admission criteria combining school results with these tests, and the weightings differ by university and by programme. No page should print a threshold or a formula: check the university's own published criteria, and plan the testing separately from the examination block.

process.description: Timed work marked against the published criteria and returned before the next session, then a written summary when the block ends.

whyPoints.title: The week is planned, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Sessions are built around a Sunday-to-Thursday school week, a real school run and the homework the school still expects.

whyPoints.title: The slot is pinned to Saudi time
whyPoints.description: Arabia Standard Time is written into the plan, so a tutor's own clock change cannot quietly move the lesson.

whyPoints.description: A Higher Level paper is taught by someone who teaches that paper. Short blocks leave no room for learning the syllabus alongside the student.

whyPoints.description: Technique is taught in the session and proved in writing afterwards, so a student can see which command term cost the mark.

whyPoints.description: If the gap is content rather than technique, we say so and quote a longer programme. No tutor can promise a grade.

faqs.question: Is a crash block ever the right tool for a Middle Years Programme student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but narrowly. The Middle Years Programme is marked against published criteria rather than external papers, so there is no timed technique to compress. What a short block can do is fix one criterion the student keeps losing marks on across several subjects, usually the one about communicating or analysing rather than knowing. If the issue is subject content, weekly work across a term does more for less money. The Personal Project stays the student's own work throughout.

faqs.question: When in the first Diploma year is a crash block actually worth buying?
faqs.answer: The end of the first year is the cheapest useful moment. Second-year Higher Level content assumes the first year is secure, so a weakness left alone compounds rather than holds steady. Twelve to sixteen hours in the break after the first-year examinations, pointed at the topics the report named, is usually worth more than the same hours bought in the final term. Bring the first-year papers, and build the block from where marks were actually lost.

faqs.question: Our child starts the second Diploma year behind in two Higher Levels - how long does a block need to be?
faqs.answer: Two Higher Level subjects means roughly twenty-four to thirty-two hours across eight weeks, split as two sessions a week in each. Less than that spreads too thin to change anything under time pressure. Do not add a third subject: the written work between sessions is where the marks come from, and a student carrying six sessions a week stops producing it. If only one subject can have a proper block, take the one with the heavier paper weighting first.

faqs.question: Is it too late to book an IB crash course in the final term before the May session?
faqs.answer: No, but the block has to get narrower the later it starts. With eight weeks left, two subjects and one question type at a time is realistic. With three weeks left it is one subject, timed papers only, and no new content unless a named topic is genuinely missing. Late blocks fail when they try to cover everything. Ask the tutor what they are deliberately leaving out; a specialist will have an answer, and that answer is the plan.

faqs.question: What should a student do in the break before the second Diploma year if a block is planned for the autumn term?
faqs.answer: Three things, none of them heavy. Read the subject guides for the Higher Level subjects so the shape of the second year is not a surprise. Settle an internal assessment topic in at least one subject, because starting that in the autumn term while everything else accelerates is where students lose time. And collect the first-year marked scripts in one place. A block that opens with the evidence already gathered spends its first session teaching rather than diagnosing.

faqs.question: What share of a Higher Level grade sits in the papers a block can rehearse?
faqs.answer: Most of it, but not all, and the split differs by subject. In the Diploma sciences the internally assessed investigation carries roughly a fifth of the grade and the written papers carry the rest; in other subjects the balance moves, and oral or portfolio components can be substantial. Your school's subject guide gives the exact weighting for each component. Check it before buying hours, because a block aimed at the smaller share is an expensive way to feel productive.

faqs.question: Which IB command terms cost the most marks when only six weeks are left?
faqs.answer: The ones that look similar and are not. State and outline want brief listable content and nothing more. Describe wants observable detail without explanation. Explain wants a causal chain, and a missing link costs the mark even when the conclusion is right. Evaluate and justify want a judgement supported on both sides. In a six-week block these deserve more attention than any single topic, because the correction transfers to every paper at once.

faqs.question: How do grade boundaries move, and why can a block not be priced against them?
faqs.answer: Boundaries are set after each session, once the examining team has seen how the cohort performed on that particular paper. A paper that ran hard produces lower boundaries; an easier one produces higher. The mark needed for a given grade is therefore not known in advance, and nobody can price a block against a boundary that does not exist yet. Work in marks rather than grades: reliable extra marks on named question types is the only honest target.

faqs.question: Our school's predicted grade is lower than the mock result - can a block change it?
faqs.answer: A predicted grade is the school's professional judgement, based on more evidence than one mock paper, and it belongs to the school. A block cannot change it directly and no tutor should suggest otherwise. What a block can do is produce more evidence: marked timed work under the same conditions over several weeks, showing a consistent level rather than one good afternoon. Take that to the subject teacher and ask what they would need to see.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Paper 2 and Paper 3 work inside a short intensive block?
faqs.answer: Paper 2 generally rewards breadth and structured written answers across the core syllabus, so block work means question-type drills and command-term discipline. Paper 3, where a subject has one, is narrower and stranger: data handling, an investigation, or the Higher Level option, and it rewards familiarity with the format. In a short block Paper 3 often gives the faster return, because a student who has never seen the format is losing marks to unfamiliarity rather than knowledge.

faqs.question: Does an IB crash course do anything for Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: No, and it is worth separating the two. Equivalency, mu'adalah, is an administrative decision by the Ministry of Education that recognises a foreign or international certificate against the Saudi secondary certificate. It depends on documents, attestations and the certificate itself, not on examination technique. A crash course helps a student earn the certificate; equivalency decides what it is worth afterwards. Start those questions with your school's coordinator and the Ministry's own published requirements well before results arrive.

faqs.question: Should Qudurat preparation sit inside the same block as Diploma revision?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment and tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content. The practice that improves it looks nothing like Diploma revision, and sharing one short block between them means neither gets enough repetition. Run them as separate pieces of work, with reasoning practice in lighter weeks and the subject block protected.

faqs.question: Why do IB students find Tahsili harder than their own Higher Level papers?
faqs.answer: Because Tahsili follows the Saudi national curriculum. It covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and an IB student has studied most of that material, but the framing, the expected method and the question style come from a different course. The overlap is real and the fit is not. Students who treat it as a new subject with familiar content do better than those who assume Diploma preparation covers it. Check the test's own published guidance.

faqs.question: What do overseas universities ask for from a Saudi school leaver, and can a block help?

intro.heading: Where you are in the two years decides what to buy
paragraphs: The single most useful thing to know about Diploma support is that its value changes completely depending on when it starts. The same tutor, the same subject and the same rate buy very different things in the first autumn term and in the final spring term. Early, the money buys foundations and an internal assessment that is started in time to be rescued. Late, it buys triage. Both are worth paying for, but a family that does not know which one they are buying usually overpays for the wrong one.

That is why this page is organised as a calendar rather than as a sales argument. Almost every IB school in the Kingdom sits the May session, so the Diploma runs on a two-year clock with a fixed sequence of milestones: subjects and Higher Levels fixed, internal assessment designed and written, Extended Essay submitted, Theory of Knowledge essay drafted, predicted grades issued, then eight weeks of technique. The dates differ school by school. The order does not, which is why this page names terms and never names a year: a month and a year printed here would be wrong for half the schools in one Saudi city, and wrong for all of them within twelve months.

The search phrase itself deserves a straight answer. A home tutor means someone who comes to the family's own home and teaches at the kitchen table. That market exists in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province and it works well for common subjects. IB Gram does not run home visits in the Kingdom; home visits are a service offered only in India. Lessons for Saudi families are one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time, and the first section compares the two honestly rather than asserting one.

The argument for teaching a Diploma subject online is specific and not about convenience. A Diploma student needs a specialist in one named subject at one named level. The number of people who can teach Higher Level Physics or Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches and also live within a twenty-minute drive of your district is small, and it shrinks further outside the three large clusters. Removing the drive removes that constraint, and the travel loading comes out of the hourly rate at the same time.

Advertised SAR figures appear throughout, always as what other providers publish and never as a price here or a market average. Where something cannot be verified - an examination date, a school count, a university's weighting - the mechanism is described and the number is left out. Everything else is meant to be checkable against your own school's Diploma coordinator, who is the person with the dates that actually bind your child. Ask for those dates in writing in the first term of the first year, because every other decision on this page hangs off them.

regions.name: Jeddah

sections.heading: What families mean by an IB Diploma home tutor
paragraphs: The phrase describes a specific arrangement: someone arrives at the family's own home, teaches one Diploma subject at the kitchen table, and leaves. It is the default across much of the Kingdom because it is what families know, and in Riyadh or Jeddah it is genuinely available for the common subjects. For a Diploma student it carries two costs that are easy to miss, and both are about time rather than about money.

The first is the travel loading. Tutor-marketplace guides advertise senior-school examination subjects in Riyadh at SAR 200 an hour and above, and an in-home rate usually carries the journey inside it; a tutor crossing a large city in evening traffic prices that hour accordingly. The second is the pool. A Diploma student needs a specialist in one named subject at one named level, and the list of people who can teach Higher Level Physics and live twenty minutes from your district is short.

So the honest position, stated once. IB Gram delivers this as one-to-one tuition over live video, timed to Arabia Standard Time, and does not run home visits in the Kingdom - home visits are a service offered only in India. The argument is not that a screen is more convenient than a kitchen table. It is that a Diploma student gets the specialist for their component instead of the nearest willing teacher, and that trade is the one worth weighing rather than the format itself.

sections.heading: The Diploma counted backwards from the May session
paragraphs: Almost every IB school in the Kingdom sits the May session, which means the Diploma runs on a two-year clock nobody prints on a wall. Working forwards from the first week produces the order families regret: content now, assessed work later, technique at the end. Working backwards from the session produces a different order, because the deadlines that actually bind a student are set by their school long before any examination timetable is published.

Three clocks run at once and families usually see only one. The board's clock governs registration and submission. The school's clock governs internal deadlines for the internal assessment, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay, and those are set by your school's Diploma coordinator rather than published centrally. The student's own clock - how long it genuinely takes to collect data, write a draft and act on feedback - is the clock that overruns, and it is the only one a tutor can help with.

The table counts the whole thing backwards in terms rather than in months, because international schools in one Saudi city run different calendars and a month named here would be wrong for half of them. Use it as a sequence rather than a diary. The order of the milestones is fixed even where the dates differ, and knowing the order is what lets a family buy help at the point where it is cheapest rather than at the point where it is urgent.

sections.heading: The first autumn term: choices that stop being reversible
paragraphs: Six subjects, three of them at Higher Level, are fixed in a window that closes early. In practice that window is shorter than the school's published date, because a change after the first few weeks means catching up on a course already running and a timetable already built. Families who treat the choice as provisional discover it was not, and the cost of discovering that late is a Higher Level subject carried unwillingly for two years.

Two checks are worth making before the window closes. First, the prerequisites for whatever the student thinks they want to study afterwards: a university course expecting a specific Higher Level subject, or a particular Mathematics route, will not accept a substitute later. Second, honesty about the gap between an IGCSE grade and a Higher Level start. A top grade establishes fluency, not the habit of justifying each step, and that habit is what the first Higher Level papers test.

This is also the cheapest term in which to buy help, which is exactly why almost nobody does. A weekly slot that starts now builds the foundations the final year will assume, and it puts someone in place who will already know the student when the assessed work begins. A family who starts here usually spends fewer total hours than a family who starts in the final term, even though it does not feel that way when the first invoice arrives. The hours are cheaper because nothing has to be undone first.

sections.heading: The internal assessment window, and why it binds
paragraphs: The middle of the Diploma is where the grade is quietly decided. Internally assessed work carries a substantial share of each subject - a fifth of the final grade in the sciences - and it is the one component the student controls completely: the question, the method, the data, the analysis, the writing. It is also the component with a school deadline rather than a board examination, which is why it slides when everything else is noisy.

The failures are predictable and nearly all happen in week one. A research question too broad to answer. A variable nobody can control. Data that cannot be collected in the time available. A design copied from a classmate's idea with the interesting part removed. None of that is visible in a finished draft, which is why the useful intervention is at the design stage and the expensive one is three days before submission.

What a tutor may do here has a hard limit, and it is worth stating plainly because the essay mills competing for this search will not. A tutor reads what the student has written, points at a criterion that is not yet met, asks questions, and hands it back. A tutor does not write, redraft or produce any part of assessed work. Keep dated drafts in the student's own account and a note of what each session covered; that record is what stands up if a school ever asks. It also protects a student who has done nothing wrong.

sections.heading: The final autumn term: the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and predicted grades
paragraphs: The heaviest term in the Diploma is the first one of the final year, and it is heavy for a structural reason: the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the first serious set of mock papers land in the same weeks. The Extended Essay is supervised at school by a member of staff, with a required set of reflection sessions, and a tutor's place is around that supervision rather than inside it.

The Theory of Knowledge essay is the piece students most often underestimate, because it looks like an essay and is not. It is assessed on how knowledge questions are handled rather than on content, and a student who writes beautifully about a topic can score poorly for never addressing the prescribed title as a question. Reading the title aloud and asking what claim it makes is usually the fastest useful hour anyone spends on it.

Predicted grades are issued in this part of the year and they shape university applications. A predicted grade is a teacher's professional judgement submitted to the board, built from work already seen, and it is neither a promise nor a target. Arguing with a prediction rarely moves it; producing better evidence sometimes does. If a prediction is below what a family expected, the first question is which component the teacher is reading it from. Ask that of the subject teacher rather than of the coordinator, and ask what evidence would change the judgement before the final set of mocks.

sections.heading: The last eight weeks, and the resit question
paragraphs: In the final eight weeks the useful work changes shape entirely. There is no time to re-teach a course, so the job becomes selection: the two question types carrying the most marks, the command terms the student keeps misreading, and the topics where a few hours convert knowledge they already have. New content is almost always the wrong purchase at this point, and a tutor who proposes it is working through a syllabus rather than working on a grade.

The routine that works is narrow and repetitive. Whole papers under timed conditions, marked against the published scheme, with the lost marks grouped by cause rather than by topic. Three faults usually account for most of the loss, and naming them is worth more than another revision guide. Two short sessions a week beat four long ones, because the marking between sessions is where the learning actually happens and that needs time to do.

Then the honest part. No tutor can promise a grade, and the ceiling in eight weeks is set by what is already in place. Where a result is not what a student needed, a resit in a later session is a real option and worth planning rather than panicking about: it needs a decision, a registration, and a different kind of preparation from a first sitting. The school's Diploma coordinator is the person to ask about the route. Decide early rather than after results, because a resit needs registration and a different kind of preparation.

sections.heading: Choosing the tutor, and naming the trouble spot first
paragraphs: A good match starts with a narrow brief. Not Mathematics, but Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Paper 1, with method marks going missing in calculus. Not Biology, but the extended-response question in Paper 2. A tutor matched against a brief like that can be checked in one trial lesson, because you can ask them what they would do about exactly that and compare the answer with your child's teacher's view.

Three questions separate a Diploma specialist from a competent generalist. Which subject guide are you teaching to, and which assessment structure? What does this school's scheme of work usually leave short of time? And where does your help stop on assessed work? The third answer should be specific and limited without being prompted. A tutor who has to be asked to name a limit has not thought about it before, and that matters more than any certificate.

Continuity is the last thing to check, and it is the one families forget. A Diploma is two years, so ask what happens if the tutor becomes unavailable mid-course, how a handover works, and whether notes travel with the student. Ask the same about your own side: a family relocating from Dhahran to Riyadh keeps an online tutor and loses an in-home one. For a two-year course, that is not a small difference. Settle it before the first invoice, alongside the notice period and what happens to unused sessions if the student drops a subject or changes level.

faqs.question: What should I ask an IB Diploma home tutor who has never taught in a Saudi school?
faqs.answer: Ask which subject guide and assessment structure they teach to, then ask them to work from your school's scheme of work rather than their own order. Saudi international schools set their own calendars and sequences, so a tutor arriving with a fixed plan will be a fortnight out of step. Ask how they will find out where the class actually is. Not having taught in the Kingdom is a small issue; not asking about the school's sequence is a large one.

faqs.question: Should a Diploma student have the same tutor for a Higher Level and a Standard Level subject?
faqs.answer: Only if the subjects are related and the tutor genuinely teaches both at both levels. The Higher Level extension is usually a different kind of work, not simply more of it, and a tutor comfortable at Standard Level may be stretched by it. Two subjects with one tutor also stacks the risk: if the match fails, two slots go with it. Where both are needed, keep the Higher Level with the stronger specialist and review at four weeks.

faqs.question: How do I check a Diploma tutor knows my child's school's scheme of work?
faqs.answer: Send them the scheme or the topic list and ask what they would expect the class to have covered by now, and what it probably has not. A tutor who knows the course will name topics that commonly run short of time and say why. One who answers generally has not read it. The second check is your child's own subject teacher: ask them what they would fix first, and compare. Matching answers are the signal worth paying for.

faqs.question: What happens if our Diploma tutor becomes unavailable between the autumn and spring terms?
faqs.answer: Ask before booking, because a Diploma is a two-year arrangement and mid-course changes happen. What you want is a handover: the session notes, the marked work, the current plan and the named components being worked on, passed to a replacement who teaches the same subject at the same level. A fortnight of overlap helps where it is possible. Continuity matters most inside an internal assessment window, so that is the period to protect in any arrangement.

faqs.question: Is a current classroom teacher a better Diploma tutor than a full-time tutor?
faqs.answer: Each brings something different. A serving teacher knows how a cohort behaves, how predicted grades are reached and what a school's internal deadlines feel like from the inside. A full-time tutor usually has more one-to-one diagnostic practice and more availability across the week. Neither is automatically better. The question that separates them is the same either way: what did you do last time a student lost marks the way mine is losing them?

faqs.question: What does a Diploma student need at home for an online one-to-one lesson?
faqs.answer: A laptop rather than a tablet, because the writing area matters for mathematics and the sciences; a quiet room with a door; a notebook and the subject's own booklet or data sheet where one is allowed. A webcam pointed at paper working helps, and a phone camera does the job for sending written work between sessions. A fast connection matters less than people assume. A room where nobody walks through matters more.

faqs.question: How is an internal assessment draft looked at during an online session?
faqs.answer: The student shares their own document or a scan of it, and the criteria are read alongside it on screen. The tutor points at a criterion that is not yet met and asks questions about the student's own reasoning: what the variable actually controls, whether the data supports the claim, where the evaluation is. Nothing is typed into the student's file by the tutor. The student makes the changes, which is both the rule and the only way the skill transfers.

faqs.question: Can a parent sit in on a Diploma lesson without changing how it runs?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth doing once early on. Most teenagers talk less with a parent in the room, so sit in for the first ten minutes and leave, or ask the tutor to record the session and watch it later. What you are listening for is whether the tutor makes the student explain things or simply explains things at them. The written note after each session tells you most of what a full hour of observation would.

faqs.question: How are graphs and working shared in an online Diploma maths lesson?
faqs.answer: On a shared whiteboard where both people can write, with the past paper open beside it. The student works and the tutor watches the lines appear, which is the point: an algebra error is usually in line three and is invisible in a finished answer. Graphs are drawn on the shared canvas or on paper held to the camera, and graphing technology is shared by screen. Nothing needs installing beyond a browser.

faqs.question: What is sent to the parent after each Diploma session?
faqs.answer: A short written note: the topic or paper covered, what the student got wrong and why, what was set before the next session, and anything the school should be asked about. Over a term those notes become the record of whether the arrangement is working, which is more useful than a single report. A note that says good progress and nothing else is a sign to ask harder questions at the four-week review.

faqs.question: Which Higher Level Physics topics have no Standard Level equivalent to fall back on?
faqs.answer: Several of the Higher Level extensions are genuinely additional rather than deeper, which means a student who has drifted has no simpler version underneath them to retreat to. That is different from most subjects, where Higher Level content extends something already learned. The practical consequence is that Physics punishes a term of absence more severely than its neighbours, and recovery has to start with the extension topics rather than with general revision of the shared material.

faqs.question: Where does weak algebra show up later in Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches?
faqs.answer: Almost never in the algebra questions. It appears in calculus, where a differentiation is correct and the simplification that follows is not, and in the method marks of long questions where a line of working is skipped because the student is unsure of it. The fix is unglamorous: timed practice on manipulation alone, separated from the topic being examined. Most students resist it because it feels like going backwards, and most see the marks move within a month.

faqs.question: Why do strong Biology students still lose marks on the extended-response question?
faqs.answer: Because they write everything they know rather than answering the command term in front of them. An outline wants a sequence, an explain wants a mechanism, and a discuss wants two sides and a judgement; a brilliant description of the topic satisfies none of them. The remedy is to read the question, name the command term aloud, then plan three points before writing. It feels slow and it is the difference between knowing the subject and being paid for it.

faqs.question: Which Diploma topic is most often rushed at the end of the final year?
faqs.answer: Whatever sits last in the school's sequence, which is why the answer differs by school rather than by subject. In practice it is often the final option or the last Higher Level extension, taught in compressed form while mock papers and the Extended Essay compete for the same weeks. Ask the teacher in the autumn of the final year what is scheduled last, then plan outside support for it early. A topic taught in a hurry is a predictable gap.

intro.heading: A perfect tutor in an impossible slot teaches nobody
paragraphs: Most arrangements for Diploma support do not fail on teaching. They fail on a Tuesday in the second month, when the tutor's own country moves its clocks, or the student's school runs a mock week, or it turns out the tutor was always teaching a full day somewhere else and the Saudi evening was the end of a long shift. The subject knowledge was never the problem. The calendar was, and nobody checked it. That is a fixable mistake, and fixing it costs one conversation at the start rather than a replacement tutor and a lost month in the middle of a term.

That is why this page runs logistics first. The school week in the Kingdom is Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend, and almost all tutoring copy on the internet was written for a country that works Monday to Friday. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and never shifts. A Diploma student carries six subjects, assessed work and CAS, which leaves about two usable evening windows a week rather than the five a parent imagines.

Once those constraints are on the table, quality can be assessed properly, and the order matters. A family that picks the tutor first and then negotiates the hour ends up choosing between a specialist at an impossible time and a generalist at a convenient one. A family that fixes the two windows first can then ask who teaches Higher Level Physics inside them, which is a question with a real answer.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an address in Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province; home visits are a service offered only in India. For a scheduling problem that is the point rather than a compromise: the hours available stop being limited by who can reach your district by six o'clock, and a family relocating between Saudi cities keeps the same tutor and the same slot.

What follows is the week from both sides, the five things that break a weekly slot and how each is handled in advance, the three different school calendars that run in a single Saudi city, what a local school can and cannot staff, what switching into the Diploma mid-course actually involves, and only then how to check that the tutor inside your chosen hour is the right one. No calendar year appears anywhere on this page, because term dates differ by school and a printed year goes stale. Advertised SAR figures appear where they are useful, always attributed to the kind of provider that published them rather than presented as a price here, and anything that could not be verified is described as a mechanism with the number left out.

sections.heading: The week your child actually has, Sunday to Thursday
paragraphs: The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. That is the single most important fact on this page and the one most tutoring copy ignores, because it was written for countries that work Monday to Friday. A family who books a Monday-and-Wednesday pattern copied from a British provider has booked the two evenings in the middle of a Saudi school week, which is the worst possible placement.

A Diploma student's usable hours are narrower than they look. School, then the run home - in a large city that is a real cost rather than a detail - then homework across six subjects, CAS commitments, and whatever assessed work is live that term. What remains is roughly two workable evening windows a week. Sunday and Tuesday are the two that survive contact with reality, because they sit before the week's work has piled up and before tiredness has.

Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time, which is UTC+3 with no daylight saving anywhere in the year. The Kingdom does not move its clocks, so a slot agreed in Saudi local time stays exactly where it was put. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service offered only in India. For a scheduling problem that is the advantage, because available hours stop being a question about who can drive to your district.

sections.heading: Who is at work when your slot runs
paragraphs: The question families almost never ask a provider is what the tutor's own week looks like. A tutor based in the United Kingdom is working on a Saudi Sunday and free on a Saudi Friday, which is precisely inverted. A tutor in India shares four of five working days and sits two and a half hours ahead of Arabia Standard Time, so a Saudi early evening is a comfortable mid-evening for them. Those two arrangements behave completely differently over a term.

Clock changes are the second half of it. Countries that move their clocks twice a year will drag an agreed slot forward or back by an hour unless the arrangement is defined in Saudi local time rather than in the tutor's. The Kingdom never moves, so the fix is simply to write the slot down in Arabia Standard Time and let the tutor absorb their own change. That should be settled when the slot is agreed rather than discovered in the autumn.

The third factor is the tutor's own term. A tutor who also teaches in a school somewhere else has their own examination season, their own reports week and their own holidays, and those will land on a Saudi Diploma student's heaviest weeks at least once. Ask where the tutor is based, what their working week is, and what in their own year might move your slot. A provider who cannot answer has not thought about it. It is also the fastest way to tell a matching service from a directory.

sections.heading: Five things that break a weekly slot, and the fix for each
paragraphs: A weekly slot is an agreement about a repeated hour, and repeated hours break in five predictable ways. The tutor's clock moves. School days shorten. The long summer arrives. A mock week or a school trip collides with the session. Or the family relocates. Each of those is cheap to handle in advance and expensive to handle in the week it happens, which is the whole argument for naming them before the first lesson rather than after the third missed one.

Ramadan deserves its own sentence, without a date attached to it. School days shorten during Ramadan and evening patterns change completely, and because it moves roughly eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar it lands in a different part of the academic year each time. Dates are confirmed by moon sighting and differ between countries, so nothing here is printed. The practical answer is agreed in advance: a later slot for those weeks, or a weekend morning.

The other four are simpler. The clock change is handled by defining the slot in Arabia Standard Time. The summer break is handled by pausing and holding the slot, or by running a short block instead of a weekly one. A mock week is handled by rescheduling inside the same fortnight rather than cancelling. And relocation between Saudi cities is handled by doing nothing at all, which is the one advantage of an online arrangement that families only appreciate afterwards. None of these five needs a long contract to handle; they need one paragraph agreed before the first lesson, and a tutor willing to write it down.

sections.heading: Three school calendars running in one Saudi city
paragraphs: Families consistently assume there is a Saudi school year. There are several. Ministry of Education schools run a two-semester year that starts in late August and finishes in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms. In the same district, a Diploma student and a cousin at a national-curriculum school will break in different weeks.

The consequence for tutoring is practical rather than academic. A slot built around one calendar collapses against another, and siblings at different schools cannot share an evening. It also means that advice about when to start support cannot be given in months. The honest unit is the term and the position in the course: the first autumn term, the internal assessment window, the final autumn term, the last eight weeks before the session.

So the instruction is the same for every family: get your own school's published calendar, in writing, at the start of the year, and give it to the tutor. Not a national calendar, not last year's, and not the one from the school website that was never updated. Term dates differ school by school within one city, and the school's Diploma coordinator is the person who knows which internal deadlines sit inside them. A tutor who has the calendar can place a slot that survives the whole year rather than the first half of it.

sections.heading: What a Saudi school can and cannot staff
paragraphs: A school offering the Diploma needs a specialist for every Higher Level it runs, and that is harder than it sounds in a small cohort. Where six students want Higher Level Physics, a school may run it with a teacher whose own specialism is elsewhere, offer it at Standard Level only, or not offer it at all that year. None of those decisions is a scandal; they are the arithmetic of a small school. They are also the real reason most families on this page are here.

The pattern repeats across the Kingdom with local variation. Dhahran is not Abha: a school-dense cluster staffs scarce subjects more easily than a city with one international school. Higher Level Physics and Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches are the two most frequently thin, with Economics at Higher Level and second modern languages close behind. Private and international schools are licensed by the Ministry of Education and evaluated through ETEC, but neither process decides who teaches this year's Higher Level group.

Before enrolling, ask four questions in writing. Which subjects are offered at Higher Level this year, and which were offered last year? Who teaches each of them, and what is their subject background? Is any subject delivered online or through a third party? And what happens if a group is too small to run? The answers tell a family more than any brochure, and they also tell you which subject to budget outside support for. Ask the same questions of a school you are already in, because the answers change year to year.

sections.heading: Arriving mid-course: switching into the Diploma
paragraphs: Relocation into the Kingdom part-way through a course is common, and what transfers depends on where the student came from. From a British school, an IGCSE background maps onto the Diploma well, although the first Higher Level papers demand a kind of justified working that IGCSE rarely asks for. A student who has already started A Levels faces a harder move, because the Diploma's breadth means picking up four subjects they had dropped.

From an American curriculum, the breadth is already there and the depth usually is not: Higher Level sciences and Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches assume a level of prior algebra and content detail that a general high-school course may not have reached. From a national-curriculum school, the content overlap is real and the assessment language is the gap - command terms, criteria and the expectation that a student justifies rather than recalls.

The hardest part of any late entry is not content, though. It is the assessed work. Internal assessments have school deadlines already in motion, the Extended Essay has a supervisor and a reflection sequence, Theory of Knowledge has a prescribed title, and CAS has a record that should already exist. A term is enough to stabilise one or two subjects and to start the assessed work properly. It is not enough to recover two. Admission is the school's decision and should be discussed with them first. Ask the Diploma coordinator which internal deadlines have already passed before agreeing to anything, because that list decides what a term can realistically achieve.

sections.heading: Then quality: checking the tutor inside your chosen hour
paragraphs: With the week, the clock and the calendar settled, the question becomes who teaches inside that hour. The brief should be narrow: one subject, Higher or Standard, and the paper or criterion where marks are going. Ask which subject guide and assessment structure the tutor teaches to, and ask what a school's scheme of work usually leaves short of time. A specialist answers with topic names; a generalist answers with adjectives about the Diploma.

The honesty question matters most and should be asked in the free trial lesson. Where does your help stop on an internal assessment draft? The answer wanted is specific and limited: they read the student's own writing, name a criterion not yet met, ask questions, and hand it back. A tutor does not write or redraft any part of assessed work, and a provider who has to be prompted to say so has not thought about the family's exposure.

Then review at four weeks against marked work rather than against impressions. Where no specialist is free for a scarce Higher Level inside your two windows, the honest options are a weekend morning, a short wait for the right person, or a narrower brief for now. No tutor can promise a grade, and a slot that cannot realistically be kept every week is worth less than a slightly later one that can. That is the whole argument of this page, put the other way round: the hour decides the teaching more often than the teaching decides the hour.
