ib-dp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The Diploma is this page's subject, but a family planning backwards usually has a younger child too, and the programme a student is in decides how early the work has to start. These are the four routes Saudi international schools run, with what each one actually asks of a student here, and where an outside specialist earns their place.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries internally assessed work alongside its written papers, and the core adds up to three points on top of the subject total. The two years are not symmetrical. DP1 builds content and the habit of writing to a mark scheme; DP2 is about finishing assessed work early enough to leave the final weeks for papers.
programmes.countryNote: Saudi schools running the Diploma are concentrated in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province, with a small number elsewhere. Cohorts are often small, which means a school may offer a subject only at Standard Level, or offer it at Higher Level with one teacher and no cover. That is the most common reason a Saudi Diploma family looks outside school, and it is a staffing problem rather than a teaching-quality problem.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of eight and reported as a grade from one to seven. There are no external papers in most schools until the optional eAssessment, so the marks a student sees are their teachers' judgements against published criteria. The Personal Project in the final year is the first piece of long independent work most students do.
programmes.countryNote: An MYP student in the Kingdom who will continue into the Diploma at the same school is building the exact skills DP1 assumes: structured writing, data handling, and the discipline of answering the command term that was asked. Where the local school runs MYP but not the Diploma, families start planning a move in MYP 4, because the receiving school's subject availability decides which Higher Levels are even possible.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, with no external assessment and no grades in the familiar sense. Progress is reported against learning outcomes and through portfolios and exhibitions. Reading fluency, number sense and the ability to explain a method out loud are what carry forward; everything later in the IB depends on them more than on any specific topic covered at this age.
programmes.countryNote: PYP support in the Kingdom is mostly about English reading age and arithmetic fluency, particularly for children who have moved between languages of instruction. Families relocating into Riyadh or Jeddah from a national-curriculum school often find the gap is not knowledge but the expectation that a nine-year-old will justify an answer in writing.

programmes.name: IGCSE and International GCSE
programmes.description: The route many Saudi international schools use before the Diploma. Cambridge IGCSE is tiered on a number of subjects: Core is graded C to G and Extended A* to E, so a student entered for Core cannot be awarded above a C however well the paper goes. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades nine to one. Both run a June series and a November series.
programmes.countryNote: IGCSE grades are what a Saudi Diploma school looks at when it decides whether a student may take a subject at Higher Level. A student holding a Core-tier pass in a science is frequently steered to Standard Level, which closes some university routes later. Confirm the tier and the component list with the school in writing, and do it before the entry deadline, because tier entry is reversible only up to that point.

ib-dp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects Saudi families ask for most, with what each one is actually assessed on. The pattern is consistent: the subjects where a school struggles to staff Higher Level are the subjects where an outside specialist makes the largest difference, and they are not always the ones a parent expects.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Three papers at Higher Level, two at Standard, plus the internally assessed exploration. The Higher Level course goes considerably further into proof, calculus and complex numbers, and Paper 3 is an extended problem-solving pair of questions with no equivalent at Standard Level. Most marks lost here are lost in method presentation rather than in arithmetic, which is a teachable failing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The statistics-and-modelling route, with a graphical display calculator assumed throughout. Students who chose it to avoid calculus still meet differentiation, and the Higher Level course adds substantial statistical inference. Universities differ sharply on whether this course satisfies a mathematics prerequisite for engineering, which is why the choice has to be made with the destination in mind.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Written papers plus the internally assessed investigation. Higher Level adds whole topics with no Standard Level counterpart and raises the mathematical demand across the rest. The scarcest Diploma teacher in almost every Saudi city is a Higher Level physicist, and schools with small cohorts often run the Higher Level set alongside the Standard one in a single room.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms are where Higher Level students separate from each other. The data booklet is allowed and most students under-use it. The internally assessed investigation rewards a narrow question with careful uncertainty treatment, and penalises an ambitious question with thin data, which is the single most common planning error.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The content volume is the problem rather than the difficulty of any one topic. Extended-response marks go to students who answer the command term that was set: explain, outline, suggest and evaluate are paid differently, and a strong student who writes everything they know about a topic scores less than a weaker one who answers the question asked.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy carries marks that no amount of prose recovers, and the internally assessed commentaries have to be built on genuinely current articles. Higher Level adds a paper of quantitative work. Students arriving from a curriculum where economics was descriptive find the diagram-plus-evaluation structure the hardest adjustment of the first year.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tool-based: the papers reward correct application of a named framework to the stimulus given, not a general discussion of the business. Higher Level adds a case study released in advance. The internally assessed research project needs a real organisation and a question narrow enough to answer, and the choice of organisation is where most projects are won or lost.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided textual analysis, a comparative essay and the individual oral, with the Higher Level essay added on top. Students with strong spoken English but little close-reading practice struggle with the unseen paper, because the mark scheme rewards attention to how a text is constructed rather than an opinion about what it says.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Papers on systems, algorithms and abstract data structures, plus a solution developed for a real client. Higher Level adds resource management and a prepared case study on a set topic. Saudi schools frequently offer this at Standard Level only, so Higher Level candidates are among the most likely to be working with an outside specialist for the whole course.

subjects.name: Arabic and second-language subjects
subjects.description: Language acquisition courses are assessed on reading, listening, writing and a spoken component, and the level a student is placed in matters more than their fluency. Arabic A and Arabic B are different courses with different demands, and a student placed in the wrong one spends two years either bored or drowning.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An essay on a prescribed title and an exhibition of three objects. Marks come from testing a knowledge claim against a counterclaim with real examples, not from philosophical vocabulary. Theory of Knowledge essay support online works well precisely because the work is argumentative structure, which is easier to coach on a shared screen than in a crowded classroom.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: An independent research essay in one subject, supervised at school, with reflection sessions that are themselves assessed. The research question is where almost every weak essay goes wrong: too broad to answer in the word limit, or too narrow to sustain an argument. Extended Essay support for Diploma candidates in the Kingdom is mostly question-shaping and source handling.

ib-dp-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Where Diploma families are, and what changes by region
ib-dp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Distance works differently across the Kingdom. In the three big markets the constraint is which Higher Level specialists exist locally; everywhere else it is whether any exist at all. These are the regions Diploma families contact us from, and what is actually different about each one.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: Roughly an hour across in traffic at the wrong time of day, which means a family in the north and a family in the centre have different school runs to the same school. The deepest Diploma teacher pool in the Kingdom, and still short of Higher Level physicists and Analysis and Approaches HL teachers.

regions.name: Jeddah and the western coast
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north towards Obhur, so a school that is twenty minutes away at one hour is fifty at another. Several IB and Cambridge schools, and a steady flow of families arriving mid-course on commercial postings.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One labour and school market behaving as three cities. Families routinely live in one and school in another, and the King Fahd Causeway puts Bahrain inside the commute. Compound and camp schooling shapes the study week here more than anywhere else in the Kingdom.

regions.name: Jubail, Ras Tanura and Al Ahsa
regions.note: Industrial and agricultural centres an hour or more from the Dammam cluster. Al Ahsa sits roughly ninety minutes inland. Local Diploma provision is limited, so families either commute towards Khobar or teach the gap subjects from home, online.

regions.name: Makkah, Taif and Madinah
regions.note: Makkah is around eighty kilometres east of Jeddah, and its calendar bends around the Hajj and Umrah seasons in a way that a tutor who has not worked here will not anticipate. Taif sits at altitude above it, and Madinah runs its own school market with few Diploma places.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Around twenty-five kilometres apart in 'Asir at high altitude, sharing one catchment. Diploma teaching at Higher Level is scarce here in every subject, and families who want it are almost always working with somebody outside the region.

regions.name: Tabuk, AlUla and NEOM
regions.note: The north-west, where the population is moving faster than the school map. Families relocating into the development corridors frequently arrive part-way through DP1 with no local Diploma school to receive them, and online teaching is the only continuity available.

regions.name: Ha'il, Buraidah, Jazan and Najran
regions.note: Regional centres where international-curriculum provision is thin and Diploma provision thinner. The practical question here is not cost but whether anybody within reach teaches the subject at the level the student needs, and usually nobody does.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST campus community
regions.note: North of Jeddah on the coast, serving a research community with an unusually international intake and a high rate of mid-year arrivals and departures. Students here often need a subject continued from a completely different curriculum until the next transfer.

schoolClusters.note: IB World Schools in the capital appear in directories across the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma programmes, and several run Cambridge alongside. Diploma cohorts are small enough that subject availability varies year to year, so a family choosing a school for DP1 should ask about Higher Level sets specifically rather than about the programme in general.

The British International School of Jeddah is both an IB World School and a Cambridge school; Deutsche Internationale Schule Jeddah runs through to Grade 12. Others appear in IB listings at various programme levels, and the long-established international schools here serve large expatriate communities with their own curricula.

schoolClusters.city: Dhahran, Dammam, Al Khobar and Jubail
schoolClusters.note: The International Schools Group operates several campuses across the Eastern Province, and the Diploma is offered at the American School of Dhahran and at ISG Jubail; not every campus runs it. Other schools here follow British and Cambridge curricula, which is why families in one city sometimes school their children in the next.

sections.heading: What an IB DP home tutor search in Saudi Arabia actually asks for
paragraphs: The phrase means something specific. A parent typing it wants a Diploma specialist working one-to-one with their child, outside school hours, on the subjects the school is not getting through fast enough. Some mean a tutor in the room. Many mean private rather than group. The honest answer to both is the same: IB Gram matches Diploma subject specialists who teach live, over video, one student at a time. Home visits are a service we offer only in India, and no page here will tell a Saudi family otherwise.

Take the in-home version seriously before setting it aside, because for some subjects and ages it works well. A parent who wants somebody sitting beside a fourteen-year-old through a worksheet has a reasonable instinct. The difficulty appears at Diploma level. A Higher Level Chemistry teacher who knows the current syllabus, has taught energetics and organic mechanisms repeatedly, and can read a mark scheme out loud is not a commodity in any Saudi city. Restricting the search to people who can drive to one address on a Tuesday evening removes almost all of them before the conversation starts.

Travel also eats the lesson. An in-home tutor crossing Riyadh at the wrong hour spends longer in the car than in the room, and that time sits in the fee whether it is itemised or not. Rates published for in-home work in the Kingdom carry that loading. Online, the same hour buys teaching, the student's own script is on screen within seconds, and the tutor can be the person who has marked that paper rather than the person who happens to live nearby. The table sets the two against each other on the terms that matter during a Diploma.

sections.heading: The Diploma year, counted backwards from the May session
paragraphs: Almost every IB school in the Kingdom enters its candidates for the May session. That single fact organises the whole two years, and it is the only fixed point a family can plan against. The IB does not publish a Saudi school's Internal Assessment deadlines; the school does, and it sets them far enough ahead of the board's own submission window to leave room for moderation and for a student who falls ill. The order of the milestones never changes. The dates move, school by school, which is why this page names none of them.

Counting backwards is more useful than counting forwards, because it tells a parent what is already too late and what is not. Eight weeks out from the session, teaching a new Higher Level topic from scratch is a poor use of the hours; rehearsing three papers under time is not. Eighteen months out, the reverse holds, and a student who spends DP1 drilling past papers on content they have not yet met will learn to produce confident wrong answers. A tutor who treats a DP2 spring term like a DP1 autumn term leaves technique exactly where it was.

The table below gives the order, not the diary. Your school's Diploma Programme coordinator holds the dates, and the examinations officer holds entry deadlines for any Cambridge or Pearson components a student is also sitting. Ask both in writing, early, and keep the answers in one place. Families who do this find the surprises are small ones. Families who do not usually discover a submission window three days before it closes, which is the week in which a tutor can do least about it and the week most families first call one.

sections.heading: DP1: what has to be in place before the second year starts
paragraphs: The first Diploma year is judged by what it leaves behind rather than by its own grades. Three things have to be true by the end of it. The student can answer the command term that was set rather than the one they wished for. They have a note system they actually return to, which for most students means something organised by syllabus statement rather than by date. And every Internal Assessment has a chosen direction, even where no data has been collected, because the ones that go wrong in DP2 are almost always the ones still unchosen at the end of DP1.

Subject levels are the other DP1 decision, and it is a decision with a deadline. A student carrying a Higher Level subject they cannot sustain will damage the other five, and the time to move down is while the change is still administratively simple rather than in the term before the session. An honest tutor says this early. The question to ask is not whether the student can pass the Higher Level course but whether they can pass it without the other subjects paying for it, which is a different and harder question.

Autumn term in DP1 is when a mid-course arrival is most recoverable. A student joining from a British, American or national-curriculum school at this point has met most of the underlying content in some form and needs the Diploma's framing rather than a second education. By the spring term the gap has compounded, and by DP2 the Internal Assessment timeline is the binding constraint rather than the content. Families relocating into the Kingdom should assume the audit takes a week and the catch-up takes a term, not the reverse.
bullets: Command terms, a working note system, and every Internal Assessment direction chosen

sections.heading: DP2: the shape of the second year, term by term
paragraphs: The second year has a different job from the first. Content continues, but the dominant constraint becomes the sequence of internal deadlines a school sets, and those deadlines all land before the papers do. A DP2 autumn term spent finishing Internal Assessments buys a spring term for mock examinations and a final stretch for papers. A DP2 autumn term spent putting Internal Assessments off produces a spring in which three subjects, the Extended Essay and the mocks all compete for the same evenings, and something is dropped.

Mock week is the most useful diagnostic of the whole Diploma, and most families waste it. The grade is the least interesting output. What matters is the paper-by-paper and question-by-question distribution of lost marks: whether a student is losing them on content they never learned, on command terms they misread, on working they failed to show, or on the final twenty minutes of a paper they never reach. Those four failures need four different responses, and only the first is fixed by more teaching.

Predicted grades go to universities in this year, and they are the school's judgement rather than a negotiation. A tutor's job around them is to make sure the evidence the school is judging from is current, which means ensuring recent work is in front of the teacher rather than lobbying for a number. The honest line to a parent is that a predicted grade is a forecast made on the evidence available, and no tutor can promise what it will say or what a university will do with it.
bullets: Internal deadlines in DP2 all land before the papers do, so they come first
Mock marks matter less than the distribution of where the marks went
Four distinct failure modes in a mock need four distinct responses

sections.heading: The last eight weeks, and what stops being useful in them
paragraphs: In the final stretch before the May session the arithmetic changes. Hours are fixed, the syllabus is not getting shorter, and the only question worth asking about any activity is how many marks it is likely to return. Teaching an untouched Higher Level topic from scratch returns very little, because the student will not have time to practise it to the point of reliability. Re-teaching a half-known topic that appears in every paper returns a great deal. A good tutor does this triage explicitly, on paper, with the student in the room.

What replaces content teaching is paper discipline, and it is a teachable skill rather than a personality trait. Reading the whole paper before starting. Allocating minutes by marks available rather than by interest. Recognising the command term and writing to it. Showing method even when the answer is wrong, because method marks survive an arithmetic slip. Leaving a question that is not working and returning to it. Students lose more marks to the last twenty minutes of a paper than to any single topic in the syllabus, and almost nobody practises that twenty minutes deliberately.

Sessions also change character. Two or three a week beats one, because the feedback loop has to be shorter than the forgetting curve. Each one starts with marked work from the last and ends with the next paper set. The student does the marking out loud under supervision at least once, against the published scheme, because a student who has applied a mark scheme to their own script writes differently afterwards. Nothing in this block should be new. If something is still new eight weeks out, it was a DP1 decision, not a DP2 one.
bullets: Rank every remaining topic by marks available, not by how much is unknown
Paper discipline is teachable: time allocation, command terms, visible method
The last twenty minutes of a paper is the least-practised part of the Diploma

sections.heading: What Diploma tutoring is advertised at in the Kingdom
paragraphs: Rates in this market are published by the people selling, which makes them advertised rates rather than a market average. They are still useful, because the spread between them tells a parent what is actually being priced. The figures below are the bands tutoring platforms, tutor marketplaces and tutoring companies publish for work in Saudi Arabia, grouped by what they claim to cover. None of them is IB Gram's price, and none should be read as what a family will finally pay.

Four things move the number, in roughly this order of weight. Subject scarcity comes first: a Higher Level Physics or Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL specialist costs more everywhere than a Standard Level mathematics tutor, because there are fewer of them and their diaries fill first. Marking or examiner experience comes second. Level comes third, with Higher Level above Standard, Standard above Middle Years, and Middle Years above IGCSE. Whether the tutor travels comes fourth, and it is the one cost online teaching removes outright.

Treat a very low advertised rate for Diploma work as information rather than a bargain. A rate well below the exam-subject band usually means a generalist teaching from a textbook rather than a specialist teaching from a mark scheme, and at Higher Level that difference shows within three lessons. Treat a very high rate the same way: ask what specifically justifies it, and expect an answer about the subject, the papers and the marking rather than about the company. A tutor who cannot name which paper their student loses marks on is not worth a premium.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week against a tutor's own working week
paragraphs: A Saudi school week runs Sunday to Thursday, and that one fact disqualifies a surprising number of otherwise excellent tutors. A tutor whose own week runs Monday to Friday is free on Saturday and Sunday, which in the Kingdom is half a weekend and a school night. Their Friday evening, which they regard as the start of a break, is the middle of a Saudi weekend. The overlap that actually exists is Sunday through Thursday, between the end of the school run and the point where a Diploma student should be asleep.

Arabia Standard Time sits at UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving, so the clock here is stable all year while the tutor's may not be. A slot agreed as a time in the tutor's country will move twice a year against a Saudi evening. The fix is simple and it has to be done at the start: agree the slot in Saudi local time, write it down that way, and let the tutor absorb the shift in their own calendar. Families who skip this discover it in the week the clocks change, which is rarely a quiet week.

The practical window for a Diploma student in Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province runs from late afternoon to mid-evening, and it narrows as the Diploma progresses because the homework load grows. Friday morning works for some families and is the only genuinely spare block in the Saudi week. During shortened school days in Ramadan the whole pattern shifts later, and the sensible move is to agree the alternative slot in advance rather than renegotiate it week by week. sections.heading: Assessed work: what a tutor may do, and what no tutor may do
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject carries internally assessed work, and that work has to be the student's own. This is not a presentational rule. A school that suspects malpractice investigates it, and a finding can cost a candidate the Diploma rather than the component. Because the market around Saudi families includes sellers who will quietly produce assessed text, the boundary is worth stating plainly on a page a parent reads before they buy anything: a tutor teaches, questions, reviews and gives feedback. A tutor does not supply sentences, data, code or analysis that then appears in assessed work.

What that looks like in a real session is less restrictive than it sounds. A tutor can teach uncertainty treatment on somebody else's published data set until the student can apply it to their own. They can read a student's own draft against the criteria and say which criterion is not yet being rewarded and what kind of evidence would satisfy it. They can argue with a research question until it narrows to something answerable. They can mark a past paper and reteach the gap. All of that is teaching, and all of it moves marks.

Keeping a record protects the student. We ask tutors to note what was discussed in any session touching assessed work, in a form the student can show a supervisor if asked. A student who can account for how their draft changed between versions, and name the teaching that caused each change, is in a straightforward position. The reverse is also worth saying to a parent directly: anyone offering to produce an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a Theory of Knowledge essay is offering to put the Diploma at risk, not to help.

sections.heading: Equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili: the part of DP2 nobody puts on the calendar
paragraphs: A family planning the Diploma year backwards from the May session usually stops at the session. For a student who may apply to a Saudi university, there is a second track running alongside, and it is the one most families discover late. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, the mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. This applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike, and it is a document process rather than an examination.

Alongside it sit the Qiyas tests, run by the National Center for Assessment under the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, measures verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and is sat in Arabic or in English. Tahsili, the achievement test, covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum. That last detail is why international-curriculum students find Tahsili harder than their own papers: the material overlaps substantially, but the framing, the vocabulary and the expected method do not.

The planning consequence is simple enough. Preparation for these tests competes with Diploma Internal Assessments and with the papers themselves, so it has to be positioned deliberately rather than squeezed into the final stretch. Universities publish their own admission criteria, combining school results with the Qiyas outcomes, and the weightings differ by university and by programme. We publish no thresholds and no formulas here, because they vary and they change; check the university's own published criteria. No tutor can promise an admission outcome, and anyone who does should be disbelieved.

process.title: Tell us where in the Diploma year you are
process.description: Not just the subject and the level, but the position: how many weeks into DP1, whether the Internal Assessment has a direction, when the school's mock week falls, what the last report said. This is the information that decides whether the first eight lessons should teach content or technique, and getting it wrong costs a month.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the proposed specialist
process.description: Sixty minutes with the tutor who would actually teach, on a topic the student is currently struggling with rather than a showcase. The student should finish it able to do something they could not do at the start. If the match is wrong, say so afterwards and we propose a different specialist without argument.

process.title: A written diagnosis, not a sales summary
process.description: After the trial you get a short written note: what the tutor saw, which paper or criterion is losing the marks, what the first block of lessons will address, and in what order. It names the things we cannot fix as well as the things we can, including cases where a level change is the honest recommendation.

process.title: Pin the slot to Arabia Standard Time
process.description: The weekly slot is agreed in Saudi local time, written down that way, and left alone. Where the tutor's own country changes its clocks, the tutor absorbs the shift. The alternative slot for shortened school days is agreed at the same time, so nothing has to be renegotiated in the week it changes.

process.title: Teach, mark, report, repeat
process.description: Work is set between lessons and marked against the published scheme rather than ticked. The parent gets a short note after each session naming what was covered and what was set. Every few weeks the tutor revisits the plan against the school's own deadlines, because those move and the plan has to move with them.

whyPoints.title: Specialists by subject and level, not by availability
whyPoints.description: A tutor on this platform teaches one or two Diploma subjects. The scarce combinations - Higher Level Physics, Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL, Higher Level Chemistry, Computer Science at Higher Level - are exactly the ones a small Saudi cohort struggles to staff, and they are the reason a family looks outside school in the first place.

whyPoints.title: The Saudi week is the default, not an accommodation
whyPoints.description: Slots are built Sunday to Thursday and agreed in Arabia Standard Time. Nothing here assumes a Monday-to-Friday week or a tutor's daylight saving. Friday morning is available where a family wants it, and the shortened-day pattern during Ramadan is planned for in advance rather than improvised.

whyPoints.title: A stated line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, review and give feedback on the student's own Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or Theory of Knowledge essay. They do not supply text, data or analysis for assessed work, and they keep a record of what was discussed that a student can show a supervisor. The boundary is explained to the student, not just to the parent.

whyPoints.title: No claims we cannot support
whyPoints.description: You will not find a success percentage, a star rating, a tutor headcount or a grade promise on this page, because none of those can be verified by the family reading them. What is here instead is the mechanism: how the year is shaped, what the market charges, what a lesson does, and what we will not do.

whyPoints.title: Honest answers about what is recoverable
whyPoints.description: A family arriving part-way through DP2 is told what the remaining weeks can realistically carry, including when a Higher Level subject is no longer the right target. Where no specialist in a scarce subject is free at the hour a family needs, we say so and give a date rather than booking a generalist into the slot.

whyPoints.title: Continuity through a move
whyPoints.description: Families in the Kingdom move - between cities, between compounds, and out again. Because the teaching is online, a transfer from Khobar to Riyadh, or out to another country entirely, does not restart the relationship. The same tutor keeps the same plan, and the only thing that changes is the hour the slot is pinned to.

faqs.question: Our child is moving into DP1 from a British school part-way through the autumn term - what has to be rebuilt first?
faqs.answer: Framing before content. A student from a British Year 12 has usually met much of the underlying material but has been assessed differently, so the first job is command terms and the shape of a Diploma mark scheme. The second is the internally assessed work, which has no counterpart in most British courses and is the thing that catches late arrivals out. The third is the core: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay both have school deadlines that were set before the student arrived. Content gaps are real but usually narrower than the parent fears, and they are the easiest of the three to close.

faqs.question: What does an American-curriculum student have to cover before Higher Level sciences in DP1 make sense?
faqs.answer: Two things, usually. The first is quantitative confidence: Higher Level Physics and Chemistry assume algebraic fluency and comfort with units and uncertainties that an American science course may not have demanded. The second is practical write-up discipline, because the internally assessed investigation is marked on how the data was gathered, processed and evaluated rather than on whether the result was right. A student arriving from an Advanced Placement science is usually closer than one arriving from a general honours course. The audit takes one session; the catch-up is normally a term of weekly work rather than a year.

faqs.question: If we relocate to the Kingdom during DP2, how much of the Diploma can realistically be recovered before the May session?
faqs.answer: It depends far less on content than on assessed work. Written papers can be prepared for in a compressed block, because papers reward technique on content that largely transfers between schools. Internal Assessments cannot be compressed in the same way: data has to be collected, drafts reviewed and submissions made to the receiving school's deadlines, and those deadlines may already have passed for some components. Ask the new school, in writing, which components it will accept from the previous one. That answer, rather than the content gap, decides whether a Higher Level subject is still the right target.

faqs.question: Does a student arriving from a Saudi national-curriculum school have to repeat IGCSE before starting the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Not as a rule, but the receiving school decides, and it will usually look for evidence that the student can cope with Higher Level demand in English. Some schools ask for IGCSE in specific subjects, others set their own entry assessment, and a few admit directly into DP1 with support. The practical constraint is English as a language of instruction across six subjects at once, which is a bigger adjustment than any single syllabus. Ask the school what it accepts as evidence before assuming a year has to be repeated.

faqs.question: What happens to Diploma coursework a student already completed at a school in another country?
faqs.answer: That is a question for the receiving school's Diploma Programme coordinator rather than for a tutor, and the answer varies by component and by how far the work had progressed. Some internally assessed work transfers with the candidate's registration; some has to be redone to the new school's supervision arrangements. Get the answer in writing early, because a family that assumes a completed Internal Assessment travels, and finds in the spring term that it does not, has lost the time that would have made redoing it comfortable. Plan the Diploma around the school's answer, not around the previous school's records.

faqs.question: Why do Saudi schools so often run Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation but not Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Cohort size. Applications and Interpretation suits a broader range of students, so a small Diploma cohort can fill one set; Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level may attract only a handful, and running it requires a teacher who can take it to the full depth including Paper 3. Schools with small year groups make the rational staffing choice. The consequence lands on the student who needs Analysis and Approaches HL for an engineering or mathematics application overseas, and that student is among the most common Higher Level cases we are asked about.

faqs.question: What should we ask a Saudi school about Diploma subject availability before we accept a place?
faqs.answer: Ask which subjects ran at Higher Level in each of the last two cohorts, not which are listed in the brochure. Ask how many students are needed to open a set, and what happens if the number is not reached. Ask who teaches the Higher Level science sets and whether there is cover if that teacher leaves mid-course. Ask whether any subject is delivered online by a third party. The answers tell you which Higher Levels are genuinely available to your child, which is a narrower list than the prospectus implies in almost every small cohort.

faqs.question: Our school's Diploma cohort is small - does that change what an outside Diploma tutor should do?
faqs.answer: Yes, in two ways. A small cohort often means mixed Higher and Standard Level teaching in one room, so the Higher Level extension content gets less class time than the shared material. An outside specialist's first job is usually that extension rather than the whole syllabus. The second effect is on practice volume: a small set generates fewer worked examples and less peer comparison, so the student has seen fewer versions of each question type. Past-paper breadth, not re-teaching, is what a tutor adds in that situation.

faqs.question: How does a compound or camp school in the Eastern Province differ from a city school for a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: The study week is shaped by the compound rather than by the city. Transport runs to a schedule, activities are concentrated inside the perimeter, and evenings are more structured than in a Riyadh or Jeddah household. For a Diploma student that cuts both ways: the routine is excellent for a standing weekly slot, but the available hours are narrower and less negotiable. Families in the Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran cluster also school across city boundaries, so the school's calendar and the compound's may not align. Agree the slot against both.

faqs.question: What does the Ministry of Education actually decide about a private international school, and what does ETEC decide?
faqs.answer: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, which is the permission to operate. School evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which operates e-services for national school accreditation and for approving international accreditation bodies. Neither body regulates private tutors, which is worth saying plainly: no tutor or tutoring company in Saudi Arabia holds a licence from either, including this one. A tutor's credibility comes from subject qualification and marking experience, which you verify directly.

faqs.question: How do Diploma lessons fit into a Sunday-to-Thursday week once the school run and homework are counted?
faqs.answer: Most Diploma families settle on one subject at a fixed hour between late afternoon and mid-evening, Sunday through Thursday, with the slot placed after the school run and before the point where a sixteen-year-old stops absorbing anything. Two subjects in the same week work; two in the same evening rarely do. Friday morning is the only genuinely free block in the Saudi week and suits a longer session on assessed work. The constraint that bites is not the lesson hour but the two hours of independent work it generates, which also have to fit.

faqs.question: Our Diploma tutor is in the United Kingdom - what happens to our slot when their clocks change and ours do not?
faqs.answer: Nothing, if the slot was agreed in Arabia Standard Time at the start. The Kingdom stays at UTC+3 all year, so a slot written down as a Saudi evening hour stays where it is, and the tutor's local time for it shifts by an hour twice a year in their own calendar. The failure mode is agreeing the slot in the tutor's time instead, which quietly moves a Saudi lesson into a school night that no longer works. Write the slot in Saudi time, confirm it that way in every message, and the problem does not arise.

faqs.question: What happens to a weekly Diploma slot during shortened Ramadan school days?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the household rhythm moves later, so the slot usually moves later with it. The practical approach is to agree the alternative hour in advance, at the same time as the regular slot, rather than renegotiating in the first week. Some families prefer to hold the subject at a reduced frequency through the period and recover the hours afterwards; others move to later evening sessions and keep the weekly rhythm. For a DP2 student close to the May session, keeping continuity usually matters more than keeping the exact hour.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the May session should intensive Diploma work start, and what does the schedule look like then?
faqs.answer: Eight weeks is the usual shape for a single subject, and it looks different from term-time work. Two or three sessions a week rather than one, each starting with marked work from the last. Every paper sat once in full under timed conditions before the block ends. Content teaching limited to the topics the mark analysis shows are costing most. A student who has not met a topic at all by this point is usually better served by securing the topics they half know. Starting earlier is better than starting intensively; starting intensively is better than not starting.

faqs.question: Can a DP1 student take two Diploma subjects in one evening, and should they?
faqs.answer: They can, and it is usually a poor trade. Two hours of tutoring after a full Saudi school day produces attention in the first and compliance in the second, and the independent work both lessons generate then lands on the same night. Spreading them across the Sunday-to-Thursday week gives each subject its own follow-up day. Where a family's hours genuinely only allow one evening, the better structure is a longer single-subject session plus a shorter review slot at the weekend, rather than two full lessons back to back.

faqs.question: What happens to a Diploma slot during the autumn break and the midyear break?
faqs.answer: That is the family's call and both choices are defensible. Holding the slot keeps the tutor and the hour, and breaks are often when Internal Assessment work finally gets attention because school homework has stopped. Pausing it frees the time and risks the hour being taken by another student, which matters most for a scarce Higher Level specialist. Our usual advice for a DP2 student is to hold the slot and change what it is used for, and for a DP1 student to pause if the family is travelling, since recovery is easier earlier in the course.

ib-dp-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start from where the Diploma year actually is
ib-dp-home-tutor.closingBody: Tell us the subject, the level, and the position in the course - how far into DP1 or DP2, whether the Internal Assessment has a direction, when the school's mock week falls. We propose a Diploma specialist in that subject, you take a free trial lesson with the tutor who would actually teach it, and you get a short written diagnosis of what the first block of lessons should do and in what order. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time, built around the Sunday-to-Thursday week. Where no specialist in a scarce subject is free at the hour you need, we will say so rather than fill the slot.

ib-dp-math-aa-hl-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level as a main subject, not as an extension of general maths. Each has worked full past papers against published mark schemes.

intro.heading: Start with the three papers, because everything else follows from them
paragraphs: A Higher Level Analysis and Approaches grade is assembled from four separate pieces of evidence, and a tutor who cannot say which piece is weak will spend the hour on the wrong thing. Paper 1 runs two hours for 110 marks with no technology permitted, and it pays for algebra written out by hand. Paper 2 runs two hours for the same 110 marks with a graphic display calculator in use throughout, and it pays for knowing when the machine helps and when reaching for it costs marks. Paper 3 runs one hour for 55 marks across two extended-response problems. The exploration is marked in school against five criteria. Those four pieces are the whole grade: 30%, 30%, 20% and 20%.

That structure is why a search for an IB DP math AA HL home tutor in Saudi Arabia so rarely ends well on distance alone. A family in Riyadh, Al Khobar or Jeddah can usually find somebody within driving range who is comfortable with Standard Level calculus. Finding somebody in the same neighbourhood who has sat with a student and worked a full Paper 3 investigation, under time, against the published mark scheme, is a different problem. The pool thins quickly outside Riyadh, Jeddah and the Dammam–Al Khobar–Dhahran cluster, and it was never deep anywhere in the Kingdom.

So the useful move is to stop filtering by address and start filtering by component. Lessons for families here are delivered one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time, which is UTC+3 and does not shift for daylight saving. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we run only in India. What that buys is a choice of Higher Level specialist rather than a choice of whoever lives twenty minutes away, and an hour that begins at the agreed minute because nobody is sitting in traffic. The trade is a real one, and this page sets out both halves of it rather than only the half that happens to favour us.

The rest of this page is built outwards from the syllabus. It sets out what each paper tests, which Higher Level topics have no Standard Level equivalent, where marks go missing in each one, and what the exploration is marked on. It then puts all of that against the Saudi school week, which runs Sunday to Thursday, because a plan that ignores when a sixteen-year-old can think is a plan that collapses by the third week of the autumn term. Where a SAR figure appears it is what a named kind of provider advertises, never what IB Gram charges. Nothing on this page is a quotation, and the trial lesson that starts any arrangement is free of charge.

ib-dp-math-aa-hl-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level does not begin in the first Diploma term. It begins wherever a student's algebra was last secure. These are the programmes feeding it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two-year course where Analysis and Approaches HL is taught and examined by three written papers plus the internally marked exploration. Higher Level carries 240 guided teaching hours against 150, and most of that difference is content with no Standard Level counterpart.
programmes.countryNote: Saudi schools authorised to run the Diploma sit the May session. Not all of them can staff Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, so some students take it in a set of three or four.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The five-year programme before the Diploma. Extended mathematics in MYP 4 and MYP 5 is the route that prepares a student for Analysis and Approaches; the standard route points at Applications and Interpretation.
programmes.countryNote: Several international schools in Riyadh and Jeddah run the Middle Years Programme but not the Diploma, so families change school at sixteen. The gap that opens is almost always algebraic manipulation.

programmes.name: IGCSE and International GCSE routes
programmes.description: The other common feeder. A student from Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Extended, or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE at higher tier, has met functions, trigonometry and basic differentiation. Additional Mathematics closes most of the remaining distance.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel candidates in the Kingdom sit the June series, with November for resits. A student entered for the Core tier was capped at a C and usually needs a term of foundation work first.

ib-dp-math-aa-hl-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is five syllabus topics plus the exploration, and requests arrive topic by topic. These are the strands students bring most often.

subjects.name: Number and algebra
subjects.description: Sequences, logarithms, the binomial theorem with fractional and negative indices, partial fractions, complex numbers in Cartesian, polar and Euler form, and proof by induction and contradiction.

subjects.name: Functions
subjects.description: Composite and inverse functions, factor and remainder theorems, rational functions with oblique asymptotes, modulus and reciprocal graphs. Paper 1 wants these sketches by hand, fully labelled.

subjects.name: Geometry and trigonometry
subjects.description: Radian measure, compound and double angle identities, reciprocal and inverse trigonometric functions, and vectors: scalar and vector products, equations of lines, and planes in three dimensions.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, discrete and continuous random variables, probability density functions, expectation and variance. Marks here are lost to notation more than method.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.description: Limits, implicit differentiation, related rates, integration by substitution and by parts, volumes of revolution, differential equations by separation and by Euler's method, and Maclaurin series.

subjects.name: The mathematical exploration
subjects.description: Individual written mathematics, recommended at twelve to twenty pages, marked in school against five criteria for 20% of the grade. Criterion E wants mathematics commensurate with Higher Level.

subjects.name: Paper 3 problem-solving
subjects.description: Not a sixth topic but a separate skill: two scaffolded problems, 55 marks in one hour, where early parts set up a structure the later parts generalise. Short-question practice does not prepare a student.

subjects.name: Proof and mathematical reasoning
subjects.description: Induction, contradiction and counterexample are examinable in their own right and appear inside other topics. A proof written without logical connectives scores a fraction of the marks available.

ib-dp-math-aa-hl-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Distance is the real constraint on Higher Level mathematics staffing here, and it bites differently in each cluster. Teaching reaches all of them over live video on Arabia Standard Time.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The deepest local pool and still thin at Higher Level. The city is roughly an hour across in evening traffic, so an in-home slot in Al Olaya and one in Al Narjis differ completely.

regions.name: Jeddah and Obhur
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur. Several schools run Cambridge and Diploma tracks together, which splits a maths department across two assessment cultures.

regions.name: Dhahran, Al Khobar and Dammam
regions.note: One school and labour market behaving as three cities. Families live in one and attend school in another, so a 6pm start depends on which ring road the school run used.

regions.name: Jubail and Ras Tanura

sections.heading: What an IB DP Math AA HL home tutor search is actually asking for
paragraphs: The phrase a parent types is about reassurance, not geography. It means: find somebody competent, make it regular, and do not make me manage it. In-home tuition answers the third part well and the first part badly, because the filter it applies is driving distance. At Higher Level that filter is brutal. A tutor who can teach Standard Level differentiation is common. A tutor who has taught Maclaurin series, vector equations of planes and the Paper 3 scaffold is not, and the odds that one lives twenty minutes away are poor.

In-home rates reflect that. Tutor-marketplace guides put general senior-school private tuition in Riyadh above SAR 200 an hour, with IB subject listings advertised from around SAR 180 and Higher Level tracks quoted at roughly SAR 200 to 220 by tutoring companies. Those are advertised figures published by providers, not a market average and not our price. Scarcity moves the number before anything else, and Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is the scarcest mathematics request here.

Our answer is to drop the distance filter. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time, to any address in the Kingdom. IB Gram does not promise home visits in Saudi Arabia; that service exists only in India. In exchange, a family in Jubail or Abha gets the same choice of Higher Level specialist as a family in north Riyadh, an hour that starts at the agreed minute, and written work returned annotated rather than discussed once and forgotten.

sections.heading: The three Higher Level papers, component by component
paragraphs: Paper 1 is two hours, 110 marks and no technology. Everything is done by hand, which means exact values, surds, logarithm laws, identities and sketches with asymptotes labelled. Students who lean on a calculator for routine arithmetic lose marks that have nothing to do with their understanding. The paper mixes short questions with longer structured ones, and the longer ones are where command terms start to matter: show that, hence, deduce and prove each demand a different kind of written answer.

Paper 2 is also two hours and 110 marks, with a graphic display calculator in use throughout. Its difficulty is judgement rather than fluency. Some questions expect a numerical solution and reward a clean answer to three significant figures. Others expect method on the page and award almost nothing for a bare number the machine produced. A tutor's job on this paper is teaching a student to read which kind of question they are in before pressing any keys.

Paper 3 is one hour, 55 marks, two extended-response problems, and it exists only at Higher Level. Each problem starts concrete and builds towards a generalisation, so part (a) is usually a gift and part (d) is usually the point. Added to the three papers is the exploration, marked in school against five criteria for 20 marks. Four pieces, four different skills, and a weak one drags the grade down whatever the other three look like. Most families only ever ask about two of them.

sections.heading: The Higher Level content that has no Standard Level equivalent
paragraphs: Parents often assume Higher Level is Standard Level with harder questions. It is not. The course carries 240 guided teaching hours against 150, and most of the difference is material a Standard Level student never meets. That matters when choosing a tutor, because somebody whose experience stops at Standard Level will be fluent for two thirds of the syllabus and silent for the third that decides the grade. Asking which Higher Level topics a tutor has taught is more useful than asking how long they have tutored.

The additions cluster in four places. In algebra: proof by induction, contradiction and counterexample, the binomial theorem with fractional and negative indices, partial fractions, and complex numbers through Cartesian, polar and Euler forms, including roots of unity. In geometry: the whole of three-dimensional vector work, from scalar and vector products to the equations of lines and planes and the angles between them. In statistics: continuous random variables, probability density functions, expectation and variance by integration, and Bayes' theorem.

The fourth cluster is calculus, and it is the largest. Implicit differentiation, related rates, integration by substitution and by parts, volumes of revolution, differential equations solved by separation of variables and approximated by Euler's method, and Maclaurin series. A student can be strong at Standard Level calculus and still be unprepared for this, because the Higher Level work is about choosing a technique from several candidates rather than applying the only one available. Families comparing tutors should ask about this cluster by name.

sections.heading: Paper 3, and why the local tutor pool rarely covers it
paragraphs: Paper 3 is the component families discover last and the one that moves a grade fastest. Fifty-five marks in sixty minutes across two problems sounds generous until a student meets the structure: a concrete case, a second case, a pattern, then a demand to prove or generalise it. Nothing in it is harder than the syllabus. What is hard is holding a thread across twenty minutes of one question while notation from part (a) is still doing work in part (d).

That is a teachable skill and it is taught almost nowhere. School time before the May session goes on content coverage and on past Papers 1 and 2, which are the familiar shapes. A tutor hired locally for general mathematics support will usually default to the same material. A student can therefore reach the examination having never worked a full Paper 3 under time, which is the equivalent of sitting an unseen essay paper having only ever written single paragraphs.

The work itself is specific. Read the whole problem before answering anything, so the generalisation at the end tells you what to record on the way through. Define notation once and keep it. Write the inductive step out properly rather than gesturing at it. When a part asks you to comment or justify, answer in a sentence rather than in symbols. None of that requires new mathematics, and all of it requires somebody who has watched students lose those marks before.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, and what each slot is good for
paragraphs: The Saudi school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. Most tutoring copy online is written for a Monday-to-Friday week and quietly assumes a Saturday morning is free and a Thursday evening is not. Here the opposite holds, and planning a Higher Level year without that fact produces a timetable the student abandons by the third week of the autumn term. The week is the constraint; the syllabus has to be fitted into it.

The second fact is the clock. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change it, so a slot agreed with a tutor in a country that does change its clocks will drift twice a year unless it is pinned to Saudi local time. A tutor in India sits two and a half hours ahead, which makes a 7pm Riyadh lesson a 9.30pm start for them. A tutor in the United Kingdom is two or three hours behind depending on their season. Pin the slot to Saudi local time and that whole problem disappears.

Within the week the days are not interchangeable. Sunday is a slow restart and suits new theory. Monday and Tuesday are the sharpest point and are worth spending on Paper 1 technique, which demands concentration with no calculator to lean on. Wednesday is tired, and suits worked examples and notation repair. Thursday evening is effectively Friday night. The weekend holds the only two-hour window, which is where a full Paper 3 under examination timing belongs.

sections.heading: Where Higher Level marks go missing, topic by topic
paragraphs: Most lost marks at Higher Level are not conceptual. They are fluency, notation and reading. In algebra the recurring failure is handling algebraic fractions and indices at speed, which turns a four-mark question into a six-minute question and costs time later in the paper. In functions it is sketching: a correct shape with no labelled asymptote, no intercepts and no indication of behaviour at infinity earns a fraction of the marks even when the student understands the function well.

In trigonometry the pattern is choosing the wrong identity first and committing to it. In vectors it is confusing the scalar and vector products, or giving the equation of a plane in a form the question did not ask for. In statistics the losses are almost entirely notational: conditional probability written ambiguously, a continuous distribution treated as discrete, or an expectation integral set up with the wrong limits. Those are cheap marks to recover, and rarely recovered without somebody reading the student's actual script.

In calculus the two reliable gaps are technique selection and justification. A student who knows substitution and parts but not how to decide between them will attempt the wrong one and run out of room. A student who finds a stationary point without establishing its nature has answered half the question. Add command terms across all five topics — show that wants a derivation, hence wants the previous result used, deduce wants a short inference — and you have most of the gap between a 5 and a 7.

sections.heading: The exploration: twenty marks that sit outside every paper
paragraphs: The mathematical exploration is an individual written investigation, recommended at twelve to twenty pages, marked in school against five criteria and worth a fifth of the Higher Level grade. The criteria reward presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics, with the last carrying the most marks. At Higher Level the mathematics has to be commensurate with the course, and that is where many otherwise tidy pieces lose most: a neat survey with a correlation coefficient is not Higher Level mathematics.

A tutor's role here is bounded, and the boundary is the most important thing on this page. A tutor may discuss whether a question has enough mathematics in it to sustain twelve pages. A tutor may read a draft and say that criterion B is weak because notation is inconsistent, or that the reflection is description rather than reflection. A tutor may teach a technique the student has decided they need. No tutor may draft, redraft or supply text for assessed work, and we decline that request.

The sequence that works is simple. Choose a question early, in the first Diploma year if possible, and test it against the use-of-mathematics criterion before investing weeks in it. Do the mathematics before writing the prose. Keep a record of what was done when, so the school's own declaration of authenticity is easy to support. Read the draft against each criterion separately rather than as a whole. Submit the student's own work, with every piece of feedback logged by whoever gave it.

faqs.question: What is Paper 1 worth in Mathematics AA HL, and why is it sat without a calculator?
faqs.answer: Paper 1 is two hours, 110 marks and 30% of the Higher Level grade, with no technology permitted. The restriction exists to examine algebraic fluency directly: exact values, surds, logarithm laws, identities and sketches done by hand. Students who have leaned on a calculator for routine arithmetic lose marks that have nothing to do with their grasp of the topic. It is also where command terms bite hardest.

faqs.question: How many marks does Paper 2 carry in Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and what does the calculator change?
faqs.answer: Paper 2 carries the same 110 marks and the same 30% weighting as Paper 1, over two hours, with a graphic display calculator available throughout. What changes is judgement rather than content. Some questions want a numerical answer to three significant figures and reward speed with the machine; others want method on the page and award little for a bare number the machine produced.

faqs.question: What does the Paper 3 investigation actually look like in Mathematics AA HL?
faqs.answer: Two extended-response problems, 55 marks, one hour, Higher Level only, and 20% of the grade. Each problem opens with a concrete case, adds a second, invites a pattern, then asks the student to prove or generalise it. The mathematics is all on the syllabus. The difficulty is sustaining one thread for twenty-five minutes while notation introduced early keeps working late.

faqs.question: Which command terms decide the marks in an AA HL extended-response question?
faqs.answer: Four do most of the work. Show that expects a derivation ending at the printed result, so the result itself earns nothing. Hence requires the previous part to be used, and ignoring it can forfeit the marks even with a correct answer. Deduce wants a short inference rather than fresh working. Justify and comment want a sentence of English. Marking a student's own script against these four is fast, cheap work.

faqs.question: How do grade boundaries move in Mathematics AA HL from one series to the next?
faqs.answer: Boundaries are set after each series by awarding committees reviewing how candidates performed against the demand of that particular set of papers, so a harder paper produces lower boundaries. That is why a mark from a past paper cannot be converted into a grade with confidence. Treat historic boundaries as a rough band rather than a target, and judge progress on which question types a student can now finish unaided.

faqs.question: How is a predicted grade for Mathematics AA HL arrived at in a Saudi school?
faqs.answer: The subject teacher sets it from the evidence they hold: internal assessments, mock papers, class work and the exploration as it stands. It is a professional judgement about likely performance in the May session, not a reward for effort and not a negotiation. A tutor can help a student generate better evidence before the prediction is made, which is the only honest way to influence it.

faqs.question: What is in the formula booklet for Analysis and Approaches, and what still has to be memorised?
faqs.answer: The booklet supplied in the examination carries the standard results: sequences and series, the binomial expansion, trigonometric identities, differentiation and integration results, vector formulae and the statistical distributions. What it does not carry is the judgement about which to reach for, or the derivations a show-that question demands. Students who assume everything is given lose time hunting for a rearrangement they were expected to produce.

faqs.question: What does a first diagnostic session for an AA HL student cover?
faqs.answer: A short set of questions sampled from all three papers rather than a general conversation. The aim is finding which of the four assessed pieces is weakest, because a student who feels generally behind is usually secure on two of them and badly exposed on one. The tutor also asks what order the school teaches in and whether exploration work has started.

faqs.question: What should the first month with a new Mathematics AA HL tutor produce?
faqs.answer: Four things: a clear statement of which component is weakest and why, repair work started on it, a timed piece marked against a published mark scheme, and a plan for the exploration with a date against each stage. You should also be able to see the student's annotated work. What the first month cannot honestly produce is a grade prediction.

faqs.question: How is progress in Mathematics AA HL reported to a parent between sessions?
faqs.answer: Work comes back annotated after each session, in the language of the mark scheme rather than in ticks, so you can see where marks were available and not taken. A short written note follows the first month and each term boundary, naming what has moved, what has not, and what the next block is for. A parent is entitled to ask for the plain version rather than a filed report.

faqs.question: What happens if the first AA HL tutor is not the right fit after three lessons?
faqs.answer: Say so and the student is moved. Fit at Higher Level is partly chemistry and partly specialism: a tutor who is excellent on calculus may be the wrong person for a student whose real problem is proof and notation. Three lessons is enough evidence. Ask for the diagnostic to be rerun by the new tutor rather than inherited, because the earlier reading may itself have caused the mismatch.

faqs.question: What should an MYP 5 student do before starting Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Secure the algebra rather than preview Diploma content. Fluency with indices, algebraic fractions, surds, rearrangement and function notation is what the first Higher Level term assumes and rarely revisits. The extended mathematics route in the Middle Years Programme is the right preparation; the standard route points more naturally at Applications and Interpretation. A summer spent on algebraic manipulation without a calculator beats a head start on differentiation, every time.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start AA HL support in the second Diploma year?
faqs.answer: No, but the plan changes. In the second year there is no room for a full content sweep, so the work becomes triage: identify the two or three topics carrying the most marks where the student is weakest, secure those, and spend the rest on Paper 3 technique and finishing the exploration. Starting in the autumn term still leaves room for all of that.

faqs.question: When should exploration work begin for a Higher Level Analysis and Approaches student?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most schools require. Choosing a question in the first Diploma year and testing it against the use-of-mathematics criterion avoids the commonest failure, which is weeks spent on a topic that cannot carry Higher Level mathematics. Do the mathematics first and the prose second, and leave a clear gap before the school's internal deadline. Late starts rarely fail outright; they lose marks inside presentation and reflection.

intro.heading: Price first, because every other question is downstream of it
paragraphs: Published Saudi rates for private tuition spread across a factor of six, and parents reasonably assume that means a quality ladder. It partly does. Mostly it means different products wearing the same word. A tutoring-platform listing advertising general online help from about SAR 55 an hour and a tutoring company advertising a Higher Level track at SAR 200 to 220 are not selling the same thing: one is homework supervision, the other is a specialist who can teach Maclaurin series and mark a Paper 3 generalisation. Those are advertised figures from the providers themselves, not a market average, and not what IB Gram charges. The practical question is never which rate is correct, but which product the rate is attached to and whether your child needs that product this term.

Four things move the number, in descending order of weight. Scarcity comes first: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is the thinnest supply line in Saudi mathematics tutoring, because the Higher Level extensions sit outside what most general maths tutors have taught. Marking or examining experience comes second. Level comes third, which is why the same tutor is quoted differently for Higher Level and Standard Level. Travel comes fourth, and an in-home visit prices it into every hour whether traffic cooperated or not. None of those four factors is about how hard the mathematics is; three of them are about supply.

An online hour removes the fourth factor entirely and widens the first. A tutor-marketplace guide puts general senior-school private tuition in Riyadh above SAR 200 an hour, and an in-home specialist carries that plus a journey. Teaching over live video means a family in Al Ahsa or Jazan draws on the same pool as a family in north Riyadh, which is how scarcity gets diluted. Lessons here are delivered one-to-one over video; IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address, and home visits are a service we run only in India. That is a real constraint and this page states it rather than burying it.

What follows is the rest of the value chain in order: why two quotes for the identical hour differ so much, what a properly used hour contains, where group teaching genuinely beats one-to-one and where it does not, and then the logistics that decide whether any of it survives a term. The logistics are not a footnote here. A slot booked without reference to the Sunday-to-Thursday week or to the tutor's own working week is a slot that quietly dies in the autumn term, and a dead slot is the most expensive purchase on this page. Read it in order, decide the budget at the end, and treat the first hour as a diagnosis rather than as lesson one of fifty-two.

sections.heading: What an AA HL hour is advertised at in the Kingdom, and by whom
paragraphs: There is no single Saudi rate for Higher Level mathematics, and anyone quoting one is describing their own price list. What exists is a set of published advertisements, each from a different kind of provider selling a different product. Reading them side by side is the only way to tell whether a quote is high because the tutor is scarce or high because the seller is confident. The figures in the table below are advertised rates, collected from provider pages and marketplace guides, and they are not a market average.

Two patterns are worth naming. First, the gap between general tutoring and subject-specialist tutoring is much larger than the gap between Standard Level and Higher Level within one provider. A platform advertising from SAR 55 an hour and a company advertising a Higher Level track at SAR 200 to 220 are four times apart; the same company's Standard Level and Higher Level figures usually sit within twenty per cent of each other. Scarcity of the specialism, not the difficulty of the content, is doing most of the work.

Second, international providers quoting in dollars, often around sixty an hour, land in the upper Saudi band once converted, and the conversion is not the interesting part. What matters is whether the hour is one-to-one, who marks the written work between sessions, and whether the tutor has taught the Higher Level extensions. A cheap hour that reviews homework and an expensive hour that marks a Paper 3 attempt are both defensible purchases. Paying the expensive rate for the cheap product is not.
