sections.heading: What the school already does, and the gap it genuinely leaves
paragraphs: Before buying anything, find out precisely what the school provides, because families routinely pay for something they already have. Most Diploma schools run mock examinations, publish a revision timetable, offer subject clinics or drop-in sessions, and give out past papers with mark schemes. Subject teachers will usually mark extra work if a student asks, and they know the examiner reports for their own subject. That is a substantial amount of preparation, and it is already paid for through fees.

The gap that remains is specific and predictable. A teacher with a class of twenty cannot spend an hour on one student's recurring error, cannot re-teach a topic from the start for one candidate, and cannot mark three papers a week for everyone. Nor can they always be neutral about a predicted grade they themselves set. Those four things are what outside help is for, and a plan that names them is a plan worth paying for.

Ask the subject teacher one question before buying hours: what would you want to see this student doing differently? The answer is usually concrete, often free to act on, and almost always a better brief than anything a tutoring provider will write from a phone call. Take that answer to whoever you hire. A tutor who starts from the subject teacher's own diagnosis wastes far fewer hours than one who starts from a sales conversation, and the teacher usually appreciates being asked rather than bypassed.

sections.heading: When a group revision course is better value than one to one
paragraphs: Group courses are dismissed too quickly by people selling one-to-one hours, and they genuinely win in some situations. If a student has missed a block of teaching across a whole topic, a group course covering that topic systematically at a lower hourly cost is efficient. If the student is motivated but isolated, a room of candidates working at pace supplies something no individual session does. And for a subject where the student is broadly fine, a group course is often all the structure they need.

Group courses lose when the gap is individual. A room cannot pause for one candidate's misconception about uncertainties, and a student who is behind will usually stay quiet rather than expose that in front of peers. They also lose on logistics in a Saudi city: a fixed afternoon timetable collides with the school day, and in Jeddah or Riyadh the journey can cost more time than the session delivers. A course that is convenient for one district is impractical from the next one over.

The sensible test is whether the student's problem is shared. If three other candidates would benefit from exactly the same explanation, a group is the cheaper way to buy it. If the explanation only helps this student, a group is the expensive way, because most of the hour is spent on other people's gaps. Families who apply that test often buy both: a group course for coverage and a small number of individual hours for the specific thing.

sections.heading: In-home tuition in a Saudi city against one-to-one online
paragraphs: In-home tuition is what many families search for first, and it is worth describing what the market actually involves rather than dismissing it. A tutor travels to the family, usually in the evening, and the journey is part of the cost whether it appears on the invoice or not. Advertised rates for senior-school examination subjects in Riyadh sit around SAR 200 an hour on a tutor-marketplace guide, and in-home arrangements typically price above the equivalent remote session because of the travel loading.

The constraint is the pool. An in-home tutor has to live within a workable drive, and Riyadh is roughly an hour across in bad traffic while Al Ahsa sits an hour and a half from the Eastern Province cluster. For Mathematics at Standard Level there may be several candidates nearby. For a Higher Level Physics specialist who has taught the current syllabus, the pool within that radius may be nobody at all. Families then either compromise on the specialist or compromise on the format.

IB Gram delivers this as one-to-one online teaching rather than visits, and the argument is the pool rather than the price. A family in Al Khobar can work with a Chemistry Higher Level specialist regardless of where that specialist lives, and the hour is not shortened by a journey at either end. Home visits are a service we offer only in India, and we would rather say that plainly than let a family discover it later. For the in-home market itself, ask any local tutor which syllabus code they have taught.

sections.heading: Self-study from past papers: strong on timing, blind on marking
paragraphs: Self-study is the most underrated option on the list and the one families abandon soonest. Past papers and their mark schemes are available through the school, and a candidate who works through them under time learns pace, format familiarity and question recognition. Those three things account for a large share of lost marks, and none of them requires a tutor. A disciplined student with a clock and a stack of papers will often outperform a less disciplined one paying by the hour.

Where self-study stalls is marking. A student marking their own script gives credit for what they meant rather than for what they wrote, which is precisely the distinction an examiner is paid to make. They also cannot see the pattern across six papers, because they are inside each one. The result is a candidate who has done a great deal of work and whose marks have not moved, which is demoralising and avoidable.

The cheapest effective plan is often self-study for volume plus paid hours for marking and diagnosis. The student sits the papers; somebody who knows the scheme marks them, names the recurring error, and teaches that one thing. That uses a small number of hours well rather than a large number loosely, and it leaves the student doing the work that actually builds stamina. Ask any provider whether they would support that plan; the answer tells you quickly enough whose interests they are actually working for.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, and the clock that decides availability
paragraphs: Schools in the Kingdom run Sunday to Thursday, and Friday and Saturday are the weekend. A final-year Diploma candidate carries six subjects, internally assessed work, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge through that week, which is why a preparation plan has to be laid out rather than simply bought. In practice, two protected evening slots plus one longer weekend session is the most that holds for a term, and any plan that assumes more will be quietly abandoned by week four.

Timing within the evening matters as much as the number of hours. The school run and homework push the workable window to roughly six until eight in the evening, later in cities where traffic is heaviest. Thursday evening carries the longest session well, because nothing is due the next morning. During Ramadan school days shorten and evening patterns change, so a plan made earlier in the year needs revisiting rather than enforcing.

Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks. A tutor in Europe will shift relative to Saudi time twice a year, and if the agreement never named a time zone the slot moves without anybody deciding to move it. Write the time down in Saudi local time. Beyond the clock, a tutor's own working week decides which hours they can actually hold, and for an eight-week programme that question is worth asking before the first session rather than after it, when replacing anyone is difficult.

sections.heading: When the school cannot staff the subject, which is more common than families expect
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which also operates services for approving international accreditation bodies. Neither of those processes guarantees that a particular school can staff a particular Higher Level subject in a particular year. A school can be well run, properly evaluated and still unable to field a specialist in Higher Level Physics when the previous teacher leaves mid-course.

What follows is familiar to anyone who has sat in these rooms. A subject gets taught by a willing non-specialist, or covered by a teacher from a related subject, or run as a supervised self-study group with a timetable slot and no teaching in it. Students in that position are usually fine on content they can read and weak on everything that requires a teacher to model it: the long explanation, the mark scheme's expectations, the parts of the syllabus a textbook handles badly.

Ask the school directly which Higher Level subjects they are running this year, who teaches each one, and whether any are offered as self-study entries. Schools answer that question honestly when it is asked early and defensively when it is asked late. If a subject is thinly staffed, outside help is not a luxury, and it should be aimed at the teaching the school cannot provide rather than duplicating the revision it can already deliver perfectly well.

faqs.question: Our child moved from a British school into the Diploma - what must examination preparation cover that a continuing student's does not?
faqs.answer: Three things. Command terms, because the IB's vocabulary of assessment is narrower and stricter than the one they are used to. The internally assessed components, which have no GCSE equivalent and arrive alongside everything else. And Theory of Knowledge, which is unlike anything in the previous system. Content is usually the smallest part of the gap; the student can read a syllabus, but nobody absorbs an assessment culture by reading about it.

faqs.question: What does an American-curriculum student have to add before Higher Level science papers?
faqs.answer: Usually depth in a narrower range rather than more breadth. Higher Level sciences examine fewer topics in far more detail than a typical high school course, and the written answers are marked against explanation chains rather than multiple-choice recall. The practical and internally assessed work is also more formal. A student arriving from a strong American programme is rarely behind on ability and often behind on the specific style the papers reward.

faqs.question: A student joined the Diploma a term late - is examination preparation realistic in the first year?
faqs.answer: Preparation in the sense of papers, no. Catching up on the taught content, yes, and that is the correct priority. A student who tries to rehearse examination technique on material they have not yet been taught produces low marks and loses confidence for no gain. Spend the first year closing the content gap and building the internally assessed work on schedule; technique work belongs in the second year, when there is something to apply it to.

faqs.question: Does moving from the Saudi national curriculum into the IB change how preparation should start?
faqs.answer: Yes, mainly in language and in assessment style. The teaching language and the technical vocabulary of each subject usually need deliberate attention early, and the shift from a content-recall model to one that rewards analysis and evaluation takes a term or two to feel normal. Mathematics often transfers well. What transfers least is the habit of writing to a mark scheme, and that is where early outside help pays for itself.

faqs.question: What happens to preparation when a family relocates between Saudi cities mid-course?
faqs.answer: Content coverage differs between schools even on the same syllabus, so the first task is a comparison of what has actually been taught, not of grades. Internally assessed work is the bigger risk: a component started under one supervisor and finished under another needs the new school's sign-off, and timelines rarely align. One advantage of online teaching is that the tutor does not change when the city does, which keeps at least one thing stable.

faqs.question: What happens to examination preparation when a Saudi school cannot run a Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: The common outcomes are a non-specialist teacher, a related-subject teacher covering it, or a supervised self-study entry with a timetable slot and no teaching. Students in that position are usually adequate on readable content and weak on everything needing a teacher to model it. Outside help should then supply the teaching rather than duplicate the revision, and the plan should be built from the syllabus rather than from a revision guide.

faqs.question: Does a school's ETEC evaluation tell me anything about its Diploma results?
faqs.answer: Not directly. The Education and Training Evaluation Commission handles school evaluation and accreditation processes, including services relating to international accreditation bodies, and that work is about institutional quality rather than about one cohort's examination performance in one subject. A strong evaluation and a thin Higher Level department can coexist. For the question you actually care about, ask the school who teaches each Higher Level subject this year.

faqs.question: How does compound or camp schooling change a Diploma student's revision week?
faqs.answer: It usually helps and occasionally hurts. Compound life compresses travel, so evening hours are easier to protect than in a city with a long school run, and study groups form naturally. The difficulty is that the community timetable is shared: when a compound schedules events, it schedules them for everyone. Families there tend to do better with two fixed early-evening slots than with anything that moves week to week.

faqs.question: What should we ask a Saudi school about Higher Level availability before the Diploma starts?
faqs.answer: Which Higher Level subjects ran last year and which are running this year, who teaches each, whether any subject is offered only as a self-study entry, and what happens if too few students choose a subject. Also ask how long the current teachers have been in post. Schools answer these questions straightforwardly when asked before enrolment, and the answers shape subject choices far more than a brochure does.

faqs.question: Why do families in smaller Saudi cities prepare for IB papers without a local specialist?
faqs.answer: Because the arithmetic does not support one. A Higher Level specialist in a narrow subject needs enough local students to make tutoring viable, and outside Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province cluster that demand is thin. Distance makes it worse: Al Ahsa is about an hour and a half from the nearest large cluster. This is the honest case for remote teaching rather than a sales argument, and it is why a family in Najran gets the same access as one in Riyadh.

faqs.question: How should a Diploma revision week be laid out across Sunday to Thursday?
faqs.answer: Put the hardest subject early in the week while energy is highest, keep one midweek evening completely free, and use Thursday for the longest piece of work since Friday follows it. Internally assessed work needs its own protected slot rather than whatever is left over. Two tutored evenings at most during term, with the rest given to independent papers. A week with nothing free in it produces cancellations rather than progress.

faqs.question: Do shorter school days during Ramadan change how examination preparation is scheduled?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is better to plan for it than to push through. School hours shorten and the useful study window shifts later into the evening or earlier into the morning, which can suit some students better than term-time evenings. The practical approach is to agree a different pattern for those weeks in advance, keep the total lower, and protect continuity rather than volume. Ramadan moves earlier each year, so it falls differently across the course.

faqs.question: What happens to preparation during study leave before the May session?
faqs.answer: The school week stops applying, which opens daytime hours and changes what a session should be. Longer sessions become possible, so a full paper plus a proper review in one sitting is the obvious use. The risk is overbooking: a candidate on study leave needs most of their day for independent work, and tutored hours that crowd that out reduce the total preparation. Two or three longer sessions a week is usually the ceiling.

faqs.question: Our tutor is in Europe - how is an evening slot protected when their clocks change?
faqs.answer: By naming Arabia Standard Time in the agreement rather than a bare hour. The Kingdom stays on UTC+3 all year, so when a European tutor's clocks shift, the Saudi time stays fixed and their local time moves instead. Without that, the slot drifts by an hour twice a year and both sides believe they are right. It takes one line in a plan and it prevents the most common scheduling dispute in overseas tutoring.

ib-exam-preparation.closingHeading: Compare the options before you buy any of them
ib-exam-preparation.closingBody: Tell us what the school already provides, what the student has tried, and what their last marked paper looked like. We will say which of the five options fits the gap, including the ones that cost nothing, and we will say so plainly if the school's own provision is already enough. If one-to-one teaching is the right answer, the trial lesson is free and comes first. Lessons are delivered live online, one student and one tutor, pinned to Arabia Standard Time; home visits are a service we offer only in India.
